docs.title: Welcome to MAGDA
docs.text:
MAGDA (Multi Agent Digital Audio) is a free, open-source digital audio workstation (DAW) for recording, editing, and mixing audio and MIDI. Built with JUCE and its own native audio engine, it is a professional-grade DAW in a lightweight, open-source package.

MAGDA includes a built-in AI assistant — describe what you want in natural language ("add a MIDI track with a bass clip", "transpose the selected notes up an octave") and MAGDA translates your request into actions. See AI Assistant to learn more.

docs.title: Three Views, One Workflow
docs.text: MAGDA is organized around three main views, each focused on a different stage of music production. Switch between them with the Session, Arrangement and Mix buttons in the footer bar.

docs.title: Session View
docs.text:
A grid-based clip launcher for real-time performance and idea sketching. Trigger clips and scenes on a grid, with a mini mixer strip at the bottom of each track.

Go to Session View →

docs.title: Arrangement View
docs.text:
A traditional timeline for composing, recording, and editing. Lay out clips on tracks along a horizontal timeline with full zoom, selection, and editing tools.

Go to Arrangement View →

docs.title: Mixer View
docs.text:
A channel-strip mixer for balancing levels, panning, routing, and adding effects. Each track gets a full-height fader with metering, I/O routing, and send slots.

Go to Mixer View →

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text:
• Tracks — Hybrid tracks that accept any clip type, with FX chains and racks for flexible routing
  • Built-in Devices — Drum Grid, Sampler, synths, and effects included out of the box
  • Modulation — LFOs, bezier curve shapes, and macros for dynamic parameter control
  • Interface Layout — Collapsible panels, context-sensitive editors, and plugin/media browsers

Visit magda.land for downloads and more information.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
New to MAGDA? Start here:

  1. Installation — Download, build, and set up MAGDA
  2. First Session — Create a project, add tracks, and make some noise

docs.title: ARA Plugins
docs.text: ARA plugins such as Melodyne or VocAlign work on a track's recordings directly rather than on the audio streaming past them. In MAGDA, inserting an ARA plugin on a track hands it every audio clip on that track, and the track plays through the plugin live. There is no transfer step and no separate render back.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
MAGDA notes whether a plugin supports ARA when it scans your plugins. If you are upgrading from an earlier version of MAGDA, rescan your plugins once so ARA plugins are recognised: click Rescan all in Settings > Plugins (see Plugin Settings). Until then an ARA plugin loads as an ordinary effect with no access to your clips.

On macOS, use the plugin's VST3 or Audio Unit version. An Audio Unit v3 plugin that runs out of process can't be bound to ARA yet; use its VST3 instead.

docs.title: Inserting an ARA plugin
docs.text:
Add the plugin to an audio track like any other effect: drag it from the Plugin Browser onto the track or into its FX chain. It can sit anywhere in the chain, including inside a rack.

As soon as it loads, every audio clip in the Arrangement on that track becomes a region in the plugin, at its position on the timeline, and the plugin starts analysing it. Clips you add, move or trim later follow automatically.

To edit, open the plugin's window from its device header. Opening the window selects the track's clips in the plugin, which is what the plugin shows and analyses. The plugin also sees the project's tempo and time signature, so its bar grid matches the arrangement.

Tracks that use the same ARA plugin share one plugin document. Each track's plugin window opens on that track's clips.

docs.title: Playing and rendering
docs.text:
The track plays through the plugin as you work:

  • The plugin's playhead follows MAGDA's transport.
  • Edits are heard as you make them, and clicking a note in the plugin auditions it.
  • Moving or trimming a clip during playback is followed without a gap.
  • Exports, Bounce To New Track and freezing the track render through the plugin.

Nothing is written back to the clips' audio files. To commit the plugin's edits to audio, bounce the clips to a new track or freeze the track.

docs.title: What happens to the clips
docs.text:
The plugin plays each clip from its source file, once and as recorded. MAGDA's own clip processing doesn't apply on that track, so the controls for it stand down:

  • Inspector - the clip's mix, loop, warp and pitch controls are greyed out, Reverse and the gain envelope included, with a note naming the plugin.
  • Arrangement and Waveform Editor - warp markers, the loop phase marker, fade and volume handles, and gain envelope editing are disabled. Shift + dragging a clip edge resizes the clip instead of stretching it, and Loop is unavailable.
  • Playback - a looping clip plays once, and a clip in beat mode or with a speed change plays the file at its own speed.
  • Drawing - each clip draws the stretch of file the plugin plays: forwards, unstretched, with no loop repeats or warping, and with a dimmed waveform. Its header shows the plugin's initial, and the Inspector shows the same chip (hover it for Played by and the plugin's name).

Your clip settings are kept. Remove the plugin and they apply again.

docs.title: Saving
docs.text:
The plugin's edits are saved with the project. Each time you save, MAGDA stores them in the project's media folder, under <Project>_Media/ara/, one file per plugin, and restores them when the project reopens.

The edits stay with the clips' sources, so relinking a missing file, collecting media into the project or moving a file doesn't lose them.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Arrangement audio clips only. Session View clips and MIDI clips on the track aren't handed to the plugin.
  • No stretching or pitch from MAGDA. Tempo following, warp, speed, pitch, reverse and looping are left to the plugin; MAGDA plays the raw file into it.
  • Use MAGDA's transport. Play, stop and locate requests from inside the plugin's window don't move MAGDA's transport.

docs.title: Arrangement View
docs.text: The Arrangement View is a traditional DAW timeline for composing, recording, and editing. Switch to it by clicking the Arrangement button in the footer bar.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
┌──────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Toolbar  │ Timeline ruler (bars / beats / time)│
├──────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Track    │                                     │
│ Headers  │   Track Content (clips on           │
│          │   the timeline)                     │
│  Name    │                                     │
│  Color   │         ▼ Playhead                  │
│  M S R   │                                     │
├──────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Aux      │   Aux track content                 │
├──────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Master   │   Song navigator                    │
└──────────┴─────────────────────────────────────┘
  • Toolbar (top left) — The corner above the track headers (see Toolbar).
  • Track headers (left) — Track name, color, mute/solo controls. Resizable width.
  • Track content (center) — Clips displayed on the timeline. Scrollable horizontally and vertically. The chord track, when there is one, is always the top row. Below the last track there is always an empty lane, so you can scroll down and drop a file there to make a new track.
  • Timeline ruler (top) — Shows bars, beats, and time markers.
  • Playhead — Vertical line showing the current playback position, always on top.
  • Aux tracks — Auxiliary/bus tracks in a fixed section above the master.
  • Master track (bottom) — The master output in its own row (see Master Track).

docs.title: Toolbar
docs.text:
The corner above the track headers holds one row of buttons:

  • Edit tool — shows the current tool; click it to pick another (see Edit Tools)
  • Add track
  • Show / hide marker lane (see Markers)
  • Show / hide seconds ruler (see Timeline Ruler)
  • Zoom to selection, Zoom to fit timeline and Zoom to loop region — on a narrow header these drop out, Zoom to loop region first
  • Toggle I/O routing — at the outer edge, over the I/O column it shows

The three track-height buttons sit above the vertical scrollbar, beside the ruler, drawn as three small dots (compact), two dots (medium) and one large dot (large). Each sets every track to that height. Right-click any of them to edit the three heights.

docs.title: Edit Tools
docs.text:
Press T to open the five edit tools at the mouse, or click the tool button in the corner. Pick one with a click or its number key:

Tool Key What it does Pointer 1 Select, move and resize clips Pencil 2 Draw a MIDI clip on an empty lane Slice 3 Split a clip where you click Glue 4 Join a clip to the next one on its track Erase 5 Click or sweep over clips to delete them

docs.title: Master Track
docs.text:
The master row at the bottom holds a mute button, the Automation button (see Master Automation), the master volume and a peak meter, with the song navigator beside them.

Three buttons beside the row set its height:

  • Compact master — the peak meter only
  • Medium master — the mute button, Automation button, volume and meter
  • Large master — the same, with a taller song navigator

In compact, only the compact button shows; click it to go back to medium. The button at the bottom of the track headers, in the scrollbar row, hides or shows the master track.

docs.title: Working with Clips
docs.text:
• Move — Click and drag a clip along the timeline or between tracks
  • Resize — Drag the edges of a clip to trim it
  • Select — Click a clip to select it; Cmd-click (Ctrl-click on Windows/Linux) to toggle clips in the selection; Ctrl+A (Cmd+A) to select all
  • Delete — Select a clip and press Del or Backspace
  • Erase — Shift+Ctrl-click a clip to delete it directly without selecting first
  • Duplicate — Ctrl+D (Cmd+D) to duplicate selected clips

Drag audio files from the Media Explorer directly onto a track to import them as clips.

While recording, the growing clip previews in real time: MIDI notes appear in the lane as you play them, and audio shows its waveform as it is captured, so you can see the take taking shape before it is committed.

docs.title: Multi-Sample Drag and Drop
docs.text:
You can drag several samples out of the Media Explorer at once — Shift-click to extend the selection, Cmd-click (Ctrl-click on Windows/Linux) to toggle individual files, then drag any item in the selection.

  • Drop on empty area — one new track is created per sample. While dragging, ghost track-header previews appear in the correct palette colours each new track will take.
  • Drop on an existing track — the samples are appended as sequential clips on that track, in selection order.

Ghost clips shown under the cursor during the drag reflect each sample's actual audio duration, so you can align the drop with the grid before releasing.

docs.title: Expanded Faceplates
docs.text:
Some devices can lend their faceplate, or part of it, to the Arrangement View when they need more room: the Step Sequencer and Poly Sequencer, the Arpeggiator's time bend, and the Sampler. Click the device's expand button (tooltip Expand into the arrangement on the sequencers and the Arpeggiator) and the faceplate fills the Arrangement View, toolbar and ruler included. The device slot shows a note in its place.

Click the collapse button (tooltip Put the faceplate back in its device slot (Esc)) or press Esc to put it back. Only one faceplate is out at a time: expanding another puts the first one back.

docs.title: Markers
docs.text:
Markers are named flags on the timeline that label sections of the song — Intro, Chorus, Drop. Toggle the marker lane with Show marker lane in the corner toolbar; it sits as a strip above the timeline ruler.

  • Add — right-click the marker lane and choose Add Marker. The marker lands at the playhead.
  • Rename — double-click a marker, or right-click it and choose Rename...
  • Reposition — right-click → Edit Position... to set an exact bar/beat.
  • Colour — right-click → Colour to pick from the palette.
  • Delete — right-click → Delete Marker.

When a marker scrolls off the left edge, its name stays pinned at the edge of the lane so you always know which section you are in.

docs.title: Song Navigator
docs.text:
The song navigator is a minimap in the master content strip showing the whole arrangement at a glance: a compressed overview of the track clips, the timeline markers as vertical lines, the playhead, and a viewport rectangle marking the part of the song currently visible in the main view.

  • Click anywhere in the minimap to jump the view there.
  • Drag the viewport rectangle to pan the arrangement.
  • Drag its left or right edge to zoom the main view in or out.

docs.title: Scrolling
docs.text:
• Horizontal scroll — Move along the timeline (mouse wheel or scroll gesture)
  • Vertical scroll — Navigate between tracks
  • Follow playhead — When enabled, the view scrolls automatically during playback to keep the playhead on screen. Turn it on in Settings > General, under Transport (Follow playhead during playback).

docs.title: Timeline Ruler
docs.text: The ruler above the tracks shows bars and beats, with the loop region and playhead in their own rows below. Toggle Show seconds ruler in the corner toolbar to add a second row that reads the same positions in seconds — useful when lining up to picture or a fixed running time. The seconds row is display-only; it sits above the bars row and disappears again when toggled off, letting the bars row fill the height.

docs.title: Zooming
docs.text:
• Horizontal zoom — Ctrl++ / Ctrl+- (Cmd++ / Cmd+- on macOS) or use the zoom scrollbar
  • Vertical zoom — Change track height using the track-height buttons (compact, medium, large)

docs.title: Toolbar Zoom Actions
docs.text:
• Zoom to fit timeline — Fit all content in the visible area
  • Zoom to selection — Zoom into the current time selection
  • Zoom to loop region — Zoom to the loop region

docs.title: Selection
docs.text:
• Time selection - Drag in the ruler's bottom row to select a time range across all tracks. The range shows there as a blue strip, and in the tracks as a spotlight: everything outside the range dims while clip colours stay true, and the range edges read as near-white. Drag the endpoint handles to adjust the range.
  • Loop region - Set from the selection with L. It is drawn in the ruler's loop row as a thin green line across the top of the loop with a wedge hanging from each end, the same in the arrangement ruler and in the clip-editor rulers; it turns grey while looping is off. Drag a wedge to move that end of the loop, or drag the line to move the whole loop.

docs.title: Playhead
docs.text:
The playhead shows the current playback position. Click on the timeline ruler to reposition it. Click Home in the transport to return to the start. The play and edit cursors are drawn a consistent near-white across every editor.

Edit Cursor

The edit cursor is a white blinking line separate from the playhead. Place it with Alt+click on the timeline ruler or inside a clip. It marks the position for operations like Split (Cmd+E). Press Esc to hide it. The MIDI editor has its own independent edit cursor — placing one in the piano roll or drum grid does not affect the arrangement cursor.

docs.title: Editing Modes
docs.text: MAGDA supports two editing modes depending on context:

docs.title: Clip-Based Editing
docs.text:
When no time selection is active, editing operations apply to selected clips:

  • Split (Cmd+E) — Splits selected clips at the edit cursor position
  • Render (Cmd+B) — Renders selected clips to audio in place
  • Cut / Copy / Paste / Duplicate / Delete — Operate on the selected clips
  • Nudge (Shift + arrow keys) — Moves selected clips one grid step along the timeline, or to the neighbouring track. See Editing Clips.

docs.title: Time Selection Editing
docs.text:
When a time selection is active (drag on the timeline ruler), operations apply to the time range:

  • Split / Trim (Cmd+E) — Splits clips at the selection boundaries and isolates the selected region. If clips extend beyond the selection, they are trimmed.
  • Render Time Selection (Cmd+Shift+B) — Consolidates everything within the time selection to a single audio clip per track
  • Cut / Copy / Paste — Operate on the content within the time range

Note

When a time selection exists, Split/Trim affects all clips that overlap the selection — not just selected clips. Clear the time selection to return to clip-based editing.

docs.title: Range Editing
docs.text:
Range edits work on a span of time and ripple everything after it, rather than editing clips in place. They act on the current time selection or the loop range.

Operation What it does Insert Time Opens a gap at the selection and pushes later clips to the right, splitting any that straddle the insert point. Duplicate Time Range Copies the selected span and ripple-inserts the copy directly after it. Duplicate Loop Range Same as above for the loop span. Settings > General has Duplicate Loop Range grows the loop (off: advances it), which chooses whether the loop grows to cover the copy or advances past it. Split All Tracks at Cursor Splits every track at the edit cursor.

A Range Editing submenu, in the Edit menu and in the right-click menus on clips and on empty arrangement space, offers Copy, Cut, Delete, and Paste (Ripple) for both the time selection and the loop range.

Range operations ripple the global tempo, time-signature, and pitch-bend curves along with the clips, so tempo and key changes travel with the music instead of staying pinned to the timeline. Beat-anchored clips keep their bar and beat position under the shifted tempo map. Markers ripple along with the clips on global operations.

docs.title: Cut, Copy, Paste
docs.text: Action Shortcut Cut Ctrl+X / Cmd+X Copy Ctrl+C / Cmd+C Paste Ctrl+V / Cmd+V

docs.title: Split and Join
docs.text:
• Split — Position the edit cursor and press Ctrl+E (Cmd+E) to split the clip at that point. If a time selection is active, clips are trimmed to the selection.
  • Join — Select adjacent clips and press Ctrl+J (Cmd+J) to merge them.

docs.title: Duplicate
docs.text:
• Duplicate clips — Ctrl+D (Cmd+D) duplicates selected clips
  • Duplicate track — Ctrl+D with a track selected duplicates the track and its content
  • Duplicate track (empty) — Ctrl+Shift+D (Cmd+Shift+D) duplicates the track structure without content
  • Duplicate track (content only) — Ctrl+Alt+D (Cmd+Alt+D) duplicates the track's clips onto a new track with an empty FX chain

docs.title: Render
docs.text:
• Render clip to audio — Select a clip and press Ctrl+B (Cmd+B) to bounce it to an audio file
  • Render time selection — Press Ctrl+Shift+B (Cmd+Shift+B) to render the selected time range

docs.title: Undo / Redo
docs.text: Action Shortcut Undo Ctrl+Z / Cmd+Z Redo Ctrl+Shift+Z / Cmd+Shift+Z

docs.title: Project Settings
docs.text: Open File → Project Settings to set options that belong to the project itself rather than the application. It has two tabs.

docs.title: General
docs.text:
Setting Options Total Length Song length in bars (16–4096, in steps of 16) Sample Rate 44100, 48000, 88200, 96000, 192000 Hz Render Bit Depth 16-bit, 24-bit, 32-bit float Bounce Bit Depth 16-bit, 24-bit, 32-bit float

These are stored per project, so different songs can carry different lengths and render formats. The values a new project starts with are set in Settings > Defaults. Apply commits your changes; Cancel closes the dialog, discarding anything you have not applied.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
The Metadata tab holds the song's title and credits: Title, Artist, Album, Original artist, Composer, Songwriter, Producer, Arranger, Year, Genre, Copyright, Website and Comment. All of them are free text and all of them are optional. The credits that describe you rather than the song — Artist, Composer, Songwriter, Producer, Arranger, Genre, Copyright, Website — are filled in for a new project from Settings > Defaults, so you only type them once.

Title is left empty by default and shows the project's name in grey. That name is what gets used, so there is nothing to fill in unless the song is called something other than the file — a song called Blue can live in blue_v7.mgd. Type a title only when you want one that differs from the name; leave it alone and renaming the project keeps carrying through.

These are the fields the DAWproject format defines, so they survive a round trip through File → Export DAWproject... and back, and credits written in another DAW come through on import.

docs.title: Automation
docs.text:
Automation is the third member of MAGDA's modulation family, alongside Modulators and Macros. Where modulators and macros generate or proxy a value continuously, automation records parameter changes into a lane and replays them in sync with the transport.

Any parameter that has a slider, knob, or fader in MAGDA can be automated.

docs.title: Automation Lanes
docs.text:
A lane is a curve drawn underneath a track in the Arrangement View that controls a single parameter over time. The parameter follows the lane's value during playback.

To open a lane:

  • Right-click any parameter slider → Show Automation Lane, or
  • Right-click an automation-aware control (macro knob, LFO Rate slider) and pick the same item.

The lane appears below the track. Drag points to edit the curve; double-click to add or remove points; right-click a point to type its value, or a segment to make it a hard corner.

Multiple lanes can stack on the same track — one per automated parameter — and modulators, macros, and automation can all drive the same parameter at once. Their effects combine.

A device parameter gets its lane from the same place you link modulation: right-click the parameter and choose Show Automation Lane. (Parameters on a post-FX device cannot be automated, so the item isn't offered there.)

docs.title: Curve Shapes
docs.text:
A segment is the line between two points. Each segment has a handle in its middle:

  • Drag the handle to bend the segment into a curve.
  • Double-click the handle to straighten it again.
  • Right-click a segment and choose Hard Corner to turn it into two straight lines meeting at a sharp apex; drag the handle to move the apex. Choose it again to go back to a curve.

Shift-click to stamp a step: a flat block one grid division wide at the value you clicked, with a sheer edge on each side.

docs.title: Editing Points
docs.text:
• Add / remove a point — double-click an empty spot in the lane to add one; double-click a point to remove it.
  • Move points — drag a point; drag across an empty part of the lane to select several, and drag any of them to move them together.
  • Draw freehand — hold Cmd (Ctrl on Windows/Linux) and drag.
  • Delete — select points and press Del or Backspace. Cmd+A (Ctrl+A) selects every point.
  • Inline value — right-click a point to type its value directly, in the lane's real units (dB, pan %, Hz, …). Press Enter to commit.
  • Simplify — select three or more points, right-click and choose Simplify Selected Points to thin them out while keeping the shape.
  • Point Inspector — select one or more points to open the inspector, which shows the target name and point count, an editable Value field, and the Position (beat) of a single selected point. Editing the value across a multi-selection applies the change as a delta, preserving the relative shape.

docs.title: Lane Header Controls
docs.text:
Each lane header carries a row of toggles:

Control Function Lane mode Switch the lane between one free-drawn curve and discrete automation clips (tooltip Lane mode: clips / free draw) Snap edits to beat grid Snap point positions to the bar/beat grid while editing Snap values to parameter grid Snap point values to the parameter's natural steps Automation on/off Bypass the lane without deleting it; the parameter ignores the curve while off Delete automation lane Remove the lane and its curve

docs.title: Automation Clips
docs.text:
A lane can hold its automation as discrete automation clips instead of one continuous curve. Switch a lane to clip mode with the Lane mode toggle in its header. Clip-based automation is handy when you want the same move to repeat, to loop, or to move and copy a shaped gesture around the timeline like any other clip.

On a clip-based lane:

  • Double-click an empty part of the lane to drop a one-bar automation clip.
  • Hold Alt and drag to draw a clip of a specific length (a plain Alt-click makes the default one-bar clip).
  • Right-click a clip for Edit Curve, Duplicate, Loop (a checkmark toggle that repeats the clip's curve to fill its length), and Delete.

Select an automation clip to see it in the Inspector: its name (double-click to rename), its Start, End and Length, and a Loop switch with the loop's length. Right-click the name to change the clip's colour.

Double-click a clip to open the automation-clip editor. Its header carries:

Control Function SNAP X Snap edits to the time grid; the adjacent division button (tooltip Snap division) sets the resolution SNAP Y Snap edits to the value grid; its division button sets the value step Overlay track content Show the underlying track's clips behind the curve for reference

Inside the editor, left-click an empty spot to add a point and drag points to move them. Right-click a point to type its exact value; right-click a segment for Hard Corner and Simplify Selected Points.

docs.title: Baking Modulation
docs.text: You can convert a live modulator (an LFO or envelope linked to a parameter) into automation you can edit by hand. Right-click the linked parameter and choose Bake Modulation to Automation to write the modulator's movement into lane points, or Bake Modulation to Automation Clip to capture it as an automation clip.

docs.title: Master Automation
docs.text:
The master channel has its own automation band above the master strip. Click the Automation button in the master header (or right-click the header) to open the master automation menu, where you can show or hide existing master lanes, hide them all, or use Add New Lane... for:

  • Track Volume — the master output level
  • Tempo — see below
  • any parameter of a device on the master chain, plus master macros and modulators

Alt-click the Automation button to show or hide every automation lane in the edit at once.

These master lanes include edit-scoped targets like tempo and master volume that aren't tied to a specific device.

docs.title: Tempo Automation
docs.text:
Tempo can be automated over time as a curve in the master automation band. Open the master automation menu, choose Add New Lane → Tempo, and the tempo lane appears in the master band. Edit it like any other lane — drag points, set curve shapes, type exact BPM values via the point inspector. The curve drives the project's tempo, so the song speeds up and slows down along the curve during playback.

Tempo automation is ignored while Ableton Link is on or MAGDA follows a MIDI clock.

docs.title: Automation Modes
docs.text:
The transport bar's automation button sits right after Record. Click it to arm automation writing: it lights up, and AUTOMATION WRITE (or TOUCH or LATCH) shows in the transport when there is room. Click it again, or press Stop in the transport, to disarm it. While it is disarmed, lanes only play back.

Right-click the button to choose the mode. The letter under the icon shows the one chosen:

Letter Mode W Write T Touch L Latch

The mode controls how parameter movements during playback are written into a lane.

Mode Behavior Disarmed No recording. Lanes play back; user gestures don't write anything. Write Record every parameter change while the transport is rolling. The classic behavior: anything you touch becomes part of the lane. Touch Record only while you're physically holding the control. Release the mouse and the lane's existing curve takes over again. Latch Same as Touch on the way in: recording starts when you grab the control. After release, the last value you held is latched and continues writing into the lane until the transport stops.

docs.title: When to use which
docs.text:
• Write for a first pass on an empty lane — sketching the shape from scratch.
  • Touch for nudging a single section of an existing curve without erasing the parts you don't touch.
  • Latch for "set and hold" gestures — sweep a filter to its destination, release, and the rest of the lane is rewritten at that target value.
  • Disarm the button when you've finished writing and want playback only. Same effect as a "Read" mode in other DAWs.

docs.title: Touch and the Override Highlight
docs.text:
In Touch and Latch modes, the parameter you're holding paints a coloured highlight around its slider. That highlight is your visual cue that the parameter is currently overriding the lane — you, not the curve, are in charge of that value right now. When you release:

  • Touch drops the highlight and lane playback resumes.
  • Latch keeps the highlight until the transport stops; the held value continues to be written.

docs.title: Recording Tips
docs.text:
• Automation only records while the transport is playing. Moving a control with playback stopped is not captured.
  • Each playback pass creates one undoable group — if a take goes wrong, Cmd+Z removes the whole pass at once.
  • The lane stays visible after stop. You can keep editing it manually with the curve editor.

docs.title: Interaction with Modulation
docs.text:
A lane can target a parameter that is also being driven by a modulator or macro. The values are summed:

final value = automation lane value + modulator output + macro output

This means a slow LFO can wobble around an automation curve, or a macro can offset the whole lane up and down — same parameter, three sources, all live.

docs.title: Duplicating Clips with Automation
docs.text: When you duplicate a clip, you can decide whether its automation comes along. Right-click a clip and choose Duplicate With Automation to carry the lane data into the copy, or Duplicate Without Automation to leave it behind. See Clips — Editing Clips.

docs.title: Removing Automation
docs.text:
• To remove a point: double-click it, or select it and press Del.
  • To remove a lane and its curve: click Delete automation lane in the lane header.
  • To hide a lane (keeping the curve): right-click the lane header → Hide Lane. Show it again from the parameter's right-click menu or the track's Automation menu.

The lane header's right-click menu also has Simplify Curve, which thins out a lane with many points.

docs.title: Chord Track
docs.text:
The Chord Track lays out a chord progression that guides the harmony of your song. You sketch the progression as a row of named chord blocks — A min7, D maj, G maj7 / B — and each block carries the actual MIDI voicing underneath, which you can audition and refine.

A project has a single chord track. Once you have added it, the menu item that creates it is disabled.

docs.title: Creating a Chord Track
docs.text:
Choose Track → Add Chord Track. It takes the top row of the arrangement and the first column on the left in the Session View and the Mixer. A separator is added right after it, unless you turn off Add a separator after a new chord track in Settings > General. In the Session View and the Mixer, click the chevron on its header to fold it to a narrow strip, and click the strip to unfold it. The chords keep playing while it is folded. The track appears with a simplified header:

  • A volume control.
  • A chord preview control (the chord icon) that sets whether the progression sounds during playback. Click it to step through Silent, Audible and Solo, or right-click it to pick one. A new chord track starts Silent, unless its project was created with New projects: chord preview on in Settings > General.

It has no mute or solo button of its own, no routing and no sends — the chord track is a guide, not an audio output.

docs.title: Editing Chords
docs.text:
The chord track's clip opens in a dedicated chord editor at the bottom of the window. The top chord lane holds the chord blocks; a piano-roll strip below shows the voiced notes for the selected chord.

  • Add — click an empty spot on the chord lane to drop a chord at the nearest bar.
  • Edit — double-click a block to open the chord popup, with dropdowns for:
    • Root — C through B
    • Quality — Major, Minor, Dim, Aug, Sus2, Sus4, 5 (Power), Dom
    • Extension — None, add2/add4, 6, 7, 9, … (the choices depend on the quality)
    • Octave
    • Inversion — Root position, Inversion 1, Inversion 2, Inversion 3
  • Move / resize — drag a block along the lane to move it, or drag its edges to change its length. Hold Alt while dragging to copy a chord.
  • Audition — click a block to hear it through the track's instrument.
  • Delete — select a block and press Del.

You can also drag a chord straight from the Chord Engine suggestion grid onto the chord lane.

docs.title: The Progression List
docs.text:
Select the chord clip and open the Inspector to see the Progression list — every chord with its bar.beat position, name, and length:

Pos Chord Length 1.1 A3 min7 1.0 bar 2.1 D3 maj 1.0 bar 3.1 G4 maj7 / B 1.0 bar 4.1 C5 maj7 / E 1.0 bar
  • Transpose — the - / + buttons shift the whole progression up or down.
  • Save to library — stores the progression in the chord progression library (see below).

docs.title: Chord Progression Library
docs.text: Saved progressions live in the media library so you can reuse them across projects. Open the Media Explorer, switch it to Library (the database icon), and click the chord progression filter to list only progressions. Browse or filter them, then drag one onto a chord track to drop the whole progression in.

docs.title: Clips
docs.text: Clips are the containers that hold audio and MIDI data on tracks. They appear as rectangular blocks in the Arrangement View timeline and as trigger pads in Session View.

docs.title: Clip Types
docs.text:
Type Description Audio Contains a reference to an audio file (WAV, AIFF/AIF, FLAC, OGG, MP3 where a platform decoder is available) with start/end points and gain MIDI Contains MIDI note and automation data

Because MAGDA uses a hybrid track system, an audio track can hold both audio and MIDI clips. Group, aux and separator tracks take no clips.

docs.title: MIDI Clip Properties
docs.text:
The Inspector shows a clip's properties in collapsible sections.

Property Description Name Display name of the clip Colour Clip colour Start / End / Length Position and duration, in bars, beats and ticks Loop Loop the clip's contents. While it loops, Phase sets where playback starts inside the loop; otherwise Offset trims the start without moving the clip Transpose Buttons that move the clip's notes down or up an octave or a semitone (−12, −1, +1, +12). The notes themselves change Time Bend Bends when the clip's notes play, and loads grooves (see Groove & Time Bend)

docs.title: Audio Clip Properties
docs.text:
The Inspector groups these into Clip, Warp & Pitch, Mix, Fades and Labels sections. The Waveform Editor's properties panel shows most of them too.

Property Description Name Display name of the clip Colour Clip colour Start / End / Length Position and duration on the timeline Loop Loop the clip, with Phase or Offset as for MIDI clips (see Looping) Warp Turn on warp markers for per-segment time-stretching Beat / Free Follow the project tempo in bars and beats, or play at the file's own rate (see Audio Clip Modes) Stretch engine The time-stretch algorithm (see Time-Stretch Engine) Transient sensitivity How readily transients are detected in the source Tempo The source file's tempo in BPM, with ÷2 and ×2 buttons, and its length in beats Speed Playback speed factor from 0.25x to 4.0x (Free only) Analog Resample instead of time-stretching for pitch changes (Free only) Pitch Pitch shift in semitones (−48 to +48) and cents Key The source's key Volume Clip volume in dB Gain Additional boost from 0 to +24 dB Pan Stereo position from L to R Reverse Play audio backwards Gain envelope Show the clip's gain envelope (see Gain Envelope) Fades Fade-in and fade-out lengths, each with a curve (Linear, Convex, Concave, S-Curve) and a behaviour (Gain Fade or Speed Ramp) Auto-crossfade Crossfade automatically where clips overlap (the switch in the Fades header) Labels Named regions and points on the source (see Labels)

docs.title: Session Clip Properties
docs.text:
Both MIDI and audio clips in Session View have additional launch and follow properties, in the Inspector's Launch section:

Property Description Quantize Quantize launch timing (None, 8 Bars, 4 Bars, 2 Bars, 1 Bar, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16) Follow action What happens when the clip finishes: None, Play Next, Play Previous, Play Random, Stop, or Play Again Delay (beats) Delay before the follow action fires (0 - 64 beats, 0.25-beat resolution) Loops Number of times the clip loops before the follow action fires

Note

Session clips do not have an absolute position property; they are not placed on the timeline. Their position is determined by the scene slot they occupy.

docs.title: Follow Actions
docs.text:
Follow actions chain session clips together for generative arrangement. Once the clip has played the configured number of loops (plus any follow delay), the chosen action fires:

  • Play Next triggers the next slot in the same track column
  • Play Previous triggers the previous slot in the same track column
  • Play Random triggers another slot in the same track column at random
  • Play Again retriggers the current clip
  • Stop stops session playback

docs.title: Creating Clips
docs.text:
• Double-click an empty area on a track to create a new 1-bar MIDI clip at that position
  • Double-click over a time selection to create a MIDI clip matching the selection length
  • Alt + drag on an empty track lane to draw a MIDI clip of variable length. The drag distance sets the clip length (snapped to the current grid). The arrangement's Pencil tool does the same.

docs.title: Selecting Clips
docs.text:
• Click a clip to select it
  • Cmd + click (Ctrl + click on Windows/Linux) to add or remove clips from the selection
  • Cmd+A (Ctrl+A on Windows/Linux) selects all clips in the arrangement, or all notes when a MIDI editor is focused
  • Double-click a clip to open the bottom editor panel on it, and double-click again to close it. Selecting a clip switches the panel to the right editor but never reopens a panel you collapsed — the panel stays as you left it until you double-click a clip or use the collapse button in the footer.

docs.title: Editing Clips
docs.text:
• Move — Drag a clip to reposition it on the timeline or move it to another track
  • Nudge — With clips selected, Shift+Left / Shift+Right moves them one grid step along the timeline, and Shift+Up / Shift+Down moves them to the neighbouring track. The whole selection moves together, keeping its spacing, and stops rather than piling up when it reaches the first track, the last track, or the start of the timeline. With snap on, the move lands on the grid; with snap off it steps by one grid unit from wherever the clip sits.
  • Resize — Drag the left or right edge of a clip to trim its start or end point
  • Duplicate — Hold Alt and drag a clip, or press Cmd+D
  • Duplicate with or without automation — Right-click a clip and choose Duplicate With Automation to copy the clip together with the automation under it, or Duplicate Without Automation to copy just the clip. Plain Duplicate behaves the same as the menu's default.
  • Split — Use Edit > Split / Trim or press Cmd+E to split the clips at the edit cursor. With a time selection, it splits them at the selection's edges instead. The clip's right-click menu has the same Split / Trim item.
  • Delete — Select the clip and press Del or Backspace
  • Erase under cursor — Shift+Ctrl + click a clip to delete it directly without selecting first. If the clip is part of a multi-selection, the whole group is erased. Acts as a rubber tool.
  • Duplicate as ghost — Right-click and choose Duplicate as Ghost, or hold Alt+Shift and drag, to create a linked copy. See Linked (Ghost) Clips.
  • Enable / disable — Right-click and choose Disable Clip or Enable Clip, or press 0. See Enabling and Disabling Clips.

Clips on a frozen track can't be edited until the track is unfrozen.

docs.title: Cut, Copy, and Paste
docs.text:
• Cmd+X — Cut the selected clip(s)
  • Cmd+C — Copy the selected clip(s)
  • Cmd+V — Paste at the playhead position on the same track

docs.title: Linked (Ghost) Clips
docs.text:
A ghost clip is a linked copy: every clip in a link group shares the same underlying content, so editing one updates them all. Use them for a chorus that repeats, a drum pattern reused across a song, or a riff you want to develop in one place and hear everywhere.

Create one by right-clicking a clip and choosing Duplicate as Ghost, or by holding Alt+Shift and dragging a copy off the original. (Plain Alt-drag makes an ordinary, independent duplicate.) The same command is available from the Edit menu as Duplicate Clip as Ghost.

Ghost clips are drawn translucently, with their waveform or notes dimmed, a small link glyph in the header, and an italic name with a per-instance index appended (e.g. Riff #2). A link group with only one clip left is inert and shows no ghost styling.

What is shared, and what is not:

Shared across the group Independent per clip Notes and audio content, takes, name Position, length, and offset Warp markers, labels and time-stretch mode Playback speed (speed ratio) and loop settings Tempo, key, and beat or free playback Colour Pitch, analog and reverse Volume, gain, pan, and fades Gain envelope, time bend, transient detection Launch and grid settings, enabled/disabled state

Editing any shared field on one member mirrors instantly to the rest; the independent fields let each ghost sit in its own place, at its own level, without disturbing its siblings.

To detach a clip from its group, right-click it and choose Make Unique. The clip keeps its current content but stops tracking, and future edits to it (or to its former siblings) no longer propagate. Splitting a ghost clip detaches both halves automatically.

docs.title: Enabling and Disabling Clips
docs.text:
Disabling a clip removes it from playback without deleting it. Right-click a clip and choose Disable Clip (or Enable Clip to bring it back), or press 0 with clips selected. A disabled clip is greyed out with a hatch, so it reads as "off" at a glance, and it is excluded from the playback graph so it produces no sound.

The enabled state is per-clip: disabling one member of a link group does not silence its ghost siblings.

docs.title: Overlapping clips
docs.text:
Arrangement clips stack rather than erase each other. Drag a clip onto one that is already there and the clip underneath keeps its position and its full contents; it is covered, not trimmed. Move the covering clip away again and the material underneath comes back on its own, because what a clip plays is worked out from the lane each time rather than stored.

The clip on top owns the span it covers, and the one underneath plays what is left. A clip covered end to end plays nothing while staying exactly where it is. Which clip is on top is set when you place or move it, so the most recently moved clip wins, and the lane draws in that same order: what you see stacked is what you hear.

Where a cover lands decides what the clip underneath becomes:

  • Overlapping an edge shortens it. The audible span pulls in to the edge of the cover, which is a shorter clip rather than a hole in one.
  • Landing strictly inside it leaves a hole. The clip keeps its start and end and goes silent across the covered span only. A MIDI clip plays around the hole by dropping the notes that start inside it; an audio clip carries the hole through to playback. Nothing is cut and nothing is split, so the material comes back intact when the cover moves away.

A clip you disabled by hand covers nothing, because it is already silent. Letting it occlude would silence the clip below on behalf of silence.

docs.title: Play Through Overlap
docs.text:
To make both clips sound where they overlap, right-click either one and tick Play Through Overlap. The lane hatches the shared span to show it is playing both.

Either clip can carry the switch, which matters because the clip you reach for when something goes quiet is the one that went quiet, and that is the one underneath.

Asking for a crossfade turns it on for you, on both clips: right-click and choose Crossfade with Previous Clip or Crossfade with Next Clip, or drag a crossfade handle. Asking for a fade region is asking for both clips to be heard across it, so the gesture sets the fade and the play-through together.

With New projects: overlap plays both on (Settings > General, under Behavior), new clips in a new project start with Play Through Overlap ticked.

The Auto-crossfade switch does not do this

Auto-crossfade marks a clip as eligible to crossfade; it does not create a fade region, and it leaves play-through alone. The same goes for New projects: auto-crossfade in Settings > General, which only decides whether new clips in a new project start with that property on.

This matters because auto-crossfade cannot keep a covered clip audible on its own. It shapes an overlap that is already playing both, so audio fades into audio instead of both running flat. Play Through Overlap is what decides whether both sound; the crossfade only decides how they meet.

docs.title: Flatten MIDI Loop
docs.text: When a MIDI clip is looping, right-click it and choose Flatten MIDI Loop to write the repetitions out as real notes. The loop cycles (including any offset phase) are baked into actual MIDI across the clip's full length, looping is switched off, and the offset resets to zero. The clip stays a MIDI clip in place, ready for per-note editing in the Piano Roll; the operation is a single undoable step.

docs.title: Audio Clip Modes
docs.text: An audio clip plays in one of two ways, Beat or Free. Choose with the Beat | Free switch in the Inspector's Warp & Pitch section, or the BEAT toggle in the Waveform Editor's properties panel. Warp markers work on top of either.

docs.title: Free
docs.text: The clip plays at the file's own rate, unaffected by the project tempo. Changing the project tempo does not stretch or compress it. Speed changes how fast it plays, and with Analog on, pitch changes resample the audio like tape instead of time-stretching it.

docs.title: Beat
docs.text:
Locks the clip to a musical length (e.g. 4 bars). When the project tempo changes, MAGDA time-stretches the audio so it always fills the same number of bars. Use this for loops, drum patterns, and rhythmic material that should stay in sync with the project.

Beat mode needs the file's tempo, shown in the Tempo field, where ÷2 and ×2 fix a detection that landed at half or double speed. If MAGDA can't detect a tempo and BEAT without a detected tempo uses the project tempo is on (Settings > General, under Behavior; on by default), the clip enters beat mode at the tempo it is heard at and a message tells you what was assumed; edit Tempo to correct it. With the option off, MAGDA asks you to type the BPM instead.

Beat mode doesn't loop the clip by itself. A beat-mode clip can follow the tempo and play once, ending where its source file ends.

docs.title: Looping
docs.text:
Only beat-mode clips loop. Turning Loop on for a free clip puts it into beat mode first, at the tempo it is heard at (the project tempo divided by its speed), so it sounds the same; a file that already has a tempo keeps it. The clip keeps its length and loops what it shows. Turning beat mode off ends an arrangement clip's loop.

Audio clips in Session View slots are always in beat mode, and BEAT can't be turned off there. Free clips that looped in a project from an earlier version of MAGDA open in beat mode and sound as they did.

docs.title: Warp Markers
docs.text:
Turn on Warp for per-segment time-stretching using warp markers. Each marker pins a point in the audio to a specific position on the timeline. The audio between markers is independently stretched or compressed. This is the most flexible mode — use it to align a free-tempo recording to the grid, fix timing, or create creative effects.

Warp markers are edited in the Waveform Editor:

  • Add a warp marker — Choose the Marker tool in the editor's toolbar and click the waveform. A dotted guide shows where it will land.
  • Move a warp marker — Drag it left or right to stretch the audio on either side. Alt + drag moves the marker without stretching.
  • Delete a warp marker — Double-click it, or right-click it and choose Remove Warp Marker

docs.title: Slicing
docs.text:
Right-click an audio clip to access slice operations. These split the clip into multiple pieces based on warp markers or the current grid setting.

  • Slice at Warp Markers In Place — Split the clip at each warp marker position, creating separate clips on the same track. Requires warp mode with at least one user-placed marker.
  • Slice at Grid In Place — Split the clip at every grid line, creating separate clips on the same track.
  • Slice at Warp Markers to Drum Grid — Create a new Drum Grid track where each slice between warp markers becomes a pad, with a MIDI pattern that reproduces the original timing.
  • Slice at Grid to Drum Grid — Same as above but slicing at grid intervals instead of warp markers.

docs.title: Time-Stretch Engine
docs.text:
When Beat or Warp mode is active (or whenever a clip is otherwise stretched or pitched), the audio is time-stretched by a selectable engine, set per clip:

Engine Notes Signalsmith Default. Modern, general-purpose stretcher with clean transients. SoundTouch Lighter-weight classic algorithm. SoundTouch HQ Higher-quality SoundTouch variant at more CPU cost. Off No stretch engine; the clip is left unprocessed.

Choose the engine from the stretch engine dropdown in the Inspector's Warp & Pitch section or from the Mode dropdown in the Waveform Editor's properties panel. New clips default to Signalsmith as soon as stretching becomes active.

docs.title: Gain Envelope
docs.text:
An audio clip can carry a gain envelope: a volume curve drawn over the clip, from silence up to +6 dB. It rides on the sound itself, so its points stay with the same audio when you trim, reverse, loop or stretch the clip. Linked ghost clips share it, and it is saved with the project.

Show it with any of these, which all set the same switch on the clip:

  • the gain envelope button in the Waveform Editor toolbar
  • Show Gain Envelope in the clip's right-click menu
  • E with audio clips selected
  • the Gain envelope toggle in the Inspector's Mix section

Showing it is a view setting, not an undo step. While it is shown, the clip's waveform dims and the envelope draws over it, both in the Waveform Editor and on the clip in the arrangement. An empty envelope is a flat 0 dB line. On the arrangement clip you edit it with the Waveform Editor's current envelope tool; the clip's trim edges and fade handles keep working, and right-clicking still opens the clip menu.

docs.title: Groove & Time Bend
docs.text:
A MIDI clip can carry a time bend: a curve that moves when its notes play, without changing the notes as written. Grooves are ready-made bends. Open it in the Inspector's Time Bend section, or with the Time Bend button in the Piano Roll toolbar.

Above the curve:

  • GROOVE loads a groove at full strength, from the Swing, Push Swing, Pull Swing, Push Snare, Pull Snare, Timing and Random families, or your own under Custom. AMOUNT sets how much of it you hear, and None turns it off.
  • BAKE writes what the bend plays into the notes and turns the bend off.

See Time Bend for editing the curve itself.

docs.title: Creating Grooves with AI
docs.text:
You can create custom grooves using the /groove slash command in the AI Assistant:

/groove funky 16th

The AI generates a groove from your description. Created grooves appear under Custom in the GROOVE menu.

docs.title: Groove via DSL
docs.text:
You can also list and apply grooves with DSL code, run through the /dsl command in the AI Assistant. strength sets the bend's AMOUNT:

groove.list()
groove.set(template="Basic 8th Swing", strength=0.5)

docs.title: Transcribe Audio to MIDI
docs.text:
MAGDA can detect the notes in an audio clip and turn them into MIDI. Right-click an audio clip and choose Transcribe to MIDI: the audio is analysed and a MIDI clip of the detected notes is created, ready to drive an instrument. It works on a single audio clip at a time and needs the clip's source file on disk.

Transcription works best on clearly pitched, reasonably clean material (a solo vocal, a bassline, a lead). Dense mixes and heavily layered audio give rougher results that usually want some cleanup in the Piano Roll.

Intel macOS

Transcription runs on the ONNX runtime, which is not part of the Intel macOS build. On those builds Transcribe to MIDI is greyed out.

docs.title: Split into Stems
docs.text:
Right-click an audio clip and choose Split into Stems to separate it onto new tracks — vocals, drums, bass and other with Demucs, vocals against everything else with Spleeter, or harmonic against percussive content with the download-free HPSS engine. The stem tracks appear in a group beneath the source, the source track is muted, and each stem clip keeps the original's position, stretch mode, and warp markers.

See Stem Separation for the engines, the model downloads, and where the rendered files land.

docs.title: Crossfades
docs.text:
A crossfade is a real overlap between two adjacent audio clips: the outgoing clip fades down as the incoming clip fades up across the shared region.

  • Create - drag one audio clip so it overlaps its neighbour. With auto-crossfade active the overlap becomes a crossfade, drawn with an X across the shared region. You can also right-click a clip and choose Crossfade with Previous Clip or Crossfade with Next Clip.
  • Resize - drag the fade handles at a crossfaded edge to lengthen or shorten the overlap.
  • Read and edit the length - the crossfade shows as an editable Crossfade in or Crossfade out value, in beats, in the clip's Fades section. Dragging it to zero leaves the row in place so you can re-create the crossfade later.
  • Remove - right-click the clip and choose Remove Start Crossfade or Remove End Crossfade.

Whether a clip crossfades automatically is its Auto-crossfade switch, in the header of the Inspector's Fades section. New projects: auto-crossfade in Settings > General decides whether new clips in a new project start with it on.

Selecting several audio clips at once keeps the Waveform Editor open in a multi-clip mode, where the fades section batch-edits all of them at once, including auto-crossfade.

docs.title: Freeze, Bounce, and Render
docs.text:
These operations render a track or clip's output to audio, useful for reducing CPU load or committing effects.

  • Freeze — Render the track's output to an audio file and play that instead, until you unfreeze it. Right-click the track header and choose Freeze Track. See Freezing Tracks.
  • Render Selected Clip — On audio clips, right-click and choose Render Selected Clip (or Render Selected Clip(s) for several) to write the clip's speed, pitch, warp, fades, gain and trim into a new audio file and replace the clip with a plain clip playing it. Track and master plugins are not included.
  • Render Time Selection — Right-click and choose Render Time Selection, or press Cmd+Shift+B, to consolidate the time selection into a single clip on each track.
  • Bounce In Place — On a MIDI clip on a track with an instrument, right-click and choose Bounce In Place to render it through the instrument only, with no effects, and replace it with an audio clip on the same track.
  • Bounce To New Track — Right-click any clip and choose Bounce To New Track to render it through the track's full chain, instrument and effects, onto a new audio track below. The original is left unchanged. With several clips selected, each gets its own track.

Bounces cover the time selection when there is one, and otherwise the selected clips.

docs.title: Exporting
docs.text:
File > Export Audio… renders your song to a stereo audio file, and File > Export MIDI… writes its MIDI clips to a Standard MIDI File. Both open a dialog for the options, then a save dialog for the file.

To hand a whole project to another DAW, use File > Export DAWproject… instead (see File Formats).

docs.title: Export Audio
docs.text: Choose File > Export Audio…, set the options, and click Export.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
Option Choices Format WAV, FLAC, Opus or MP3. The dialog opens on the format you exported last Sample Rate 44.1 kHz, 48 kHz, 96 kHz or 192 kHz. It starts at the project's sample rate, rounded down to one of these. MP3 goes up to 48 kHz Bit Depth WAV: 16-bit, 24-bit or 32-bit Float. FLAC: 16-bit or 24-bit. It starts at the project's Render Bit Depth from Project Settings Dither Off, TPDF (the default) or Noise Shaped. Not available at 32-bit Float, which needs none Bitrate Opus and MP3 only, in place of Bit Depth and Dither. Opus: 64 to 320 kbps, 160 kbps by default. MP3: VBR V0, V2 or V4, or CBR at 128, 192, 256 or 320 kbps; VBR V2 by default. MAGDA remembers the last bitrate you used for each

See File Formats for what each format stores.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Normalize to 0 dB (peak) — Raises or lowers the whole file so its loudest peak sits at 0 dB. Off by default.
  • Real-time render (slower, avoids plugin glitches) — Renders at playback speed rather than as fast as possible, for plugins that misbehave when run faster than real time. Off by default.
  • Lead-in Silence — Up to 2 seconds of silence before the audio, in steps of 0.1 s. 0 s by default.

docs.title: Export Range
docs.text: Range What it exports Entire Song From the start of the arrangement to the end of its last clip. The default Time Selection The arrangement's time selection. Available when there is one; a selection made only on automation lanes doesn't count. A selection over some of the tracks still exports the whole mix over that time Loop Region The loop region. Available while looping is on

docs.title: What goes into the file
docs.text:
The export is the whole mix as it reaches the master, through every track's chain and the master's own effects. A powered-off device stays off in the file (see Device Power), and a disabled track renders nothing. The chord track is left out.

If the project holds a routed External FX or External Instrument, MAGDA first plays the export range once in real time to record the hardware, in a box titled Capturing External Hardware with a Cancel button, and then renders.

Opus and MP3 files carry the Title, Artist, Album, Year, Genre and Comment from the Metadata tab of Project Settings as tags; empty fields are left out. A WAV file instead carries the tempo, the time signature and the project's key, when one is set, in the loop information that samplers and loop-aware DAWs read. An Entire Song export is marked as a one-shot and a Loop Region export as a loop. With lead-in silence the tempo is left out, since the file no longer starts on the beat. FLAC files carry no tags.

docs.title: Where the file goes
docs.text:
After Export, a save dialog opens in the folder set under Settings > Rendering (Documents unless you chose another), with a name built from the Export pattern there, <project-name>_<date-time> by default. See Rendering. In an export, <track-name> reads master and <clip-name> reads the project name, and spaces in the project name become underscores. MAGDA adds the format's extension and asks before replacing an existing file.

A progress window, Exporting Audio…, follows the render and has a Cancel button. Playback stops while MAGDA renders and starts again afterwards if it was playing. When the file is written, a message gives its full path.

docs.title: Export MIDI
docs.text:
File > Export MIDI… writes the MIDI clips in the arrangement to a .mid file.

Option Choices MIDI Format Type 1 (Multi-Track), the default: a track per MAGDA track that has MIDI clips, named after it, after a first track holding the tempo and time signature. Type 0 (Single Track): everything in one track Export Range Entire Song, Time Selection or Loop Region, available as for audio. Entire Song runs from the start of the arrangement to the end of its last MIDI clip

The file holds the clips' notes, CC and pitch bend, all on MIDI channel 1. The range starts at the beginning of the file, and notes that cross its end are cut there. The tempo is written once, the project tempo, with the project's time signature. Session view clips and automation lanes aren't exported.

The save dialog opens in your Documents folder with the project's name. If no MIDI clip has anything in the range, MAGDA says so instead.

docs.title: Other ways to render
docs.text:
• Edit > Render Selected Clip(s) and Edit > Render Time Selection render to audio clips in the project; see Render.
  • Freezing a track renders it to a file that plays in its place.
  • Programs connected through the Remote API can render a range with engine.renderRange.

docs.title: FX Chain & Racks
docs.text: Each track has an FX chain — an ordered list of audio processors applied to the track's signal.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The FX chain is displayed in the bottom panel when a track or device is selected. Signal flows left to right through the chain. The header above the chain holds the track's own controls and presets; see Track Chain for each button.

The chain can contain:

  • Plugins — VST3, AU, or VST effect and instrument plugins
  • Built-in devices — MAGDA's own processors (see Built-in Devices)
  • Racks — Container devices with nested chains and parallel routing, including multiband racks

docs.title: Working with Devices
docs.text:
• Drag plugins from the Plugin Browser onto the chain to add them, or click the + at the end of the chain (Add a device) to pick one from a menu: Internal devices first, then plugins grouped by manufacturer
  • Drag devices to reorder them in the chain; hold Alt while dragging to copy instead of move (the cursor shows a copy badge)
  • Click a device to select it; the selected device is highlighted in the accent colour. Cmd-click adds or removes a device from a multi-selection, Shift-click selects a range
  • Cmd+D duplicates the selected device(s) in place
  • Backspace or Del deletes the selected devices and racks. Devices have no delete button of their own
  • Right-click a device for Add to New Rack (or Add Selection to New Rack when several are selected) and Delete. Both act on the whole selection when the device you click is part of it, and deleting several devices is a single undo step
  • Double-click the background of a selected device to collapse it to a narrow strip; double-click again to expand it
  • Plugin devices have a Locate button that finds the parameter matching a control you move in the plugin's own window — see Plugin Parameters

See Plugin Parameters for per-plugin parameter visibility, custom units and ranges, and AI-assisted classification.

docs.title: Device Layout
docs.text:
Every device in the chain has the same height. Its parts:

  • Header — on the left, the Macros and Mods buttons that open the device's macro and modulator panels, plus routing buttons when the device has them (MIDI thru, sidechain source, multi-output routing). Then the preset box and the device name. On the right, plugin devices carry Locate and a button that opens the plugin's own window. A small MIDI light flashes green when a note arrives on the track's MIDI input, but only while the track monitors its input. With monitoring off, incoming notes leave it dark.
  • Sidebar — down the left edge of the body, the toggles for the device's panels (for example its parameters or its faceplate) and the arrows that page through its parameters.
  • Side strip — down the right edge, the device's power button at the top, then its peak meter with the gain fader over it. Effects with a dry/wet mix also show a Dry / Wet Mix knob, and effects carry the Δ delta-solo button at the bottom. MIDI devices show a strip of incoming notes in place of the meter.

A plugin's parameter grid shows one row fewer when the plugin sits inside a rack or a Drum Grid pad, so each value still fits under its name.

docs.title: Device Power
docs.text:
The power button at the top of a device's side strip takes the device out of the signal path. A chain's power button does the same for every device in it. Both states are part of the project: they survive save and reload, and they are honoured when you render — a device that is powered off is powered off in an exported or bounced file too.

The gain fader in a device's or rack's side strip ignores the scroll wheel until you click it. This keeps a stray trackpad gesture over a device scrolling the chain rather than changing its gain. Once you have clicked the fader the wheel adjusts it, until the pointer leaves.

docs.title: Delta Solo
docs.text:
The Δ button at the bottom of an effect's side strip (tooltip Delta Solo: processed signal minus dry input) lets you hear only what that device changes: MAGDA subtracts the device's latency-aligned dry input from its processed output, so you audition the difference alone. It is the direct way to check exactly what a compressor, EQ, or saturator is doing to the signal.

Delta solo and bypass are mutually exclusive: turning on delta solo powers the device on, and powering the device off clears delta solo. The button lights cyan while active.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text: Every device, and the track chain header, shows a preset box naming the current preset, with a floppy disk beside it. On both headers the preset sits before the name, between separators. The name of the current preset is saved with the project, so the box still shows it after you switch tracks or reopen the project.

docs.title: MAGDA Presets (.mps)
docs.text:
A MAGDA preset captures everything MAGDA knows about the device — parameter values, plugin state, macros, modulators, sidechain wiring, gain — in a single .mps file.

  • Load — click the preset box. The menu lists the device's MAGDA presets, with categories as submenus and the current preset ticked. Loading replaces the device's state in place, keeping its slot in the chain.
  • Save — click the floppy disk. It always asks for a name, pre-filled with the current preset's, and an optional category, which becomes a folder under the preset directory. Keep the name and press Enter to overwrite the preset (MAGDA asks first); type a new name to save a copy.
  • Reveal in Finder at the bottom of the menu opens the device's preset folder.

.mps is portable across MAGDA installations. The format is plugin-aware — loading a preset onto a slot whose plugin id doesn't match is rejected with a one-line error rather than silently overwriting state.

docs.title: Plugin Presets
docs.text:
A third-party plugin (VST3 / AU) uses the same menu, with its own entries after your MAGDA presets:

  • Plugin Presets — the plugin's .vstpreset / .aupreset files, scanned from the standard preset directories. Your existing factory and user banks are picked up without a copy step.
  • Built-in Programs — the programs the plugin itself exposes, when it has more than one.
  • Save as .vstpreset... / Save as .aupreset... — save the plugin's current state as a plugin preset in its user preset folder.
  • Reveal Plugin Preset Folder and Rescan.

The floppy disk always saves a MAGDA preset, on plugins as on every other device.

docs.title: Track Chain Presets
docs.text:
The preset box on the track chain header holds track presets. A track preset captures the entire chain — every device, every nested rack, every modulator binding — for a single track. Useful for stashing a finished mix-bus chain, a vocal chain, or a synth-and-FX combo and dropping it onto a fresh track later.

The box lists your track presets; loading one replaces the track's chain. The floppy disk asks for a name, pre-filled with the current one; use / to file it in a folder (for example Bass/808 Stack). Saving over an existing name asks first.

You can also drag a preset from the media browser onto the chain: a track preset replaces the chain, and a device preset is inserted where you drop it.

docs.title: Rack Presets
docs.text: Racks keep a small chevron beside their name. Its menu lists your rack presets, followed by Save "name" (once a preset is loaded), Save as MAGDA Rack Preset... and Reveal in Finder.

docs.title: Racks
docs.text: A rack is a container that holds one or more parallel chains. Signal flows into the rack, splits across chains, and mixes back together at the output.

docs.title: Creating a Rack
docs.text:
• Click Add rack in the track chain header, or Add multiband rack for a rack that splits the signal into frequency bands
  • Right-click a device and choose Add to New Rack to wrap it in a new rack (Add Selection to New Rack wraps every selected device)

docs.title: Chains
docs.text:
A rack lists its chains on its left. With the MIX tab selected, each chain row has:

  • Volume — Level control for the chain's output
  • Pan — Stereo positioning of the chain
  • Mute (M) / Solo (S) — Mute or solo individual chains
  • Power and remove buttons

The KEY, VEL and FADE tabs show each chain's key range, velocity range, and range on the rack's Chain select control instead. The VEL tab also holds the round-robin switch. A rack inside a Drum Grid pad has no KEY tab, since the pad plays a single note.

Click Add chain at the bottom of the list to add a new parallel chain. Double-click a chain's name to rename it. The selected chain's devices show beside the list.

Select multiple chains with Cmd-click (toggle) or Shift-click (range). When more than one chain is selected, editing volume, pan, mute, solo, or bypass on any selected chain applies to the whole selection — volume and pan shift each chain by the same amount from its own value, so their relative balance is preserved.

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• Parallel processing — Blend dry and wet signals (e.g., parallel compression)
  • Multi-band processing — Split signal into frequency bands with different processing
  • Organized grouping — Keep related devices together in a collapsible container

docs.title: Rack Controls
docs.text:
• Header — the rack's Macros and Mods buttons, which open its own macro and modulator panels, then the name and the rack's preset chevron. The rack header spans only the rack's left panels, so the headers of the devices inside it sit level with it.
  • Sidebar — toggles that show the chain list and the selected chain (and, on a multiband rack, its faceplate), with the Chain select control at the foot.
  • Side strip — the rack's power button, peak meter, and gain fader (Rack Gain (dB)).
  • Collapse/Expand — double-click the background of a selected rack.

Racks have no delta-solo button. Delete a rack the same way as a device: Backspace, or right-click and choose Delete.

docs.title: External Hardware Inserts
docs.text:
MAGDA can route a track's signal out to outboard gear and back, treating a hardware unit as an insert in the chain. Two entries live under the External category in the Plugin Browser, and in the Internal list of the chain's + menu:

  • External FX — sends audio out to an outboard effect and returns its processed audio.
  • External Instrument — sends MIDI out to a hardware synth and returns its audio.

Add either to a track's chain, then set it up on its faceplate: the routing along the top, a row of MIDI CC knobs under it, and a status line at the foot.

docs.title: Routing
docs.text:
Control Purpose Send to External FX: the audio output that feeds the effect MIDI to External Instrument: the MIDI output the synth listens on, then its MIDI channel, Ch 1 to Ch 16. MAGDA moves the track's notes onto that channel. The channel can be changed once a MIDI output is chosen Return from The audio input the hardware comes back on Latency Extra delay in milliseconds to line the return up with the rest of the mix (default 0.0 ms). Click the value to type a new one. MAGDA already allows for the latency your audio interface reports, so this is only the time the hardware itself adds

The port pickers start at None. Send to and Return from list the channels ticked under Settings > Audio & MIDI, and MIDI to lists your computer's MIDI outputs. To check a route, put a Test Tone before an External FX: it replaces the track's signal with a tone, so you know exactly what reaches the hardware.

For an External Instrument, the track's own MIDI-out and audio-in selectors become read-only mirrors of the insert's routing; change them on the insert. When the track takes all MIDI inputs, MAGDA ignores the synth's own MIDI port while the track isn't armed, so notes the synth sends back don't double or loop. Arm the track to play and record from the synth's keyboard.

docs.title: MIDI CC knobs
docs.text:
The MIDI CC row puts knobs for the hardware's own controls on the faceplate. Each knob sends one CC number, with values from 0 to 127.

  • On an External FX, whose send is audio, the row has its own MIDI output and channel pickers: choose where the unit listens for CCs.
  • On an External Instrument, the CCs go to the same MIDI output and channel as its notes, and the row shows where.

Click the dashed + tile (Add a CC knob) to add a knob. It takes the lowest CC number the insert isn't sending yet. Knobs sit eight to a page, up to 32 on four pages; once there is more than one page, arrows at the right end of the row page through them. Click a knob to select it: a CC picker (CC 0 to CC 127) and Remove appear in the status line, to change the number it sends or delete it.

To pick the number by ear, click the Learn icon (Learn: click a knob, then turn a hardware control), click a knob, then turn a control on the hardware. The knob takes that control's CC number, and from then on the control moves the knob, like any MIDI Learn mapping. Choosing another number in the CC picker, or removing the knob, drops that link. Click the icon again to stop listening.

Each knob is a device parameter named after its CC number (for example CC 74), so you can automate it or drive it from a macro or a modulator. MAGDA sends the CC each time the knob's value changes.

docs.title: Status line
docs.text:
The line at the foot of the faceplate says what the insert is doing:

Status Meaning send → return, green dot Both ends are routed No return chosen, amber dot A send but no return No send chosen / No MIDI port chosen, amber dot A return but no send (External FX / External Instrument) Not routed Neither end is set

The dot turns amber and the line names the clash when the return uses the same port as the send (Return uses the same port as the send), or another switched-on insert uses the same send or return (for example Send port also used on Bass). While Learn is on, the dot is blue and the line prompts you through the steps instead.

A preset saved from an External FX or External Instrument brings back its routing, latency and CC knobs, along with the knobs' values.

Export captures the hardware automatically

Because outboard gear isn't part of an offline render, MAGDA captures it for you. When you export a project that contains a routed insert, it first plays the export range once in real time to record the hardware returns (a progress box titled Capturing External Hardware appears, with a Cancel button), then substitutes those captures into the offline render. If the capture can't be set up or fails, the export stops with a message instead of writing silent hardware into the file. Nothing is added to your project and there is no freeze step to manage.

docs.title: Post-FX Section
docs.text:
In addition to the main FX chain, every track and the master have a post-FX area, a stage that runs after the main chain. It is the natural home for meters and analyzers, but any effect can live there.

Show or hide the post-FX panel with the post-FX button in the track chain header (Show/hide the post-FX panel). The Oscilloscope, Spectrum Analyzer and Levels buttons beside it add that analyzer to the post-FX area, or remove it; each button is lit while its analyzer is there. You can also drop any effect into the panel. The panel opens automatically when you select a track that has post-FX devices.

docs.title: Which side of the fader it runs on
docs.text:
By default the post-FX area runs after the track fader, so a meter there reads the level you are actually sending on. The PRE FADER / POST FADER tag under the + button on the panel's add strip shows the current side and switches it for that track. The whole section moves together; sends keep their own pre/post-fader setting either way.

Master is always pre-fader, so the tag does not appear there. To choose the side tracks start on in new projects, use New projects: post-FX after fader in Settings > General.

Note

Each analyzer kind is unique per track in the post-FX area — one Oscilloscope, one Spectrum Analyzer and one Levels meter at most — while regular effects can repeat.

docs.title: Gain Staging
docs.text:
Gain staging trims the output of every device in a chain so the whole chain holds a target headroom, without adjusting each one by hand.

Open it from the gain-staging button in the track chain header, set your target peak (default -12 dBFS), play a representative section of the song, and stop. MAGDA works out the trims:

  • It only attenuates, never boosts.
  • It carries the gain forward down the chain, so later devices see consistent levels.
  • Every fader it moves stays marked so you can see the pass at a glance, until you change it or run another pass.

The whole pass is a single undoable step. An optional AI pass can weigh limiters and saturators in the chain instead of applying a flat target.

docs.title: Is MAGDA Right for You?
docs.text:
MAGDA may be a good fit if:

  • You enjoy experimenting with new workflows.
  • You like exploring ideas rather than following fixed templates.
  • You are interested in AI-assisted creativity and automation.
  • You are comfortable with software that evolves rapidly.
  • You enjoy discovering new musical ideas and refining them yourself.
  • You see AI as a creative assistant rather than a replacement for musicians.
  • You enjoy participating in a project and helping shape its direction through feedback and discussion.

MAGDA may not be the right fit if:

  • You expect AI to generate finished songs with minimal input.
  • You are looking for a mature commercial DAW with decades of refinement behind it.
  • You are unwilling to spend time learning new workflows or troubleshooting occasional issues.
  • You expect every feature to work exactly as imagined without experimentation or iteration.

docs.title: MAGDA Is an Open Source Project
docs.text:
MAGDA is not a product developed by a large company with dedicated support, QA, marketing and engineering teams. It is an independent open-source project under active development.

Open source works best when it is collaborative. Users contribute by:

  • Reporting bugs.
