  • Providing reproduction steps.
  • Suggesting improvements.
  • Testing new features.
  • Sharing ideas and feedback.
  • Making music and sharing their experiences.

Constructive feedback is always welcome, and many features in MAGDA exist because of community suggestions.

Because MAGDA is developed by one person, time and attention are limited resources.

If you encounter a problem, please provide as much information as possible. Feedback that includes details, reproduction steps, screenshots, logs, examples, or concrete suggestions helps move the project forward and has a direct impact on future releases. By contrast, reports that provide little information are often difficult or impossible to act upon, regardless of whether the underlying problem is real.

The goal is not to create a customer-vendor relationship, but a collaborative one where users and developers work together to understand a problem and improve the software.

The best results usually come from users who enjoy exploring, experimenting, learning and contributing to the project in whatever way they can.

docs.title: Localization
docs.text: MAGDA's interface can be displayed in several languages. Alongside English (en), MAGDA ships with community translations into Spanish (es), Japanese (ja), Russian (ru) and Simplified Chinese (zh), and more are added as translations are completed.

docs.title: Switching Language
docs.text:
Set the UI language in Settings > General, under Language, with UI Language. The dropdown lists every language MAGDA ships with, by language code. The new language is loaded when you click Apply or OK; restart MAGDA for it to apply everywhere.

Chinese and Japanese text is drawn a little larger by default. Adjust it with Localized Font Size in the same group.

docs.title: Contributing Translations
docs.text:
MAGDA's translations are managed on Crowdin:

https://crowdin.com/project/magda

To contribute:

  1. Request access on the Crowdin project page.
  2. Once approved, translate strings directly in the browser editor.
  3. Approved translations sync back to MAGDA through an automated pull request — no manual file handling required.

New locales appear in the UI Language dropdown once their translations are complete and shipped in a release.

docs.title: What is Not Translated
docs.text:
Some strings are deliberately kept in English across every locale:

  • Brand names (plugin names, company names, MAGDA's own name)
  • File-format designators such as "WAV 24-bit", "FLAC", "MIDI"
  • The MAGDA subtitle

Leave these untouched when translating — they are excluded from the Crowdin source strings.

Some parts of the interface, such as parts of the AI settings, have not been moved into the translation files yet, so they show in English whatever the language.

docs.title: Mixer View
docs.text: The Mixer View provides a channel-strip interface for balancing levels, panning, routing, and applying effects. Switch to it by clicking Mix in the footer bar.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
┌──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬─────────┐
│ Track 1  │ Track 2  │ Track 3  │ Aux 1    │ Master  │
│          │          │          │          │         │
│ [Routing]│ [Routing]│ [Routing]│          │         │
│ [Sends]  │ [Sends]  │ [Sends]  │          │         │
│          │          │          │          │         │
│  ┃  ┃    │  ┃  ┃    │  ┃  ┃    │  ┃  ┃    │  ┃  ┃   │
│  ┃██┃    │  ┃█ ┃    │  ┃  ┃    │  ┃█ ┃    │  ┃██┃   │
│  ┃██┃    │  ┃██┃    │  ┃█ ┃    │  ┃██┃    │  ┃██┃   │
│  ┃██┃    │  ┃██┃    │  ┃██┃    │  ┃██┃    │  ┃██┃   │
│  [Pan]   │  [Pan]   │  [Pan]   │  [Pan]   │         │
│  M S R   │  M S R   │  M S R   │  M S     │ [Mute]  │
│ Track 1  │ Track 2  │ Track 3  │ Aux 1    │ Master  │
└──────────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────┴─────────┘
  • Channel strips — One per track, scrollable horizontally
  • Chord channel strip — The chord track, always the first strip on the left
  • Aux channel strips — Auxiliary/bus tracks, in a fixed section next to the master with a small gap before it
  • Master channel strip — Final output, fixed on the right
  • Resizable width — Drag the edge of a channel strip to resize

Click a channel strip to select it. Drag plugins onto a channel strip to add them to the track's FX chain. Drag a strip by its name to move it: a line shows where it will land between strips, including inside or out of a group, and an outline shows a group it will join.

docs.title: Toggle Rail
docs.text:
A vertical rail of toggles runs down the left edge of the mixer. Each button shows or hides a row across every channel strip, so you can pare the mixer back to just the controls you need:

  • Sends — the send section
  • I/O — input and output routing selectors
  • Monitor — the record-arm and input-monitoring row
  • Oscilloscope — a mini oscilloscope per strip
  • Spectrum — a mini spectrum analyzer per strip
  • FX Chain — the strip's mini FX chain

The rail's on/off state is remembered between sessions. Below the toggles sits the Analyze button — see Mix Analysis.

docs.title: Channel Strip Controls
docs.text: Each channel strip provides:

docs.title: Volume Fader
docs.text: Drag the fader to adjust the track's output level. The fader sits over the track's peak meter, with the current level shown as a dB readout below the thumb.

docs.title: Level Meters
docs.text: The peak meter sits directly behind the fader and shows the real-time signal level. A peak value displays the highest level reached — watch for clipping. Click the peak readout to reset it.

docs.title: Pan
docs.text: The pan control positions the track in the stereo field, from hard left to hard right.

docs.title: Mute, Solo, Record
docs.text:
• Mute (M) — Silence the track output
  • Solo (S) — Solo this track, muting all others
  • Record (R) — Arm the track for recording
  • Monitor — Enable input monitoring

docs.title: Track Name and Color
docs.text: The track name and color bar are displayed at the bottom of each strip for identification.

docs.title: Mini FX Chain
docs.text: With the FX Chain toggle on, each strip shows a compact version of the track's FX chain, one row per device (a rack shows as one row with its name). Click a row's dot to bypass the device. Click its chevron to unfold up to three of its parameters as faders, so you can tweak an effect without leaving the mixer. Choose exactly which parameters appear per device from the Mini FX column in the Configure Parameters dialog — if none are chosen, the row falls back to the device's first visible parameters. Third-party plugins also show a button to open their own window; native MAGDA devices do not. The same rows appear in the FX section of the track and master inspectors.

docs.title: Mini Analyzers
docs.text: With the Oscilloscope or Spectrum toggle on, a mini analyzer appears on each strip that carries the matching device. Click the expand chevron to unfold its controls beneath the trace, or the pop-out button to open the full analyzer in its own floating window.

docs.title: Master Channel Strip
docs.text: The master strip controls the final output level of the mix. It has its own volume fader and meters, and a speaker button that mutes the master. It has no pan control and no solo or record buttons.

docs.title: Mix Analysis
docs.text:
The Analyze button at the bottom of the toggle rail runs a measured analysis of the mix and shows the findings in a small panel anchored to the button.

  • Scope — with no channels selected, the whole mix is analysed; select channel strips first to scope the measurement to just those tracks. The panel title shows the scope and the range (the loop region if one is active, otherwise the whole song).
  • Findings — a per-track table of measured values (integrated loudness, peak, peak-to-loudness ratio, stereo correlation and width, with a row for the master) followed by any detected collisions: frequency ranges where two tracks mask each other, with a severity rating.
  • Re-run the analysis after changes, or Stop a run in progress.

The same measurements feed the mixing agent: once an analysis exists, the AI console in the mixer view picks it up as context, so you can ask for mix feedback grounded in real numbers rather than guesswork.

docs.title: I/O Routing
docs.text:
Each channel strip has routing selectors for:

  • Audio input — Select which physical input or bus feeds the track
  • Audio output — Choose where the track's audio is sent (master, aux bus, etc.)
  • MIDI input — Select the MIDI input device and channel
  • MIDI output — Route MIDI to a specific device or virtual instrument

docs.title: Sends
docs.text:
Each channel strip has a send section for routing audio to auxiliary buses. Show or hide it with the Sends toggle in the rail.

  • Add a send — Create a new send slot to route signal to an aux track
  • Send level — Adjust how much signal is sent to the aux bus
  • Remove a send — Click the remove button on a send slot to delete it

The send section sizes itself to the number of sends across your tracks, so every strip stays aligned.

docs.title: Multi-Output Plugins
docs.text:
When an instrument has multiple output pairs activated, each output appears as its own channel strip in the mixer — just like any other track. You can route these strips to groups or aux sends independently. See Multi-Output Plugins for setup details.

The device's multi-out menu lets you toggle several pairs in one go: the menu stays open as you tick pairs, and Activate All / Deactivate All bring every output in or out with one click.

docs.title: Drum Grid Pad Channels
docs.text:
Every Drum Grid pad that holds a sound has its own mixer channel, nested under the strip of the grid's track. Click the chevron on the track's strip to fold the pad channels away or show them again. Empty pads have no channel.

A pad channel works like any other channel: volume, pan, mute, solo, sends, automation, effects, and a meter. Its output goes to the Drum Grid by default, so the pads are summed into the grid before any effects that come after the grid on its track. Route a pad's output somewhere else and it leaves the grid's mix.

  • Solo — soloing a pad channel keeps the grid's track audible, so you hear the pad through the rest of the track
  • Chain — select a pad channel to show that pad's chain in the bottom panel. Devices you add to it land in the pad's chain
  • Pad mix — the pad's level, pan, mute, and solo on the Drum Grid device and its pad channel are the same controls

Projects saved with pad bus outputs are converted when you open them: a bus that carried one pad becomes that pad's channel, keeping its effects, sends, automation, and output, and a bus that carried several pads becomes a group that their channels route into.

docs.title: Plugin Parameters
docs.text:
Third-party plugins rarely tell a host what their parameters actually mean — most expose every knob as a generic 0–100 % value. MAGDA takes a first pass at interpreting those values for you, and the Configure Parameters dialog lets you refine or override the result for any plugin.

The configuration is saved per plugin (by plugin unique ID), so it's applied automatically every time the plugin is loaded.

docs.title: Automatic Inference
docs.text:
When a plugin is scanned, MAGDA looks at each parameter's name, value shape, and typical range and guesses a sensible unit and range. Common cases like cutoff frequencies (Hz), envelope times (ms), gain (dB), pitch (semitones), and mix amounts (%) are detected automatically. Parameters it can't classify fall back to a generic 0–100 % display.

You can override or extend the inferred configuration in the dialog described below.

docs.title: Configure Parameters Dialog
docs.text:
Open the dialog from the Plugin Browser: right-click a plugin and choose Configure Parameters….

The dialog shows one row per parameter with the following columns:

Column Description Parameter Parameter name as reported by the plugin. Visible Toggle whether the parameter shows up on the device in MAGDA's chain and in AI prompts. Hide parameters you never touch to reduce clutter. Mini FX Show the parameter in the device's row of the mini FX chain, in the mixer and the track inspector. Up to three are shown. AI Agent Allow the AI sound designer to set this parameter. Independent of Visible. Unit Display unit — Hz, dB, ms, %, semitones, or any custom string. Range Minimum, centre, and maximum values in the parameter's own domain. Narrow the range so sliders and AI-generated values stay in the useful zone.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
• Select All / Deselect All — Toggle every row in the column chosen by the dropdown beside them (Visible, Mini FX, or AI Agent).
  • Detect — Run the deterministic heuristic pass (instant, offline). Picks up units and ranges that the plugin's own display strings give away.
  • AI Detect — Run the heuristic pass and then send anything it couldn't resolve to the configured LLM (see below).
  • AI Prompt... — Standing instructions added to every sound-design request for this plugin. The button shows a checkmark once a prompt is saved.
  • Controls — How this plugin's parameters draw on its device: Text fields, Knobs, or Sliders. Use global keeps the default, text fields.
  • Reset — Discard all inferred units, ranges, AI parameter selections, and the custom prompt for this plugin, putting every parameter back to a plain 0–100 % view.
  • Apply — Save changes without closing the dialog.
  • OK / Cancel — Save and close, or discard.

Internal devices

MAGDA's own devices report proper units and ranges already, and their sound designers introspect every parameter, so the dialog drops the Visible and AI Agent columns and the AI Prompt... button for them, and offers only the Mini FX choice.

docs.title: AI Detect
docs.text:
Typing units and ranges by hand for a plugin with dozens of parameters is tedious. AI Detect runs the heuristic pass first, then sends each remaining parameter — name plus a sample of display values — to the configured LLM, which returns a unit, range, and scale.

The results populate the dialog so you can review them before applying — tweak anything you disagree with and hit Apply.

Note

AI Detect uses whichever provider is configured in Settings > AI. It works with both cloud providers and local inference.

docs.title: Locating a Parameter
docs.text:
Big plugins can have hundreds of parameters spread across many pages in the device slot. Finding the one you want is tedious. The Locate button lets you point at a control in the plugin's own window and have MAGDA jump straight to its slot.

On any plugin device slot in the FX chain:

  1. Open the plugin's own window.
  2. Click the Locate button in the device header — it highlights.
  3. Move any control in the plugin's window.
  4. MAGDA navigates to the parameter page that contains the matching parameter and highlights its slot.

Click Locate again to stop. Use it to find the right parameter before setting up automation, modulation, or a macro link.

Note

Locate is only enabled while the plugin's own window is open, and is hidden for MAGDA's built-in devices. Closing the plugin window turns it off.

docs.title: Recording Takes & Comping
docs.text: When you loop-record over a section, MAGDA keeps every pass as a separate take instead of overwriting the previous one. You can then comp the takes together, swiping in the best part of each to build a single composite performance. This works for both audio and MIDI clips.

docs.title: Recording takes
docs.text:
1. Set the loop region over the part you want to record (see Transport).
  2. Enable Loop in the transport bar.
  3. Arm the track and record.

Each pass around the loop is captured as its own take. Nothing is lost between passes, so you can keep playing until you have a take you like.

A live Recording... preview is drawn over the timeline as you record, showing the incoming waveform (audio) or notes (MIDI) growing under the playhead so you can see what was captured before recording stops.

docs.title: Capturing what you just heard
docs.text:
MAGDA can keep what you play, so an idea you played without recording is not lost. While capture is on, it keeps the master output and the notes you play on MIDI devices, whether or not the transport is running. Capture is off until you turn it on.

Click MEM's dot or its caption in the transport bar to turn capture on or off; the meter beside them doesn't respond to clicks. Turning capture off stops it writing but keeps what it already holds, so you can still open, play, select and import it. Turning it on again carries on from where it stopped.

The MEM meter shows what is held: its level, with what you just played drawn bright, then how long that is and how full the buffer is. It reads off while capture is off. The dot is lit while it is recording.

Click the capture button beside the meter (Cmd+Shift+C, or Transport > Recent Capture) to open the capture panel under the transport. It shows the audio and the notes over the whole buffer, oldest at the left, with what you just played already selected:

  • With the transport stopped, that is your last phrase, back to a pause of a few seconds, with a second of tail for the release.
  • Along with the transport, it is the last bars of that pass. A stop or a loop wrap ends a pass.

Zoom and scroll with the ruler and scroll bar, as in the waveform editor. The play button plays the selection, or what is in view when nothing is selected. Drag across the lanes to select something else (click to clear, double-click to go back to what you just played), then press Import Audio to put the master audio on a new Capture Audio track, or Import MIDI to put the notes on a new Capture MIDI track. Notes from several MIDI devices go on a track each, named after the device. A stretch the transport played lands at the bars where you heard it; anything else lands at the playhead. The click is never included. Notes stay in the buffer after their MIDI device is unplugged.

Settings > General, under Engine, has the same switch (Keep what you play, so it can be captured afterwards) and two lengths:

  • Capture Buffer — how much is kept: 5 minutes by default, up to 4 hours. The first minute is held in memory and anything longer in a file on disk; the setting shows the size each length takes.
  • Capture Length — caps what is selected for you, 8 bars by default.

The file goes in the folder set under Capture History in Settings > Paths, in a MAGDA Capture subfolder; by default that is the system's temporary folder. Point it at a drive with room for long buffers. If the folder can't be used or is short of space, the history stays in memory, up to 30 minutes. Changing Capture Buffer or the folder starts a new history.

docs.title: Selecting a take
docs.text:
Select the recorded clip and open the Inspector. The Takes section lists the captured passes:

  • The take selector reads Take N / M — choose which take plays back.
  • Expand take lanes / Collapse take lanes toggles the stacked take view in the editor.
  • Clear Comp removes the comp and returns to a single selected take (shown only while a comp is active).

When a comp is assembled, the selector reads Comp instead of a take number.

docs.title: Comping audio
docs.text:
Expand the take lanes on an audio clip to open the Waveform Editor take view. Each take is drawn as a stacked lane labelled Take 1, Take 2, and so on, with the active take marked by an accent bar down its side.

To build a comp, swipe horizontally across a take lane over the range you want from that take. The swiped region is added to the comp and shaded in the clip colour; swipe a different range on another lane to pull that section from a different take. MAGDA renders the selected regions into a single composite clip as you go.

docs.title: Comping MIDI
docs.text:
MIDI clips comp the same way. In the Piano Roll, click Show take lanes in the editor header to reveal the folded take strip below the grid. Each take gets its own mini-roll, and all lanes share a single folded pitch axis (the union of every take's pitches) so notes line up across takes on the same beats.

  • Click a lane to bring that take to the front as the active take.
  • Swipe across a lane over a beat range to assign that range of the comp to that take.
  • Right-click a lane to clear the comp.

As with audio, the result is a single MIDI clip assembled from the chosen regions.

docs.title: Session View
docs.text: The Session View is a grid-based clip launcher for real-time performance and idea sketching. Switch to it by clicking the Session button in the footer bar.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
The Session View is organized as a grid:

  • Columns represent tracks
  • Rows represent scenes
  • Each cell is a clip slot that can hold an audio or MIDI clip

The chord track is always the first column on the left. Aux tracks sit in their own section on the right, next to the scenes column, with a small gap between them and your other tracks. They stay put while the other columns scroll.

     Track 1    Track 2    Track 3   │ SCENES
    ┌──────────┬──────────┬──────────┼──────────┐
    │ ▶ Clip A │ ▶        │ ▶ Clip D │ 1 ▶ Scene│
    ├──────────┼──────────┼──────────┼──────────┤
    │ ▶        │ ▶ Clip B │ ▶ Clip E │ 2 ▶ Scene│
    ├──────────┼──────────┼──────────┼──────────┤
    │    +     │    +     │    +     │    +     │
    ├──────────┼──────────┼──────────┼──────────┤
    │    ■     │    ■     │    ■     │ STOP ALL │
    ├──────────┼──────────┼──────────┼──────────┤
    │ meter    │ meter    │ meter    │ MASTER   │
    │ vol  pan │ vol  pan │ vol  pan │ meter    │
    │  M    S  │  M    S  │  M    S  │ vol      │
    └──────────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────┘
  • Track headers run across the top — click to select a track
  • Scene buttons in the SCENES column on the right launch every clip in their row
  • The + row below the last scene adds a scene
  • The stop row has a stop button (■) for each track, and STOP ALL stops every playing clip
  • Mini mixer strips at the bottom provide quick mixing controls, with the master's in the scenes column
  • The toggle rail runs down the left edge (see Toggle Rail)

docs.title: Clip Slots
docs.text:
Each cell in the grid is a clip slot. A slot can be empty or contain a clip.

  • Click the launch triangle (▶) at the left of a slot to trigger its clip. Clicking it again while the clip plays triggers it again.
  • Click the left edge of an empty slot to stop the clip playing on that track, or to start recording into the slot when the track is armed.
  • Click the track's stop button (■) in the stop row to stop its clip.
  • Only one clip per track plays at a time — triggering a new clip in the same column stops the previous one.
  • Double-click a clip to open it in the editor at the bottom of the window. Double-clicking an empty slot creates a MIDI clip there.
  • Right-click a slot for Create MIDI Clip, Copy, Cut, Duplicate, Paste, Delete Clip, Add Scene and Remove Scene.

A queued clip's border blinks until it starts, and a playing clip shows its progress across the slot.

Not every track takes clips. An aux track's slots stay empty, and a group track's slots launch the clips of the tracks inside it rather than holding any of their own.

While recording into a slot, the clip previews in real time — incoming MIDI notes and captured audio peaks draw in the slot as the take happens.

docs.title: Selecting Clips
docs.text:
• Click a clip's name to select it
  • Shift-click another slot to extend the selection to a rectangular range
  • Cmd-click (Ctrl-click on Windows/Linux) to toggle individual slots in or out of the selection
  • With several clips selected, Duplicate and Delete Clip in the right-click menu act on all of them

docs.title: Launch Fade
docs.text: Each session clip has an optional launch fade — a per-clip crossfade applied when the clip launches over the clip it replaces on the same track. Set its length with Launch in the Fades section of the clip's Inspector. Useful for pad and atmosphere clips where the hard cut between launches is jarring.

docs.title: Scenes
docs.text:
A scene is a horizontal row across all tracks. Launching a scene triggers all clips in that row simultaneously, which is useful for transitioning between song sections during a live performance.

  • Click the number or triangle (▶) on a scene button to launch the scene; click its name to select it
  • Click + below the last scene to add one, or right-click a slot for Add Scene and Remove Scene
  • Use STOP ALL to stop all playing clips at once

docs.title: Mini Mixer
docs.text:
At the bottom of the Session View, each track has a mini channel strip for quick mixing without leaving the clip launcher. From top to bottom:

  • Peak meter — a horizontal meter across the top of the strip
  • Volume and Pan — side by side; drag a value to change it
  • Mute and Solo
  • Record arm and Monitor — in their own row, shown with the rail's record/monitor toggle

With several tracks selected, dragging one strip's volume or pan moves every selected track by the same amount.

The master's strip sits in the scenes column, level with the track strips: the MASTER label, its peak meter and its volume.

docs.title: Toggle Rail
docs.text:
The rail along the left edge of the Session View shows or hides parts of the view, the same way the Mixer View does:

  • Show sends — the sends section above the mixer strips. Drag the handle above it to make it taller or shorter.
  • Narrow / Medium / Wide track width — set every channel to that width. Right-click any of the three to edit the widths.
  • Show I/O routing — the input and output selectors
  • Show record/monitor row — the record arm and monitor row in each strip

Right-click the sends or I/O area for the same choices in a menu: Show I/O, Show Sends and Show Record/Monitor.

docs.title: Drag and Drop
docs.text:
• Drag audio files from the Media Explorer onto a clip slot to import them
  • Drag plugins onto a track to add effects

docs.title: Multi-Sample Drag and Drop
docs.text:
Select multiple samples in the Media Explorer (Shift-click to extend, Cmd-click / Ctrl-click to toggle) and drag them into the grid:

  • Drop on empty area — one new track is created per sample, with each clip placed in a separate scene row so the samples stack vertically down the grid.
  • Drop on an existing track — clips stack down consecutive scene slots on that track, starting from the drop target.

docs.title: Adding Clips
docs.text:
• Drag and drop audio or MIDI files from the Media Explorer onto an empty clip slot
  • Double-click an empty slot, or right-click it and choose Create MIDI Clip, to make a new MIDI clip
  • Record into an empty slot on an armed track

Note

Clip launching quantize and follow-action settings are configured in the Clip Inspector.

docs.title: Stem Separation
docs.text:
Stem separation splits one audio clip into several, each carrying a different part of the sound: vocals on one track, drums on another, and so on. MAGDA does this offline on your own machine, writing real audio files into the project.

Right-click an audio clip and choose Split into Stems, then pick an engine.

docs.title: Engines
docs.text:
Three engines are available, trading quality against speed and download size.

Engine Stems Needs a download Harmonic / Percussive (HPSS) Harmonic, Percussive No Vocals / Drums / Bass / Other (Demucs) Drums, Bass, Other, Vocals Yes, 301 MB Vocals / Accompaniment (Spleeter) Vocals, Accompaniment Yes, 74 MB

HPSS is plain signal processing with no machine-learning model behind it. It separates sustained, pitched content from transient content, so it is the right tool for pulling a drum layer away from a pad or a guitar, and the wrong tool for isolating a singer. It needs no download and works in every build.

Demucs gives the best separation of the three and is the slowest. It produces the familiar four-way split.

Spleeter is quicker and lighter than Demucs, at the cost of quality, and only splits two ways: the vocal and everything else.

Intel macOS

Demucs and Spleeter run on the ONNX runtime, which is not part of the Intel macOS build. On those builds the submenu offers HPSS only.

docs.title: Downloading the models
docs.text:
Demucs and Spleeter weights are not bundled with MAGDA — they are fetched on demand.

An engine whose weights are missing shows in the menu with a trailing .... Choosing it opens Settings > AI on the Local models tab, with Stem separation chosen as the type, rather than failing. You can also go there directly at any time to install or remove either model. See Settings > AI.

Downloads come from HuggingFace, are checked against a pinned SHA-256, and land in MAGDA's application data folder under StemSeparation/models. The Local models tab shows the source repository for each one as a clickable link, and lets you remove weights you no longer want to keep on disk.

docs.title: What a split produces
docs.text:
Clicking an engine starts a two-phase operation.

Immediately, one empty audio track per stem appears directly beneath the source track, wrapped in a group named after the source file (Guitar Take 3 Stems). The track area reflects the operation as soon as you click, so you can see what is coming.

When separation finishes, a clip lands on each stem track. Each one is a duplicate of the source clip with its audio file swapped for the rendered stem, so start position, offset, loop, stretch mode, and warp markers all stay exactly where they were on the original. Take and comp data is not carried over — that belongs to the original recording, not to a stem of it.

Finally the source track is muted, so the stems do not play on top of the material they came from. Unmute it whenever you want to compare.

A loading banner reads Splitting into stems... with a live percentage while the split runs. A toast confirms completion, or reports the failure.

docs.title: Undo
docs.text:
The split lands as two undo steps: Split into Stems creates the tracks and the group, and Add Stem Clips adds the clips and mutes the source. Undoing the second restores the source track's mute state along with the clips.

If separation fails part-way, the empty tracks and group created in the first phase are removed for you.

docs.title: Where the files go
docs.text:
Stems are written as 32-bit float WAV into a stems/ folder inside the project's media directory, one subfolder per split named after the source and the engine:

<project media>/stems/Guitar Take 3 - htdemucs/
    Guitar Take 3 - Drums.wav
    Guitar Take 3 - Bass.wav
    Guitar Take 3 - Other.wav
    Guitar Take 3 - Vocals.wav

Splitting the same clip twice never overwrites an earlier result; the second run gets its own folder.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• One clip at a time. The menu item is unavailable for a multiple selection.
  • One split at a time. Engines are greyed out while another split is running.
  • The source file must be on disk. Clips whose audio has gone missing cannot be split.
  • Very long files are refused. Separation decodes the whole file into memory, and MAGDA rejects anything that would need more than about a gigabyte rather than attempting it.

Separation is CPU-intensive and runs off the audio thread, so playback keeps going while it works, but expect a Demucs pass over a full song to take a while.

docs.title: Time Bend
docs.text:
Time Bend changes when notes play by drawing a curve. The notes stay where they are written; the curve decides when each one is heard, so a part can rush ahead, drag behind, hold still or even run backwards. Grooves are time bends too, and a bend can also carry dynamics: a level per step that scales how hard each note lands.

Time Bend works on MIDI clips (in the Piano Roll, the Drum Grid Editor and the clip Inspector) and in the Arpeggiator, the Step Sequencer and the Poly Sequencer.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Picture a read head moving through the part. Without a bend it moves at a steady pace and every note plays where it is written. The curve tells the head where to be at each moment: time runs from left to right, and the position in the part runs from bottom to top.

  • Rising — the head moves forward and notes play as written.
  • Steeper — the head moves faster, so the notes it passes bunch together.
  • Flat — the head holds still and nothing plays until it moves on.
  • Falling — the head reads backwards and plays the notes it passes again.

A note plays wherever the head crosses it and keeps its written length. The straight diagonal is the part as written.

docs.title: The Editor
docs.text:
The same editor appears everywhere Time Bend does: a header row of controls over the curve.

Control What it does Power button Turns the bend on or off (tooltip Play through the bend). Drawing on the curve, picking a shape or loading a groove turns it on. While it is off the curve is dimmed and the part plays as written. TIME / DYNAMICS Switches between the curve and the dynamics. SHAPE Replaces the curve with a starting shape (see Shapes). SPAN 1 / 2 / 4 How long one pass of the curve lasts, in bars. Grid division The grid's division: 1/4, 1/8, 1/8T, 1/16, 1/16T, 1/32 or 1/64. It sets the grid lines and what points snap to. A clip starts on 1/16; a device starts on its own step length. SNAP Snaps points to the grid. On by default. GROOVE Loads a groove (see Grooves). In the header on the Step and Poly Sequencers; above the editor on a clip. AMOUNT How much of the curve you hear: 0% plays the part as written, 100% plays the full curve. Below 100% a fainter line shows the curve you actually hear. CYCLES Repeats the curve 1 to 8 times across the span.

On a narrow editor, such as a sequencer's faceplate, the header takes two rows and AMOUNT, CYCLES and DYNAMICS shorten to AMT, CYC and DYN.

Behind the curve, the dashed diagonal shows the part as written, with beat and bar lines across it and a faint row for each grid step. On a device, a playhead line moves across the curve during playback.

docs.title: Drawing the Curve
docs.text:
Gesture Effect Double-click empty space Add a point Double-click a point Delete it Drag a point Move it, together with any other selected points. The first and last points stay at the start and end of the pass. Drag the handle in the middle of a segment Bow the segment Double-click a segment's handle Straighten the segment Right-click a segment or its handle Toggle a hard corner: two straight lines meeting at a sharp apex. Drag the handle to move the apex. Drag across empty space Select the points inside the lasso Shift-click a point Add it to, or remove it from, the selection Cmd-drag (Ctrl-drag on Windows/Linux) Draw freehand Del / Backspace Delete the selected points Cmd+A (Ctrl+A) Select every point

A curve holds up to 32 points.

docs.title: Shapes
docs.text:
SHAPE replaces the curve with one of these, keeping the span, cycles and amount:

Shape What you hear Straight The part as written Rush Notes bunch toward the start of each pass Drag Notes bunch toward the end of each pass Rush, then drag Rush over the first half, drag over the second: notes bunch at both ends of the pass Hold, then catch up Silence for half the pass, then the whole part at double speed Backwards The pass plays in reverse There and back Forward at double speed, then back over the same notes

docs.title: Span and Cycles
docs.text: SPAN sets how long one pass lasts: 1, 2 or 4 bars. CYCLES divides the span into equal parts and repeats the curve in each, so in 4/4 a 1-bar span at 4 cycles bends every beat the same way.

docs.title: Dynamics
docs.text:
Click DYNAMICS (DYN on a narrow editor) to draw how hard each step lands. The view shows a bar per step of one pass: sixteenths on a clip, the device's own step on a device, up to 64 bars. Draw to add dynamics shows until you draw.

  • Drag across the bars to draw their levels. Hold Alt to set a bar to full.
  • A full bar plays notes at the velocity they were written with; a lower bar plays them softer.
  • Drawing turns the dynamics on. In this view the power button turns the dynamics on or off (tooltip Apply the dynamics), separately from the curve.
  • AMOUNT sets how much of the drawn levels you hear: at 0% every note plays as written.
  • Right-click the bars and choose Remove dynamics to delete them.

Dynamics scale each note's velocity as it plays, in MIDI clips, the Step and Poly Sequencers and the Arpeggiator. The velocities written in the clip or the steps don't change. They also work on a straight curve, so you can use dynamics without bending time at all. Because the bars cover one pass of the bend, timing and dynamics repeat together.

docs.title: Grooves
docs.text:
Grooves are time bends. Click GROOVE to open the groove library: None first, then the grooves grouped into Swing, Push Swing, Pull Swing, Push Snare, Pull Snare, Timing and Random, with any others under Custom.

Picking a groove loads its curve at full strength, replacing the bend you had (dynamics included), and AMOUNT sets how much of it you hear. None turns the bend off. Once loaded, a groove is an ordinary curve: edit it like any other. A project saved with a groove opens with that groove's curve.

docs.title: MIDI Clips
docs.text:
A MIDI clip carries its own time bend, and it is live: the notes stay where you wrote them and play where the bend puts them. You can edit it in two places:

  • Inspector — select one or more MIDI clips and open the Time Bend section. The editor grows with the Inspector's width. Edits apply to every selected MIDI clip.
  • MIDI editors — the Time Bend button in the Piano Roll or Drum Grid Editor header (tooltip Show the clip's time bend) opens the editor in a panel on the right of the editor. Drag the panel's edge to resize it. The button lights while the clip has a bend in force.

Each gesture on the curve is one undo step.

Above the editor sit GROOVE (see Grooves) and BAKE. BAKE writes what the bend plays into the notes and turns the bend off: each note moves to where it plays, a note the head crosses twice is written twice, and a note it never reaches is removed. It is available while a timing bend is in force and writes the timing only; dynamics stay as they are. Ctrl+Z undoes it.

docs.title: Piano Roll
docs.text: In the Piano Roll, the written notes are dimmed while a bend is in force, and each note is also drawn where it plays. The drawing follows the curve as you drag it.

docs.title: Drum Grid Editor
docs.text: The Drum Grid Editor works the same way: open the panel with its Time Bend button, and the hits show where they play.

docs.title: Arpeggiator
docs.text:
The Arpeggiator's faceplate is its time bend, under TIME BEND. The bend reshapes when each note of the arpeggio plays: the notes keep their order, but the rhythm changes.

Its amount and cycles are the Bend and Cycles parameters among the device's controls rather than in the editor's header, so they can be automated and linked to Macros and modulators like any other parameter. Beside the curve, Quantize pulls bent notes back toward a grid, and Subdivision sets how many divisions of the bend's cycle that grid has.

The Arpeggiator has no GROOVE button.

docs.title: Step Sequencer
docs.text:
The Step Sequencer and the Poly Sequencer show their time bend in a column beside the steps. The time bend toggle on the device slot (tooltip Show the time bend) shows or hides it, and the choice is saved with the device.

The bend redistributes when the steps fire within each pass. AMOUNT and CYCLES in its header are the device's bend parameters, so they can be automated and linked to Macros and modulators. The grid starts on the sequencer's step length.

On the Arpeggiator and both sequencers, the expand button in the editor's header (tooltip Expand into the arrangement) lends the editor to the Arrangement View for more room. Click the collapse button or press Esc to put it back.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Swing — load a groove from the Swing family, then lower AMOUNT for a lighter swing.
  • Rushing or laying back — pick Rush or Drag, then bring AMOUNT down until it feels right.
  • Stutters and repeats — a falling segment plays notes again. Start from There and back and shorten the falling part.
  • Cross-rhythms — set CYCLES to 3 over a 1-bar span in 4/4 to repeat the shape three times a bar.
  • Accents without moving anything — leave the curve straight and draw dynamics: higher bars on the beats, lower ones between.

docs.title: Tracks
docs.text: Tracks are the fundamental building blocks in MAGDA. They appear in all three views — as columns in Session View, rows in Arrangement View, and channel strips in Mixer View.

docs.title: Hybrid Track System
docs.text: MAGDA uses a hybrid track system: there is no strict distinction between audio and MIDI tracks. Any track can contain any combination of audio clips, MIDI clips, and other clip types. The track's behavior adapts based on the clips and devices it contains.

docs.title: Track Types
docs.text:
Type Description Audio The regular track. It holds audio and MIDI clips, instruments, effects and live input, and can send MIDI out to hardware or to another track Group Bus that sums the child tracks inside it (see Grouping Tracks). It holds no clips Aux Send-return track for shared effects, fed by other tracks' sends. It holds no clips Chord Guide track holding a chord progression — one per project (see Chord Track) Separator A divider in the track list, with an optional name (see Separators) Output One stereo output of a multi-output instrument, created from the device (see Multi-Output Plugins) Master Final stereo output — one per project

The chord track sits at the top of the Arrangement View and at the far left of Session View and the Mixer. Aux tracks sit in their own section above the master in the Arrangement View, and on the right beside the master in Session View and the Mixer.

docs.title: Track Controls
docs.text:
Every track provides the following controls. They render identically in the track header and the track Inspector, and reflow responsively to the width available rather than to fixed height presets, so no control is ever hidden.

  • Volume fader — Adjust the track's output level
  • Pan knob — Position in the stereo field
  • Mute (M) — Silence the track. Shortcut: select the track and press M
  • Solo (S) — Solo the track. Shortcut: select the track and press Shift+S
  • Record arm (R) — Arm the track for recording
  • Input monitor — Monitor the live input signal through the track (see Input Monitoring)
  • Automation — Toggle automation read/write for the track
  • Sends - Level to each aux / return the track feeds
  • Routing - Input and output routing for the track (see Track-to-Track Routing)
  • Meter - Peak level meter for the track

The Automation button lights purple when the track holds automation.

Tracks that don't take input show fewer controls. An aux track has no record arm, input monitor, routing or sends; the chord track has only its volume and its chord preview; a separator has none.

docs.title: Input Monitoring
docs.text:
The input monitor button has three modes:

Mode Colour Behavior Off Grey The live input is not monitored In Green The live input is always monitored, whether or not the track is record armed Auto Blue The live input is monitored only while the track is record armed

Click the button to cycle Off → In → Auto, or right-click it to pick a mode from a menu.

To play an instrument without arming its track, for example to practise before recording, set its monitor to In.

With Auto-monitor selected track enabled (Settings > General, under Behavior), selecting a track sets its monitor to Auto and turns the previously selected track's monitor Off. This overrides a mode you set by hand. The option is off by default.

docs.title: Multi-Output Plugins
docs.text:
When an instrument plugin has more than two output channels (e.g. Kontakt, Battery, Drum Machine Designer), MAGDA can create separate output tracks for each stereo pair.

  • Open the multi-out menu on the device (the button) and activate the output pairs you need
  • Each activated pair creates an independent track placed directly after the instrument track
  • Output tracks behave like any other track — you can rename, reorder, route to groups, and apply FX
  • An output track's lane takes MIDI clips only, and they play the parent instrument
  • To organize them, select the output tracks and move them into a Group using the right-click menu

Note

Multi-out tracks receive audio from the parent instrument's rack — their input routing is fixed. Output routing (to master, groups, or aux sends) works normally.

docs.title: Track-to-Track Routing
docs.text:
A track can take another track's output as its own input. Every other track appears in the audio-input and MIDI-input selectors, listed after a separator alongside the hardware inputs, in the Inspector, the track headers, the Mixer, and Session View.

From the source side, MIDI Out can name another track instead of a hardware port. Each track has one MIDI Out, but any number of tracks can send to the same track, which still takes its own MIDI input as well.

docs.title: MIDI channels
docs.text:
In the Inspector's routing section, the input and output icons beside the selectors open each track's MIDI channel menu. Once a channel is set, the icon lights up and shows its number.

  • Input passes only one channel (1–16) of what the track hears from its MIDI devices, for both monitoring and recording. Any passes them all.
  • Output moves everything the track's MIDI Out sends, to a port or to another track, onto one channel. As is leaves channels alone. A chosen channel puts all of an MPE clip's notes on that one channel.

Together these drive a multitimbral instrument: give each part its own track, set each track's MIDI Out to the instrument's track and its output channel to the part's channel. A hardware synth works the same way, with each track's MIDI Out on the synth's port.

Self-routing and feedback loops are detected and blocked. Routings are saved with the project, and input monitoring works normally for an internally-routed track.

docs.title: Track View Manager
docs.text:
Each of the three views — Session, Arrangement, and Mixer — maintains its own independent track visibility and layout. This means you can show a different set of tracks in each view.

Open the Track Manager from the View menu to configure track visibility per view. Each column (Live, Arrange, Mix) has independent checkboxes — toggle them to control which tracks appear in each view.

Per-view track settings include:

  • Visible — Whether the track appears in this view
  • Locked — Prevent editing the track in this view
  • Collapsed — For group tracks: collapse or expand children
  • Height — Track row height (Arrangement View)

docs.title: Example: Multi-Output Workflow
docs.text:
A common use case is keeping the Arrangement View clean while having full control in the Mixer. With a multi-output instrument like Addictive Drums, you can hide the individual output tracks from the Arrangement and show only the MIDI track you compose on:

Arrangement View — Only the group and the instrument's MIDI track are visible, keeping the timeline uncluttered:

Mixer View — All output tracks are visible for independent level, pan, and effects control per drum voice:

docs.title: Adding and Managing Tracks
docs.text:
• Press Ctrl+T (Cmd+T on macOS) to add an audio track after the selected one, or Ctrl+Shift+T (Cmd+Shift+T) to add a group track
  • Click the + button in the Arrangement View's corner, or right-click the empty area below the tracks, for the add-track menu: Add Audio Track, Add Group Track, Add Aux Track, Add Chord Track and Add Separator. Add Chord Track is greyed out once the project has one. The Track menu offers the same items
  • Right-click a track header for options: add a track, grouping, sends, freeze, enable or disable, duplicate, delete
  • Double-click the track name to rename it

docs.title: Multi-Track Selection
docs.text: Click a track header to select it. Hold Shift and click another header to extend the selection to a contiguous range; Cmd-click (Ctrl-click on Windows/Linux) to toggle individual tracks in or out of the selection. Most track-level actions — mute, solo, delete, group — apply to every selected track in one operation. Freeze applies to the track you right-clicked.

docs.title: Disabling a Track
docs.text:
Right-click a track header and choose Disable Track, or use the power switch in the track inspector. A disabled track renders nothing. Its clips, devices, sends and output all fall silent, and anything routed into it stops there. This applies to exports and bounces too. Its header dims and reads Disabled. Choose Enable Track to bring it back.

A track is also disabled when its chain holds a MAGDA device this copy of MAGDA does not have, for example one from an extension that is not installed, or one from a newer version. Rather than play the chain without it, the track stays silent. Its header names the missing device, and the device's slot reads Not in this build. The track can't be enabled until the device is removed or replaced. Until then the device keeps its settings and saves them unchanged, so the project opens as it was in a copy of MAGDA that has it.

docs.title: Separators
docs.text:
A separator divides up the track list. It has no header, controls, signal or clips: it is a thin row across the arrangement and a vertical line in the Session View and the Mixer.

Choose Track → Add Separator to add one after the selected track, or choose Add Separator from the add-track menu, then drag it where you want it in the arrangement or the Session View. A separator starts without a name. Double-click it, or right-click it and choose Rename Separator..., to give it one.

With Add a separator after a new chord track on (Settings > General, under Behavior; on by default), adding a chord track also adds a separator after it. Drag its edge to make it a little taller or wider. Separators don't take a position on control surfaces, and they aren't exported to DAWproject files.

docs.title: Grouping Tracks
docs.text:
Group tracks collect several tracks under a single bus so you can fold them away and control them together. Right-click a track header for the grouping actions:

  • Group tracks — with two or more tracks selected, collects them into a new group track.
  • Ungroup tracks — on a group track, dissolves it and promotes its children back to the top level.
  • Remove from Group — moves a track out of its group, back to the top level.
  • Move to Group — a submenu listing the existing group tracks; pick one to move the track into it.

Collapse or expand a group's children from the Track Manager or the group header. The chord track and separators can't join a group.

docs.title: Duplicating Tracks
docs.text:
MAGDA offers three duplication modes, available from the Track menu, the track header right-click menu, and via keyboard:

Mode Shortcut Copies clips Copies FX chain Duplicate Track Ctrl+D / Cmd+D yes yes Duplicate Track Without Content Ctrl+Shift+D / Cmd+Shift+D no yes Duplicate Track Content Only Ctrl+Alt+D / Cmd+Alt+D yes no

Duplicate Track Content Only is useful when you want the clips on a clean signal path — the new track has the same structure and name, but its FX chain is empty.

docs.title: Freezing Tracks
docs.text:
Freezing renders a track to an audio file and plays the file in its place, so the track's instruments and effects stop costing CPU. Right-click the track header and choose Freeze Track; a progress window shows while it renders. Choose Unfreeze Track to go back to the live chain.

  • The file holds the track's signal up to its fader, together with every track routed into it, from the start of the project to the last clip plus the tail its devices declare.
  • Devices after the fader keep running live.
  • Tracks routed into the frozen track stop playing on their own, since the file already holds them, and their devices show greyed out.
  • A frozen track's header dims, with a cyan strip on its outer edge, and its clips can't be edited until you unfreeze it.
  • Only audio tracks can be frozen. A disabled track can't be, and neither can a track that outputs into another track: freeze the track it feeds instead.
  • The file is kept in the project's renders folder, under freeze.

docs.title: Unloading plugins on freeze
docs.text:
With Unload plugins when freezing, to free their memory on (Settings > General, under Engine; on by default), freezing also closes the plugins whose sound the file now holds: those before the fader and those on tracks routed into the frozen track. Unfreeze Track loads them again with their settings. A large sampler takes as long to come back as it takes to open, and an instrument stays silent until it has loaded. Devices after the fader stay loaded.

With the option off, the plugins stay loaded until the project closes. Either way, a project reopened with a frozen track doesn't load that track's plugins until you unfreeze it.

docs.title: FX Chain
docs.text:
Each track has an FX chain — an ordered list of audio processors applied to the track's signal. See FX Chain & Racks for full details.

An ARA plugin such as Melodyne inserted on a track takes over that track's audio clips and plays them live. See ARA Plugins.

docs.title: Clips
docs.text: Tracks contain clips — audio and MIDI data blocks arranged on the timeline. Group, aux and separator tracks take no clips. See Clips for details on editing, splitting, duplicating, and rendering clips.

docs.title: Transport
docs.text: The transport bar sits at the top of the window and is available in all views. It is a single row, with each group of controls in its own well.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
From left to right:

Group Contents Transport buttons Home, Previous, Next, Play, Stop, Record, Automation, Loop, Back to Arrangement Punch Punch In and Punch Out Tempo The Ableton Link chip, the tempo, the count-in, the time signature and the metronome Playhead The playhead position in bars, beats and ticks, with the same position as a clock beside it SEL The time selection, start → end LOOP The loop region, start → end Grid Grid division, AUTO and SNAP MEM The capture switch, meter and button (see Capturing what you just heard) QWERTY keyboard Plays notes from the computer keyboard CPU The audio engine's load

Hover the CPU readout for the audio device, sample rate, buffer size, peak load and dropouts (Xruns).

docs.title: Narrow Windows
docs.text: When the window is too narrow for everything, the transport makes room in steps: the MEM meter shrinks to its dot and capture button, the clock beside the playhead goes, the Link chip shrinks to its LED, and SEL and LOOP show only their starts (hover a start to see the end). After that, whole groups leave the bar. A menu button appears at the right end, and the controls that left are in its menu: the QWERTY keyboard (Virtual MIDI Keyboard), Recent Capture and the CPU load, then Loop and Back to Arrangement, Punch In, Punch Out and Punch Range..., Auto Grid and Snap, and Go Home, Previous and Next.

docs.title: Navigation & Playback
docs.text:
Button Action Shortcut Home Return to the start Previous Return to the start Next Jump to the end Play Start/stop playback Space Stop Stop playback and disarm automation writing Record Start/stop recording Automation Arm automation writing; right-click to choose the mode (see Automation Modes) Loop Toggle loop playback Back to Arrangement Return from session clip playback to the arrangement position

To jump between markers, use Transport > Previous Marker (Cmd+Alt+Left) and Transport > Next Marker (Cmd+Alt+Right); on Windows and Linux, use Ctrl+Alt with the arrows.

Hovering a transport button shows its name and shortcut in the footer's info line.

docs.title: Loop
docs.text:
Enable looping with the Loop button. The LOOP readout shows the loop's start and end in bars, beats and ticks, in green while looping is on. Editing either value turns looping on.

  • Set loop from a time selection — Make a time selection in the arrangement and press L to set the loop region to match it. With no time selection, L sets the loop to the selected clip.
  • Set loop from a clip — Select the clip and press Ctrl+Shift+L (Cmd+Shift+L)
  • Go to the loop's start or end — Press [ or ]. Shift with the same keys goes to the time selection's start or end.

docs.title: Punch In/Out
docs.text:
Use punch in and punch out to record only within a specific time range. Punch In and Punch Out are two toggles. Right-click either one to set the punch range's start and end, or use Punch Range... in the menu when the window is narrow.

You can also right-click the timeline ruler and choose Set Punch In Here or Set Punch Out Here.

docs.title: Position Displays
docs.text:
The transport shows editable displays for:

  • Playhead position — Current playback time in bars, beats and ticks. The clock beside it shows the same position in minutes and seconds.
  • SEL — Start and end of the current time selection
  • LOOP — Start and end of the loop region

docs.title: Tempo
docs.text:
The tempo (BPM) is displayed in the transport bar. You can change it by:

  • Dragging the tempo value up or down
  • Double-clicking it and typing a new value

docs.title: Time Signature
docs.text:
The time signature sits to the right of the tempo. You can change it by:

  • Dragging the numerator or denominator up or down
  • Alt-clicking a value and typing a new number

Double-click a value to reset it to 4.

docs.title: Metronome & Count-In
docs.text:
The metronome (click track) is the icon after the time signature. Click it, or press C, to turn it on or off.

The small circle between the tempo and the time signature sets the count-in (pre-roll) before recording starts. Click it to open the count-in menu:

Option Description Off Recording starts immediately 1 Beat One beat of click before recording 2 Beats Two beats of click before recording 1 Bar One full bar of click before recording 2 Bars Two full bars of click before recording

Once a count-in is set the circle lights up, and it stays dim while count-in is off. Hovering it shows the current setting.

During count-in, the metronome plays but recording does not begin until the count-in period is complete.

docs.title: Ableton Link
docs.text:
The Link chip at the start of the tempo group switches Ableton Link on and off. With Link on, MAGDA plays in time with the other apps on your network that have Link switched on: every app shares one tempo, and tempo automation is ignored.

  • The chip lights while Link is on, and its LED flashes on each beat of the session, brighter on the downbeat.
  • Play waits until the session reaches the same point in the bar as your start position, never more than a bar. While it waits, the chip's LED and the Play button blink. Clips launched from stopped in the Session View wait for the same downbeat.
  • The footer shows Ableton Link · N, where N is the number of other apps in the session. Its dot turns green once one joins. Click it to open Link's settings in Settings > Connections.

Start Stop Sync and the output latency offset are set in Settings > Connections > Ableton Link (see Ableton Link settings).

docs.title: MIDI Clock
docs.text:
MAGDA can drive hardware with MIDI clock, or follow a clock from another device. Both are set in Settings > Connections > MIDI Clock (see MIDI Clock settings).

  • Send clock to — Tick each MIDI output that should receive clock. While the transport plays, MAGDA sends 24 clocks per beat, with Start, Continue, Stop and Song Position as playback starts, stops, loops and jumps. Clock leaves when the audio it belongs to is heard, so external gear lines up with what comes out of the speakers. A device joins on the next sixteenth note after a start or a jump, since Song Position counts in sixteenths.
  • Follow clock from — Pick the MIDI input whose clock MAGDA follows. The project tempo follows the incoming clock, and Start, Stop, Continue and Song Position start, stop and move the transport. Playback stays locked to the clock's beat as it plays.

Only one sync source is followed at a time: choosing a clock input switches Ableton Link off, and switching Ableton Link on stops following the clock. While a clock is followed, tempo automation is ignored, as it is under Link. Sending clock works with either.

docs.title: Capture (MEM)
docs.text: MEM keeps what you play, so you can capture it after the fact. Click MEM's dot or caption to turn capture on or off, and click the capture button beside the meter (Cmd+Shift+C) to open the capture panel. See Capturing what you just heard.

docs.title: QWERTY MIDI Keyboard
docs.text: A small keyboard-icon toggle on the right side of the transport enables the computer-keyboard MIDI input. When on, typing on the QWERTY keyboard sends MIDI notes to the currently selected instrument track. Right-click the toggle to see the key layout.

docs.title: Key layout
docs.text:
Two rows of keys cover just over an octave. The lower row maps to the natural notes of the current base octave, the upper row extends one octave above.

Row White keys (naturals) Black keys (sharps) Lower (base octave) A S D F G H J → C D E F G A B W E _ T Y U → C♯ D♯ F♯ G♯ A♯ Upper (base +1) K L → C D O P → C♯ D♯

Octave shift:

  • Z — move the base octave down one
  • X — move the base octave up one

The base octave defaults to 3, so A plays C3. Range is clamped to 0–8.

Modifier combinations (⌘, ⌃, ⌥) and the spacebar always pass through to regular shortcuts, so transport control and edit shortcuts keep working while the keyboard is on.

On a narrow window the toggle moves into the transport's menu as Virtual MIDI Keyboard.

docs.title: Grid & Snap
docs.text:
The grid controls how clips and edits snap to musical divisions. The grid group in the transport bar has three parts:

  • Grid division — Click the division button (tooltip Grid division) to pick a fixed resolution from the menu:

    Section Divisions Straight 1/1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32 Triplet 1/4T, 1/8T, 1/16T, 1/32T Dotted 1/2., 1/4., 1/8., 1/16., 1/32.

    Custom... at the bottom opens a numerator/denominator editor that shows the nearest named division as you type.

  • AUTO — When on, the grid resolution follows the current horizontal zoom: it picks a finer division as you zoom in and switches to whole bars when you zoom far out. The division button is dimmed while AUTO is active.

  • SNAP — Enable or disable snapping to the grid.

The same picker is used by the bottom-panel editors (Piano Roll, Drum Grid Editor, and the automation-clip editor), each with its own AUTO button.

docs.title: AI in MAGDA: Philosophy and Expectations
docs.text:
MAGDA's automation features are not exclusively about music generation.

In fact, pure musical content generation is almost a side effect of a much broader goal: helping users automate repetitive tasks and interact with the DAW more naturally.

Examples include:

  • Creating tracks.
  • Selecting clips.
  • Manipulating arrangements.
  • Building chord progressions from explicit instructions.
  • Generating scales, melodies or rhythms.
  • Assisting with workflow and experimentation.

docs.title: Different Levels of Automation
docs.text: Not all requests are content generation.

docs.title: Functional requests
docs.text:
These describe exactly what you want.

Examples:

  • Create a new MIDI track.
  • Create a drum track and insert a step sequencer.
  • Generate the progression Cmin, Amaj, Bdim.
  • Create a 16-bar drum pattern using the selected kit.

In these cases, the AI is primarily acting as an assistant or automation layer.

docs.title: Creative requests
docs.text:
These leave part of the decision-making to the model.

Examples:

  • Generate a jazzy chord progression.
  • Create an uplifting melody in C major.
  • Suggest a bassline that complements the selected chords.

In these cases, the AI contributes musical ideas rather than simply executing instructions.

docs.title: What Should I Expect?
docs.text:
The quality of AI-generated results depends heavily on:

  • The selected model.
  • Whether the model is local or cloud-based.
  • The quality of the prompt.
  • The capabilities of your hardware.

A small local model running on your machine will generally produce lower-quality results than large commercial models today, though the gap is narrowing as local inference improves (see Local Models vs Cloud Models below).

The trade-off is privacy, cost, and control.

docs.title: AI Is a Starting Point, Not a Replacement
docs.text:
The purpose of content generation in MAGDA is to provide a foundation for further work.

The generated material is intended to be:

  • Edited.
  • Rearranged.
  • Reinterpreted.
  • Combined with your own ideas.

This is particularly useful for:

  • Exploring chord progressions you may not have considered.
  • Generating variations.
  • Discovering happy accidents.
  • Using step sequencers as intelligent random generators.

Think of the AI as a collaborator, not as a finished-product generator.

docs.title: Prompting Tips
docs.text:
Instead of:

"Write a melody in C."

Try:

"Generate an uplifting 8-bar melody in C major suitable for liquid drum and bass. Include rhythmic variation and a memorable motif."

The more context you provide, the better the results are likely to be.

Good prompts often include:

  • Genre.
  • Mood.
  • Musical references.
  • Desired complexity.
  • Instrumentation.
  • Structure.

docs.title: Local Models vs Cloud Models
docs.text:
MAGDA supports both cloud AI providers and local AI models. They sit at different points on a quality, privacy and cost trade-off rather than one simply being better than the other.

Cloud providers generally offer the highest-quality results today, but require an account and API credentials, send your prompts to a third party, and bill per use.

Local models run entirely on your machine. There are no API keys, nothing leaves your computer, and there is no per-request cost. MAGDA provides a small default GGUF model fine-tuned specifically for its DSL (downloadable under Settings > AI > Local models), and you can also point MAGDA at any GGUF model or a local OpenAI-compatible server such as LM Studio, Ollama, GPUStack or a llama.cpp server. See AI for configuration.

Local results vary with the model you choose and the hardware you run it on. Smaller quantised models are fast and light but less capable; larger models close the gap with cloud at the cost of more memory and slower responses.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Running a language model locally is demanding, and your hardware sets a hard ceiling on what is realistic. Be honest with yourself about your machine before expecting cloud-level results from it.

  • Memory. Treat 16 GB of RAM as the practical minimum for local inference. 32 GB or 64 GB is what you want to run larger, more capable models comfortably and to keep the rest of your DAW session responsive while a model is loaded. Below 16 GB you may only be able to run the smallest, most heavily quantised models, with correspondingly limited results.
  • CPU instruction set. On Windows and Linux, MAGDA's embedded local model uses the best instruction set your processor supports (AVX2, AVX-512 and so on), chosen when the model loads, so a newer CPU runs it faster. On an Intel Mac it uses SSE 4.2 and AVX. None of this affects cloud providers or local-server mode.
  • GPU. Local inference is far more responsive with GPU acceleration: Metal on macOS, and Vulkan on Windows and Linux when a Vulkan driver is installed. An Apple Silicon Mac or a dedicated GPU with plenty of VRAM makes a large difference. Without a GPU it runs on the CPU, just slowly.
  • Larger general-purpose models need correspondingly more RAM (when running on CPU) or VRAM (when offloaded to a GPU). A bigger model on an underpowered machine will be slow, or simply fail to load.
  • If responses are slow or a model fails to load, choose a smaller or more heavily quantised model, switch GPU layers to Custom with a lower count, or reduce the Context length under Settings > AI > Local models, with Type set to Local LLM.

If your machine does not meet these specs, do not expect usable local AI from it. Use a cloud provider instead: it will give far better results than a local model struggling on limited hardware.

docs.title: Local inference is improving
docs.text: Local inference in MAGDA is an area of active development. The fine-tuned model is updated over time, and the distance between local and cloud quality continues to narrow as both the models and the surrounding tooling improve. Choosing local today is a deliberate trade for privacy, cost and control, not a dead end.

docs.title: What You Should Not Expect
docs.text:
Do not expect the AI to create a smash hit for you.

That is not the goal of MAGDA's automation features and it is unlikely to ever be.

The most successful workflows are usually those where the user provides direction, evaluates the results, and iterates.

The AI can generate ideas.

The creative decisions remain yours.

docs.title: Analysis (Oscilloscope, Spectrum & Levels)
docs.text:
MAGDA ships three real-time analysis devices: an Oscilloscope, a Spectrum Analyzer, and a Levels meter. They tap the signal passing through them and draw it; they do not change the audio. Drag any of them from the Plugin Browser onto any track's FX chain, or add them to the post-FX area of a track or the master.

The Oscilloscope and Spectrum Analyzer also appear as compact mini analyzers on the mixer strips, and can be popped out into their own always-on-top windows from the open-in-window button in the device header.

In the device chain, the Oscilloscope's and Spectrum Analyzer's plots take the whole body. Click the settings gear in the device header to fade their control row in over the foot of the plot, and again to hide it. The pop-out windows keep the row in view.

docs.title: Oscilloscope
docs.text:
The Oscilloscope draws the waveform in the time domain. It locks onto a rising edge, placed between samples, so a steady tone holds still even with noise on it, down to 20 Hz. Busy material such as a drum mix scrolls along with the audio instead of holding and then jumping. Zoomed in, the trace is a smooth curve through the samples; zoomed out, it is a filled min/max envelope.

Control What it does Time How much time the display spans, from 1 ms to 5 s. Drag the value or type one (250 ms, 1.2 s). Shorter shows individual cycles; longer shows the overall envelope. Color Five dots: Green, Blue, Yellow, Red and Purple. Click one to pick the trace colour; the current one is ringed, and hovering a dot names it. The choice is saved with the device.

Reference lines at 0, -3, -6 and -12 dBFS mark the amplitude scale so you can read level at a glance.

docs.title: Spectrum Analyzer
docs.text:
The Spectrum Analyzer draws the frequency content of the signal. It runs a windowed FFT on overlapping frames, averages them, and plots magnitude against a logarithmic frequency axis. Each pixel column shows the loudest frequency it covers, and where the analysis is coarser than the screen, as in the low end, a smooth curve runs between its points. A tone reads at its true level wherever it falls.

Control What it does FFT 2k, 4k or 8k: the resolution of the analysis. Larger gives finer frequency detail, most useful in the low end, at the cost of a slower response. Slope dB/oct 0, 3, 4.5 or 6: tilts the display by that many dB per octave, so a natural spectrum reads flatter and high-frequency detail is easier to see. Time Slow, Med or Fast: how quickly the curve reacts. Slower is steadier, faster is more responsive. Color Five dots, as on the Oscilloscope.

A peak-hold line sits on top of the live curve, marking the highest level reached in each band. The frequency axis runs across the audible range with a dB magnitude scale down the side.

Hover over the plot for a readout of the frequency under the pointer, the nearest note with its offset in cents (440 Hz reads A3 +0c), and the level there.

docs.title: Track Overlay & Masking
docs.text:
The Overlay picker, in the device header (and at the top of the pop-out window), overlays another track's spectrum on the display as a neutral grey trace, so you can see how two tracks share the frequency range. When an overlay is active, MAGDA also runs its masking detector between the two tracks: frequency ranges where they fight for the same space are shaded in a warm tint behind the curves, with the shading intensity following the severity of the clash. Pick No overlay to remove it.

The same collision data appears in the mixer's mix analysis findings.

docs.title: Levels
docs.text:
The Levels meter gives broadcast-grade numbers for the signal at its insert point — drop it on the master for the mix, or on any track. Its readings sit in three columns, LOUDNESS, PEAK / DYNAMICS and STEREO:

Reading What it tells you Integrated, Short-term, Momentary Loudness in LUFS (BS.1770) — the perceived level streaming services normalise to. True peak Inter-sample peak, caught by oversampling — what a converter actually hits. PLR Peak-to-loudness ratio — how dynamic the signal is. PSR Peak-to-short-term ratio — how squashed the loudest moments are. Correlation Stereo phase relationship — negative values warn of mono-compatibility problems. Width Stereo width, from mono to fully wide.

The device is a transparent pass-through, and only spends CPU on measurement while its meter is actually visible. Reopening it resets the integrated readings, and RESET restarts integrated loudness, peak hold and PLR at any time.

Note

The analyzers refresh continuously and add no latency or gain to the signal, so you can leave them inserted anywhere in a chain. In the post-FX area, only one of each analysis device can exist per track, and an analyzer there has no power button or preset box, since it never changes the signal.

docs.title: Arpeggiator
docs.text: The Arpeggiator is a MIDI device that takes held chords and plays them back as a rhythmic pattern — one note at a time, in a chosen order and rate.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Arpeggiator sits on a track's device chain before an instrument. It intercepts incoming MIDI chords and outputs arpeggiated note sequences. Hold a chord on your keyboard and the arpeggiator cycles through its notes at the configured rate and pattern.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: The parameters sit in the device's grid; the sidebar's Show the parameters toggle hides or shows them.

docs.title: Pattern & Timing
docs.text: Parameter Range Description Pattern Up, Down, Up/Down, Down/Up, Random, As Played Note order within each cycle Rate 1/4D to 1/32, with dotted (D) and triplet (T) values Speed of the arpeggio steps Octaves 1–4 How many octaves the pattern spans before repeating Gate 1–100% Note length as a percentage of the step duration. Lower values produce staccato; higher values produce legato. Swing 0–100% Delays every other step for a shuffle feel Latch Off / On When on, the arpeggio continues playing after you release the keys

docs.title: Velocity
docs.text: Parameter Range Description Vel mode Original, Fixed, Accent How output velocity is determined. Original uses the played velocity; Fixed uses the Fixed vel value; Accent plays every fourth step harder than the rest. Fixed vel 1–127 Velocity used when Vel mode is Fixed. It is dimmed in the other modes.

docs.title: Time Bend
docs.text:
The Arpeggiator's faceplate is its Time Bend panel, shown or hidden with the Show the time bend toggle in the device's sidebar. It reshapes when each arpeggiated note plays within the cycle: instead of evenly spaced steps, notes can accelerate, decelerate, or cluster. Notes still play in the same order; only the rhythm changes.

The panel holds the time bend's read-head curve. Drag its points and bend its segments, right-click a point for a hard corner, or start from a SHAPE. The TIME | DYNAMICS switch draws a level per step instead, which scales each note's velocity as it plays; the arpeggiator's own velocities are left as they are. See Time Bend for the editor itself.

Parameter Range Description Bend 0–100% How much of the time bend is heard (in the parameter grid) Cycles 1–8 Repeats the curve within each arpeggio cycle (in the parameter grid) Quantize 0–100% Pulls the bent notes back toward the Subdivision grid (beside the curve) Subdivision 16–512 Divisions of the bend's cycle that Quantize pulls toward (beside the curve)

The expand button in the panel's header moves the time bend into the arrangement, where it has room to be edited in detail. Its collapse button, or Esc, puts it back.

Bend and Cycles can be linked to Macros for automatable timing modulation — morph from straight to bent patterns in real time.

docs.title: MIDI pass-through
docs.text:
The Arpeggiator replaces the notes you play with its own pattern, and passes everything else on the channel to the instrument behind it — mod wheel, expression, sustain, pitch bend, aftertouch and program change all reach the synth unchanged. Sustain still holds the arpeggiated notes, and the wheel still bends them.

Turn on MIDI thru in the device header only when you want the chord itself to play alongside the pattern: thru passes the raw input on, notes included.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
1. Place the Arpeggiator before an instrument on a track's device chain
  2. Play or input a chord — the arpeggiator breaks it into individual notes
  3. Adjust Pattern, Rate, and Gate to shape the basic rhythm
  4. Use the time bend to add rhythmic variation beyond simple swing
  5. Enable Latch to keep the arpeggio running while you change chords

docs.title: Built-in Devices
docs.text: MAGDA ships with its own native MIDI devices, instruments, and effects. All built-in devices are managed through the same rack wrapper layer that hosts third-party plugins, so macros, modulators, and presets behave identically across the device set.

docs.title: MIDI Devices
docs.text: Device Description Arpeggiator MIDI arpeggiator with pattern, swing, and time bend. See Arpeggiator. Chord Engine Real-time chord detection, suggestion, and AI progression generator. See Chord Engine. Step Sequencer Monophonic step sequencer, up to 32 steps, with time bend and AI pattern generation. See Step Sequencer. Poly Sequencer Polyphonic step sequencer with up to eight notes per step and a keys or drum-lane grid. See Poly Sequencer. Strum Turns a held chord into a strum, roll or arpeggio shaped by a curve, for any instrument. See Strum.

docs.title: Instruments
docs.text: Device Description Poly Synth 16-voice subtractive synth: four oscillators with unison, and two filters in series or parallel. See Poly Synth. FM0 Four-operator FM synth with a modulation matrix and a filter that can sit inside it. See FM0. Drum Kit Five synthetic drum voices: Kick, Snare, Hat, Tom, Clap. See Drum Kit. Physical Models Struck Marimba, Djembe, and Bell physical models. See Physical Models. Materia / Halo / Nimbus Ports of Mutable Instruments Elements, Rings, and Clouds. See Mutable Ports. Drum Grid Pad-based drum instrument: each pad has its own device chain and its own mixer channel. See Drum Grid. Sampler 8-voice sample player with zones, a pitch envelope and a filter per voice; imports SFZ, DecentSampler and SoundFont instruments. See Sampler. Faust Instrument 16-voice synth that plays a Faust DSP you write and compile at runtime. See Faust Instrument.
