docs.title: Effects
docs.text: The MAGDA FX bank is a set of native effects compiled from Faust DSP and shipped with every MAGDA installation. See Effects for the full list, grouped by category. The bank is joined by native devices that are not compiled from Faust, among them Convolution, a convolution reverb that plays the signal through an impulse response you load, Spectral FX, four FFT effects over a scrolling spectrogram, and Sidechain, a MIDI-triggered volume shaper keyed from another track.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text: Real-time analyzers — an Oscilloscope, a Spectrum Analyzer and a Levels loudness meter — that tap the signal without changing it, on the FX chain or in the post-FX area. See Analysis.

docs.title: External Plugins
docs.text:
In addition to built-in devices, MAGDA supports external plugins in the following formats:

  • VST3 - Cross-platform
  • Audio Units (AU) - macOS only

Use the Plugin Browser to find and add plugins to your tracks.

docs.title: Chord Engine
docs.text: The Chord Engine is MAGDA's built-in chord analysis, suggestion, and generation device. It detects chords from incoming MIDI, identifies the musical key, and suggests what chord to play next — all in real time.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Chord Engine is a MIDI device that lives on an instrument track's FX chain. Its suggestions tie straight into note editing: you can drag chords onto the Piano Roll, where they land as notes with a chord annotation, and the same panel docks beside the Piano Roll and the chord track's editor (docked, it has no keyboard). This tight integration between harmonic analysis and note editing is central to the workflow.

It analyses incoming MIDI notes and provides:

  • Real-time chord detection — identifies the chord you're playing
  • Key and scale detection — determines the tonal centre from your playing
  • Context-aware chord suggestions — recommends chords based on music theory and voice leading
  • AI-generated progressions — uses a language model to compose chord progressions in a given style
  • Drag-and-drop to Piano Roll — drop suggestions directly onto the timeline as MIDI notes with chord annotations

The suggestions column has two tabs, chosen with the icons at its top: K&S (Krumhansl-Schmuckler analysis and suggestions) and AI (LLM-generated progressions).

docs.title: K&S Tab
docs.text:
The K&S tab uses the Krumhansl-Schmuckler algorithm to detect the key from your playing and generate chord suggestions from music theory rules. The interface has three columns:

Column Content Chord (left) The chord you are playing, with its degree in the detected key and a keyboard lighting its voicing, then the History of recent chords Suggestions (centre) Suggestion tiles in two groups, Diatonic (in key) and Beyond the key (secondary, borrowed and substitute chords). Each tile shows its Roman numeral degree and a dot for its harmonic function: tonic, pre-dominant or dominant. Key / Scales (right) Detected key, a button to browse scales, and the matching scales

Press any chord tile, in the suggestions or the history, to hear it through the track's instrument; drag it onto the Piano Roll to place it (see Placing Chords). The C button in the Chord header switches note names between letters (C), solfège (Do) and both (C/Do).

docs.title: Chord Detection
docs.text:
Play notes on the track and the panel displays the detected chord name in real time. Detection uses pitch-class set matching against a library of known chord shapes (triads, sevenths, ninths, elevenths, thirteenths, augmented, diminished, suspended, and slash voicings).

Recent chords appear in the History section as a chain of chips, ending on the chord just played. The bin button beside it clears the history and resets detection.

docs.title: Key Detection
docs.text:
The detected key (e.g. "D# minor") is shown at the top of the right column. It uses the Krumhansl-Schmuckler key-finding algorithm:

  1. A pitch-class histogram accumulates every note you play, weighted by an exponential time decay (recent notes matter more; decay constant is 5 seconds).
  2. The histogram is correlated against Krumhansl major and minor profiles — empirically derived distributions of pitch-class frequency in tonal music.
  3. All 24 possible keys (12 roots x major/minor) are scored. A small bias toward the third of each candidate helps disambiguate major vs minor.
  4. The highest-scoring key wins.

docs.title: Scale Detection
docs.text:
Below the key, the panel lists the top matching scales (Ionian, Aeolian, Dorian, Mixolydian, Pentatonic, etc.), ranked by how well your pitch content matches each scale's note set.

  • Click a scale to see all diatonic chords built from it
  • Shift-click a scale to select it for filtering (it highlights). Multiple scales can be selected — their pitch classes are merged to filter suggestions

The browse button beside the key swaps the suggestions for a list of scales, with root-note buttons to narrow it to one key; the back arrow returns to the suggestions.

docs.title: Suggestion Generation
docs.text:
Suggestions are generated from:

  • Diatonic candidates — chords built from scale degrees I–VII, with optional extensions (7ths, 9ths, 11ths, 13ths)
  • Non-diatonic candidates — modal borrowings, secondary dominants, and altered chords
  • Voice leading — suggestions are voiced to minimise movement from the last chord played

Recently played chords are filtered out so suggestions always point forward.

docs.title: Footer Controls
docs.text: Control Description Novelty Slider from safe to wild: the balance between diatonic (0%) and non-diatonic (100%) suggestions Extensions Toggles for the extensions the suggestions may use: 7th, 9th, 11th and 13th. Alt adds borrowed chords and tritone substitutes. Scale filter The funnel button: filter suggestions by the detected scales

docs.title: AI Tab
docs.text: In AI mode, a language model generates full chord progressions based on a text description. Type a prompt describing the style, mood, or harmonic flavour you want, and the AI returns a sequence of chords.

docs.title: Using AI Suggestions
docs.text:
1. Type a description in the prompt at the foot of the panel (Describe a chord progression...). This can be a qualitative mood description (e.g. "soulful and jazzy", "dark ambient") or a functional one using chord grades (e.g. "I-iv-V7 progression", "ii-V-I turnaround")
  2. Press Enter or click the send button
  3. The AI returns one or more labelled progressions as rows of chord buttons
  4. Press a chord to audition it
  5. Drag a chord onto the Piano Roll to place it as MIDI notes

The model in use is named beside the tabs. Each progression row also has a copy button (Click to copy chords, drag to timeline) for taking the whole progression at once.

AI progressions are labelled with a short description (e.g. "Dim pull with warm iv and V7", "Backdoor cadence into Dim").

docs.title: AI with Key Context
docs.text: The AI receives the currently detected key as context, so its suggestions are harmonically relevant to what you've been playing.

docs.title: Suggestion Pipeline
docs.text:
The K&S tab's suggestion engine uses the following pipeline:

flowchart TD
    A["MIDI Note Input"] --> B["Pitch-Class Histogram<br>(time-decayed, τ = 5s)"]

    B --> C["Krumhansl-Schmuckler<br>Key-Profile Correlation<br>12 rotations × major/minor/modal"]

    C --> D["Detected Key + Mode"]

    D --> E["Diatonic Candidates<br>Scale degrees I–VII<br>+ 7ths / 9ths / 11ths / 13ths"]
    D --> F["Non-Diatonic Candidates<br>Modal borrowings<br>Secondary dominants<br>Alterations / Slash chords"]

    E --> G["Mix by Novelty<br>0.0 = diatonic, 1.0 = chromatic"]
    F --> G

    G --> H["Filter Recently Played Chords"]

    H --> I["Voice-Leading Optimizer<br>Minimize centroid distance<br>from last played chord"]

    I --> J["Top-K Suggestions"]

    style A fill:#2d2d2d,stroke:#7c4dff,color:#fff
    style D fill:#1b5e20,stroke:#4caf50,color:#fff
    style G fill:#4a148c,stroke:#ce93d8,color:#fff
    style J fill:#0d47a1,stroke:#42a5f5,color:#fff

docs.title: Chord Timeline
docs.text: When a Chord Engine is present on a track, the Piano Roll shows a chord row above the note grid. This row displays chord annotations that are linked to their MIDI notes. The Chord track button in the Piano Roll's rail shows or hides it, and the clip remembers your choice.

docs.title: Placing Chords
docs.text:
Drag a chord from the suggestions grid and drop it onto the Piano Roll:

  1. Drop sets the start position — a blinking indicator appears
  2. Move the mouse to preview the chord length
  3. Click to confirm the length, or press Enter to use the default length
  4. Press Escape to cancel

The dropped chord creates both MIDI notes and a chord annotation in the timeline. These are linked — moving, resizing, or deleting the notes automatically updates the annotation.

docs.title: Detecting Chords
docs.text: Click the refresh button in the chord row (Recalculate chords from notes) to auto-detect chords from existing notes. The detection scans notes at each bar boundary, identifies chords with 2+ simultaneous notes, and creates linked annotations.

docs.title: Note Tracking
docs.text:
Chord annotations track their associated MIDI notes in real time:

  • Move notes — the annotation follows
  • Resize notes — the annotation length updates
  • Delete notes — the annotation shrinks or disappears
  • Transpose notes — the chord name re-detects automatically
  • Undo/redo — annotations revert along with their notes

docs.title: Drum Grid
docs.text: The Drum Grid is MAGDA's pad-based drum instrument. Each pad holds its own chain of devices, and each pad that holds a sound is its own mixer channel, giving you independent processing and mixing per drum voice.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Drum Grid maps incoming MIDI notes to 64 pads, 16 to a page. The device shows three panels side by side: the pads, the selected pad's panel with its mix, and the selected pad's chain. The sidebar's Show the pad panel and Show the pad's chain toggles hide or show the last two, and its arrows turn the pages of pads. Like other devices, the Drum Grid has a side strip with a meter and gain fader.

docs.title: Pads
docs.text:
• Each pad is mapped to a specific MIDI note and shows that note and the name of the sound it holds
  • Pads can be triggered from the Piano Roll, the Drum Grid Editor (bottom panel), or a MIDI controller
  • Click a pad to select it and show its panel and chain; the play button on a loaded pad auditions it
  • Drag a pad onto another to swap the two
  • Right-click a loaded pad for Analyze pad role, which classifies its sample with the Sample Analyzer models to set the pad's role, and Delete, which clears the pad

Pad labels, instrument roles, and drumkits are managed by right-clicking rows in the Drum Grid Editor.

docs.title: Pad Chain
docs.text:
Each pad has one chain of devices, just like a track. Its instrument comes first, typically a Sampler playing the pad's sample; effects follow it, so you can put distortion on a snare without affecting the kick. To layer several sounds on one pad, put a rack in its chain.

  • Drop an instrument, a MAGDA one or a plug-in, on a pad to make it the pad's instrument. This replaces the pad's whole chain, effects included.
  • Drop effects or samples on the chain panel to add them to the selected pad's chain. An empty pad's chain panel also has a + button for building a chain from scratch.

Plug-ins inside a pad's chain show one row of parameters fewer than at the top of a track's chain, so each value still fits under its name.

docs.title: Pad Channels
docs.text:
Each pad that holds a sound is a mixer channel nested under the Drum Grid's track. It appears as a row under the track in the arrangement, with no clip lane, and as a strip under the grid's strip in the Mixer View. A pad channel has volume, pan, mute, solo, sends, automation and a meter, like any track, and its device chain is the pad's chain: select the channel and the bottom panel shows the pad's chain, and devices you add while it is selected land there.

Empty pads have no channel. Clearing a pad removes its channel, and undo brings it back with its settings.

The pad panel in the device mixes the selected pad's channel:

  • Gain — level, -60 to +6 dB
  • Pan — stereo position
  • Mute pad, Solo pad and Pad power

A pad channel's output goes to the grid by default: the pads are summed where the Drum Grid sits, before any effects that follow it on the track. Route a channel's output elsewhere and it leaves the grid's mix. Soloing a pad keeps the grid's track audible.

Projects with pad buses

Earlier versions routed pads to bus tracks. Those projects open with each bus converted: a bus that carried one pad becomes that pad's channel, keeping its effects, sends, automation and output, and a bus that carried several pads becomes a group that their channels route into.

docs.title: Adding Samples
docs.text: • Drag audio files from the Media Explorer onto a pad to load a sample. The pad's chain is replaced by a Sampler playing it, rooted on the pad's note. To add a sample to a pad's chain instead, drop it on the chain panel.

docs.title: Multi-Sample Drop
docs.text: Select several samples in the Media Explorer or Media Library and drag them onto any pad. Samples fill consecutive pads in selection order, starting from the drop target. While dragging, every pad that will receive a sample lights up so you can see the range before releasing.

docs.title: Pad Envelope and Macros
docs.text:
Each pad's Sampler has an amplitude envelope you can shape per pad: Attack, Decay, Sustain and Release.

These envelope controls are full modulation targets. You can link them to the Drum Grid's macros and modulate them with LFOs or envelopes the same way as any other parameter (see Linking Parameters). Slicing a sample across several pads gives each slice its own envelope, so a single macro can, for example, tighten every slice's release at once.

docs.title: MIDI Mapping
docs.text: The 64 pads run chromatically from C0 on the first pad, so the General MIDI drum notes land where drum maps expect them: kick on C1, snare on D1, and so on.

docs.title: Drum Kit
docs.text:
The MAGDA drum kit is five synthetic drum voices: Kick, Snare, Hat, Tom, and Clap. Every voice is synthesised, not sampled. Drop them onto Drum Grid pads to build a kit, or add any one to a track and play it standalone.

All five are 8-voice, MIDI-gated instruments. The played note only triggers the hit: each voice is tuned by its own controls, not by the key you play.

docs.title: Faceplate
docs.text:
Each voice is built from layers, such as a kick's transient, body, and click. The layers sit behind tabs, and the selected tab shows that layer's controls.

Beside the controls, a plot draws the rendered hit, with each layer's envelope traced over it in its own colour; the selected layer's is bright and the others dimmed. Drag a layer's handles to set its attack, where the layer has one, and its decay. Scroll over the plot to bend the curve of the layer nearest the pointer.

The sidebar's Show the parameters toggle hides the controls, and the other toggle hides the plot. One of the two always shows.

There is no gain control on the faceplate: set the voice's level with the fader on the device's side strip.

docs.title: Curve
docs.text: Layers with a decay have a Curve control (-50 to 50) that shapes it. At 0 the decay is linear, positive values swell and slow the tail, and negative values make it faster and more concave.

docs.title: Kick
docs.text:
Three layers: a pitched sine TRANSIENT sweep, a tuned sine BODY with pitch-snap into a saturator, and a noise CLICK.

docs.title: Macros, modulation, and presets
docs.text: Each drum voice is a standard MAGDA device, so its parameters accept macros and modulators, and patches save and recall through the preset system. On a Drum Grid, each pad chain can carry its own macro and modulator links.

docs.title: AI sound design
docs.text: Click the AI icon in the device header and describe the sound you want. The agent reads this device's own parameters and their real-world ranges, then writes values into them. See Per-Device AI Panel.

docs.title: Effects (MAGDA FX Bank)
docs.text: The MAGDA FX bank is a set of native effects compiled from Faust DSP and shipped with every MAGDA installation. They appear in the Plugin Browser under the MAGDA vendor and can be dragged onto any track's FX chain.

docs.title: Dynamics
docs.text: Device Description Compressor Two engines. Clean: feedforward with peak/RMS detection, soft knee, stereo link, sidechain HPF, external audio sidechain, parallel mix, output safety limiting. Glue: Brouns FBFF compressor with Detector (Peak/RMS), Style (Pre/Post), and FBFF blend. On the faceplate the knobs sit in four tabs: Curve (Threshold, Ratio, Knee), Timing (Attack, Release), Level (Makeup, Output) and Detector (Link, SC HPF, FBFF). Multiband Compressor OTT-style 3-band compressor. LR4 crossover split, two OTT stages in series per band, symmetric expander, per-band brickwall limiter, editable crossover frequencies and per-band thresholds in the curve editor. The graph always shows, since it selects the band; the sidebar's Show the band and Show the global controls toggles hide the band editor and the whole-device controls. Limiter Native lookahead limiter / autonormalizer. Threshold drives the signal into a fixed 0 dB ceiling, Attack and Release shape gain movement, and Output is a post-limiter trim that can only reduce level. Clipper Antialiased multi-mode clipper with five ADAA curves: Hard (brickwall), Soft (quadratic), Tanh (tube-style), Hyperbolic, and Sine. Drive pushes input into the curve, Output trims after. Gate Stereo-linked gate / downward expander with range, timing (attack / hold / release), mix, and output gain.

docs.title: EQ & Filter
docs.text: Device Description EQ 8-band parametric EQ. Each band is a low cut or high cut (12 or 24 dB/oct), low shelf, bell, high shelf, or notch. The curve view draws the live signal spectrum behind the response curve — a dim trace for the input and a brighter one for the output — so you can see what each band is doing to the actual material. See EQ band editor below. Filter Seven-model multimode filter. SVF: clean LP/BP/HP/Notch with 2, 4 or 6 Poles, plus Notch+, a notch at the cutoff between two resonant peaks. Ladder: 4-pole low-pass with driven resonance. Korg 35: MS-style LP/HP with analog bite. Oberheim: SEM-style LP/BP/HP/Notch. Sallen-Key: smooth 2nd-order LP/BP/HP. Diode: resonant 4-pole diode ladder with input drive. Comb: peaks at the cutoff and its harmonics, with Resonance as feedback; mode + puts the peaks on the harmonics, - on the odd half-harmonics, an octave down and hollow. The Poles control shows only on the SVF.

docs.title: EQ band editor
docs.text:
Each band has a chip under the curve. The chip's dot turns the band on or off; click the rest of the chip to edit that band. At the device chain's standard height the band editor opens over the curve, and Esc closes it. Given more height, it sits under the chips.

The editor holds the band's type (LC, LS, Bell, Notch, HS, HC), a 12 | 24 slope switch for LC and HC, and Note, Freq, Gain and Q, with the device's Output beside them. The Note tile shows the band's frequency as a note and cents. Click it and type a note (C3, F#1, Bb0) to set the frequency exactly.

The expand button in the device header moves the curve and chips into the arrangement, where there is room to work; the band editor stays in the device.

docs.title: Reverb & Space
docs.text: Device Description Reverb Three engines. Plate: Dattorro diffusion network. Hall: Zita 8-tap FDN. Room: Freeverb Schroeder/Moorer network. Dimension Stereo widener with three engines. Dimension: Roland Dimension D-style anti-phase modulated delays. Haas: short fixed delay on one channel. M/S: pure side-channel gain, no time smear. Convolution Convolution reverb that plays the signal through an impulse response you load. See Convolution below.

docs.title: Delay
docs.text: Device Description Delay Stereo delay with sync (or free time), tone, feedback, and crossfeed. Grain Delay Granular delay for smeared repeats, pitch motion, and texture.

docs.title: Modulation
docs.text: Device Description Chorus Stereo chorus with 1-3 modulated voices per channel. Free-Hz or tempo-synced rate, depth, feedback, mix, stereo width. Flanger Stereo flanger with short modulated delay, heavy feedback for the classic comb-sweep, and sync- or free-rate LFO. Phaser Phaser with selectable stage count, feedback, and sweep window. Mod Tremolo / vibrato / auto-pan sharing one LFO. Free-Hz or tempo-synced; sine, triangle, square, or sample-and-hold shape. Ring Mod Stereo ring modulator. Sine, triangle, or square carrier from 1 Hz (tremolo) to 5 kHz (metallic clang). Sync- or free-rate. Freq Shift Stereo single-sideband frequency shifter. Hilbert-pair Bode design. Fixed-Hz offset, feedback for resonant artefacts, Spread for stereo width.

docs.title: Distortion
docs.text: Device Description Saturator Waveshaper with drive, mode, bias, tone, mix, and output. Grit Bit-depth and sample-rate reduction. Bitcrusher Lo-fi bitcrusher. Rate (sample-rate reduction), Bits (bit depth), Drive (quantization landing point), Tone (post-crush low-pass).

docs.title: Pitch
docs.text: Device Description Pitch Three engines, all using ef.transpose. Shifter: single voice, +/-24 semitones. Detuner: two voices hard-panned L/R for chorus-style thickening. Harmonizer: shifted voice summed with dry at a chosen interval.

docs.title: Spectral
docs.text: Device Description Spectral FX Four FFT effects in series: spectral gate, contrast, phase-coherent frequency shift and phase scramble, over a scrolling spectrogram. See Spectral FX below.

docs.title: Utility
docs.text:
Device Description Utility Gain, pan, stereo width, mono sum, low-frequency mono, left/right swap and per-channel polarity flip. Pan, Width, Low mono and Gain sit in a row over the Mono, Low mono, Swap, Ø L and Ø R toggles. Beside them is a picture of the stereo field: drag the band to pan, drag its edges to change the width, and double-click it to reset both. An amber tick marks the low-mono crossover. The sidebar's Show the stereo field toggle hides the picture. Gain is the device's output level, so its side strip has a meter but no fader. Test Tone Tone generator for calibration and routing checks. Waveform picks Sine, Triangle, Saw Up, Saw Down, Square or Noise; Frequency runs from 20 Hz to 20 kHz and Level from -60 to 0 dB. The noise colour (White, Pink, Brown) applies to Noise, and Frequency is dimmed while Noise plays. Turn on Transport only to keep it silent while the transport is stopped.

Note

Devices that bundle multiple engines (Compressor, Reverb, Dimension, Filter, Pitch) expose an engine selector at the top of the editor and switch DSP in place. Macros and modulator links survive the switch.

docs.title: Convolution
docs.text:
The Convolution device (called IR Reverb in earlier versions) is a native MAGDA device, not part of the Faust FX bank, that sits under Reverb in the Plugin Browser. Where the Reverb device synthesises a space from an algorithm, this one convolves your signal with a recording of a real one: an impulse response captured in a hall, a stairwell, a plate, a spring tank, a guitar cabinet, or any object you have measured. Anything an impulse response can describe, it will reproduce, which also makes it the device to reach for when you want a specific room rather than a plausible one.

No impulse responses ship with MAGDA, so the device starts empty and passes the signal through until you load one.

The faceplate has three panels side by side:

  • IMPULSE RESPONSE draws the loaded impulse response's waveform, in dB so the tail shows. Its title gives the file's name, its length and whether it is mono or stereo.
  • FILTER draws the live response of the low and high cut filters over the Low Cut, High Cut and Q tiles.
  • OUTPUT holds Gain and Mix. The sidebar's Show the output toggle shows or hides this panel.

Loading an impulse response. Click the IMPULSE RESPONSE panel, or the folder button in its title, and pick a file. You can also drag an audio file onto the panel; its border lights up blue while a file is over it. WAV, AIFF, FLAC and Ogg are all accepted, mono or stereo.

The impulse response is stored inside the device, not referenced from disk, so a project stays self-contained: it opens with its reverb intact on a machine that has never seen the original file. Long impulse responses make for large project files.

Controls:

Control Description Low Cut High-pass on the reverb, 10 Hz to 20 kHz. Clears mud out of the tail. High Cut Low-pass on the reverb, 10 Hz to 20 kHz. Darkens the tail so it sits behind the dry signal. Q Resonance of both cutoff filters, 0.1 to 14, shared between them. Gain Output trim, -12 to +6 dB. Mix Dry/wet balance, 0 to 100%. At 0% the device is a straight passthrough.

Note

The device reports no latency, so it needs no delay compensation and can be used freely on a live-monitored track. A long impulse response is still expensive to convolve, though: if the CPU meter climbs, a shorter one costs less.

docs.title: Spectral FX
docs.text:
Spectral FX is a native MAGDA device in its own Spectral category of the Plugin Browser. It splits the signal into its frequency content and runs four effects on it, always in this order: Gate, Contrast, Shift, then Scramble. At their defaults all four are off and the device is transparent.

Controls:

Control Description Gate Mutes frequencies quieter than the threshold, from -80 dB (Off) to 0 dB. The threshold reads in the same dBFS as broadband material, so a gate at -40 dB cuts what sits below -40 dBFS. Contrast -100 to 100%. Above zero it sharpens the peaks and lowers the floor; below zero it flattens the spectrum. The overall level stays the same. Shift Moves every frequency by the same number of hertz, -2000 to +2000 Hz. The shift is phase-coherent, so it is exact in Hz; like Freq Shift, it pulls harmonics out of tune with each other. Scramble 0 to 100%. Randomises the phase of each frequency for a smeared, washed-out texture, with the level kept steady. Output Output level, -24 to +24 dB.

The dry/wet balance is the mix box at the top of the device's side strip.

The faceplate is a scrolling spectrogram of the device's own output, low frequencies at the bottom, with 100 Hz, 1 kHz and 10 kHz marked. The strip at its right shows the colour scale and marks the Gate threshold, and a non-zero Shift is shown in the top-right corner.

Note

The device delays the signal by its FFT size, 2048 samples (4096 at sample rates above 50 kHz), and reports that latency so MAGDA's delay compensation keeps the track in time.

docs.title: Sidechain
docs.text:
The Sidechain device is a native MAGDA device (not part of the Faust FX bank) that sits under Dynamics in the Plugin Browser. It is a MIDI-triggered volume shaper: the device holds its own gain at unity and a retriggerable curve ducks it toward silence, keyed from the notes of another track. This is the classic "sidechain pump" effect without a compressor — the curve is the gain envelope, so you draw exactly the ducking shape you want.

Choosing the trigger source. The device faceplate has no source picker; pick the source from the sidechain button in the device header (tooltip Sidechain source). It turns orange once a source is routed. Clicking it opens a menu with None, an Audio Sidechain section, and a MIDI Source section listing the other tracks; the Sidechain device keys off a track chosen under MIDI Source.

Controls:

Control Description Curve The gain envelope. Edit it directly to shape how the level ducks and recovers on each trigger. DEPTH How far the curve pulls the gain down, 0–100%. SYNC Trigger sync division, which also sets the length of the duck curve. MODE 1-Shot (run the curve once per trigger) or Loop (repeat it). CH ST ducks the full stereo signal; SD ducks the side channel only. ATK Attack, 0–50 ms. REL Release, 0–500 ms.

Placement

The Sidechain device can go on the master track as a destination, but the master can never be a source (it has no notes to key from). The device cannot run in the post-FX area, since ducking has to happen before the fader.

docs.title: Faust (Custom DSP)
docs.text:
The Faust device hosts a Faust DSP that you compile and load at runtime. Unlike the rest of the MAGDA FX bank, where each device wraps a fixed pre-compiled .dsp source, this device accepts any Faust program.

Both this and the Faust Instrument live under Custom DSP in the device browser. Reach for the instrument instead when you want MIDI to play your DSP as a synth rather than process an incoming signal.

The device's title is the name of the loaded patch ("Drive", say); hover it to see the patch's credits.

docs.title: Patches and presets
docs.text:
A Faust patch is a .dsp file, and it holds source code only. Patches live in the Patches submenu of the device's preset box:

  • Built-in - the patches that ship with MAGDA, grouped by category.
  • My Patches - the .dsp files in Faust Patches/Effects inside your presets folder (set under Settings > Paths; by default Documents/MAGDA/Presets). The Faust Instrument lists its own from Faust Patches/Instruments.
  • Load .dsp File... - open a patch from anywhere on disk.
  • Save .dsp File... - save the current source as a .dsp, by default into My Patches.

Loading a patch compiles it and swaps it in immediately. It replaces the code and nothing else, so your modulators and macros stay, and the preset box clears its name, since no preset describes the device any more.

A MAGDA preset, saved with the floppy-disk button, is a full snapshot: the source, the parameter values, modulators, macros and gain. Loading one brings back the patch it was saved with.

Patches kept in the FaustEffects folder of earlier versions are no longer listed; they stay on disk and open with Load .dsp File....

docs.title: Editing and controls
docs.text:
• The code icon beside the floppy (Edit the patch's source) opens an in-app code editor. Compile recompiles the source and hot-swaps the DSP.
  • If a patch fails to compile, the error shows in a strip along the foot of the device.
  • The parameter grid is up to eight columns by two rows. Faust groups in the source become named page tabs.
  • A patch with a custom view, such as Drive, shows it to the right of the grid, and the grid takes only as many columns as its controls fill. The sidebar's Show the parameters and Show the patch's view toggles hide either side; one of the two always shows.

Parameters live in a stable pool of slots that persist across recompiles, so macro links, modulator routings, MIDI Learn assignments, and automation lanes survive a code change as long as the slot ordering is preserved. This makes the device practical for iterative DSP development without losing your patch state on every compile.

docs.title: How your code is run
docs.text:
Your DSP is compiled to WebAssembly and then JIT-compiled to native machine code by wasmtime, so it runs as real compiled code rather than being interpreted.

Two things follow from that. It is fast enough to play with rather than merely audition, though it still carries more overhead than the ahead-of-time compiled MAGDA FX bank, which has no sandbox boundary and is optimised by your system compiler. And it is sandboxed: the DSP runs inside the WebAssembly memory model, so a patch that misbehaves cannot take the application down with it. That matters most when you are iterating quickly or loading code an AI wrote.

Still evolving

This device is newer than the rest of the FX bank and its surface is still settling. For a patch you rely on in finished work, ask for it to be promoted into a compiled device.

docs.title: Writing Faust with AI help
docs.text:
faust-mcp-magda is an optional companion tool that exposes the Faust compiler and standard library to AI assistants. MAGDA uses it to validate AI-generated Faust code before loading it into this device, so syntax errors and bad library references get caught up front instead of failing at compile time.

Enable it from Settings > AI, on the Assistant tab, by turning on the Faust DSP toggle under Tools. When Faust validation is used, MAGDA will start the MCP server on-demand via npx; no manual install step is needed. npx must be available on the system PATH (it ships with Node.js).

The MCP server carries its own copy of the Faust compiler, so no separate Faust installation is required either. This is a separate thing from how the device runs your DSP during playback, described above; the server only checks that code compiles before MAGDA loads it.

The server can also be wired into a separate MCP-aware AI assistant (Claude, Cursor, and similar) directly, by adding it to that client's MCP config; see the project README for details. This is independent of the MAGDA-side toggle.

docs.title: Faust Instrument
docs.text:
The Faust Instrument is the instrument counterpart to the Faust effect. Where that device runs a Faust program as an insert on an audio signal, this one reports as a synth: it takes MIDI in, allocates voices, and plays your DSP once per held note.

Authoring is shared with the effect. The device's title is the patch's name; hover it to see the credits the patch declares (declare author, version, license, description). Load a .dsp from the Patches submenu of the preset box (see Patches and presets). The code icon beside the floppy-disk button (Edit the patch's source) opens the in-app code editor: click Compile to recompile and hot-swap the running DSP. If a patch fails to compile, the error shows in a strip along the foot of the device.

Your code is compiled to WebAssembly and JIT-compiled to native machine code by wasmtime, sandboxed the same way, as described under How your code is run.

docs.title: Writing a polyphonic patch
docs.text:
The instrument follows the Faust polyphonic convention. Three control names are reserved:

Control Driven by freq the pitch of the note being played, in Hz gain note velocity gate note on and note off, for triggering envelopes

Declare them as ordinary sliders and read them in your DSP. MAGDA drives them per voice and does not expose them as user parameters, so they never appear as knobs or automation targets. Every other control you declare becomes a parameter as usual.

A minimal patch looks like this:

import("stdfaust.lib");

freq = hslider("freq", 440, 20, 20000, 0.01);
gain = hslider("gain", 0.5, 0, 1, 0.01);
gate = button("gate");

cutoff = hslider("Cutoff", 2000, 50, 12000, 1);

process = os.sawtooth(freq) * gain
        : fi.lowpass(2, cutoff)
        * en.adsr(0.01, 0.2, 0.7, 0.3, gate)
        <: _, _;

A patch that produces one output channel is fanned to both; there is no need to split it yourself.

The device plays up to 16 voices at once. When they are all busy, the oldest released voice is reused first, then the oldest still playing.

The parameters sit in a grid of up to 8 by 2 controls, on pages named for the groups in your patch and shown as tabs.

docs.title: Voice controls
docs.text:
Three host parameters sit on the Voice page, alongside whatever your patch declares:

  • Voice Mode - Poly allocates a fresh voice per note. Mono plays one note at a time and retriggers the envelope on each new note. Legato also plays one note at a time, but overlapping notes slide to the new pitch without retriggering, so the envelope keeps its shape.
  • Glide - portamento time, from instant up to 2 seconds. In Legato it gives the classic slide between overlapping notes, and releasing back to a note you are still holding glides back to it.
  • Bend Range - how far the pitch wheel moves the note, in semitones each way, up to 24. The default of 2 matches most synths.

All three can be automated. Glide and Bend Range can also be linked to macros and driven by modulators like any other control; Voice Mode follows automation only.

Pitch bend is applied by MAGDA to the same freq your patch already reads, so the wheel works without your DSP doing anything to support it. There is no need to declare a bend control or tag anything with [midi:pitchwheel]. Stopping the transport recentres the wheel, so a bend held at the moment you stop does not carry over into what you play next.

docs.title: MPE
docs.text:
The instrument plays per-note expression, as an MPE clip plays it (see Pitch Glides).

Pitch bend on a member channel (2 to 16) moves only the note on that channel, at a fixed range of ±48 semitones, and works for every patch through freq. The wheel on channel 1 is the ordinary wheel: it moves every note, by Bend Range. A keyboard set to send on any other channel has its wheel read as per-note bend.

Two more control names are reserved for patches that want them:

Control Driven by timbre CC74 on the note's channel, 0 to 1, resting at the middle (64 of 127) pressure channel pressure on the note's channel, 0 to 1, resting at 0

Declare a timbre or pressure slider and each voice gets its own note's value. Like freq, gain, and gate, they stay out of the parameter list.

docs.title: Parameters across recompiles
docs.text: Parameters live in the same stable slot pool the Faust effect uses, so macro links, modulator routings, MIDI Learn assignments, and automation lanes survive a recompile as long as slot ordering is preserved. You can keep editing the DSP without losing the patch you built around it.

docs.title: Patches and presets
docs.text:
A .dsp file holds source only. The preset box's Patches submenu handles them:

  • Built-in - the instrument patches that ship with MAGDA, grouped by category.
  • My Patches - the .dsp files in Faust Patches/Instruments in your presets folder (set in Settings > Paths). Instrument and effect patches are kept apart, since an instrument patch can't load into the effect.
  • Load .dsp File... - open any .dsp from disk.
  • Save .dsp File... - save the current source as a .dsp, into My Patches by default.

Loading a patch replaces the source and nothing else: your mods and macros stay, and the preset box clears its name, since no preset describes the device any more.

A MAGDA preset, saved with the floppy-disk button, is a full snapshot: the source, the parameter values, mods, macros, and gain. Loading one brings its patch back with it.

The FaustInstruments and FaustEffects folders earlier versions saved patches to are no longer listed. Their files stay on disk; open them with Load .dsp File....

docs.title: FM0
docs.text: FM0 is a 16-voice, four-operator FM synthesizer built into MAGDA. Every operator can phase-modulate any operator through a full 4x4 modulation matrix, including self-feedback on the diagonal. Each operator has its own ratio, level, and waveform, feeding a shared amplitude ADSR. An optional filter can sit after the operators or join the matrix as a fifth node. It plays in poly, mono, or legato modes.

docs.title: Faceplate
docs.text:
The faceplate has three panels:

  • OPS, AMP ENV, and VOICE - three tabs sharing the first panel: the operators, the amplitude envelope, and the performance controls
  • MATRIX - the modulation amounts
  • FILTER and FILTER ENV - the filter and its envelope

The sidebar's Show the operators toggle hides the first panel and Show the matrix hides the matrix, to make the device narrower.

docs.title: Operators
docs.text:
The OPS tab has a row per operator, under the column heads WAVE, RATIO, LEVEL, and RST.

Parameter Range Default Description Ratio 0.25 to 16 1 (Op2 = 2) Frequency ratio, a multiple of the played note Level -60 to 6 dB 0 (Op2-4 = -60) Operator output level Wave Sine / Triangle / Saw / Square / Noise Sine Operator waveform

Click the waveform's icon to pick another wave from a menu. The dot beside it turns the operator on and off (on by default); a disabled operator stops both sounding and modulating, and its row greys out. Tick RST to reset the operator's phase on note-on.

The last row, Filter, holds the filter's F Level (see The filter in the matrix).

docs.title: Modulation matrix
docs.text:
The MATRIX panel routes operator outputs into operator phase inputs. Rows are sources, labelled 1 to 4, and columns are destinations, labelled →1 to →4. The cell in row 2, column →1 is "operator 2 modulates operator 1"; its parameter is named M21. The diagonal cells (M11, M22, M33, M44) are self-feedback.

Parameter Range Default Description M11 ... M44 0 to 8 0 (M21 = 2) Modulation amount for each matrix cell

A default patch has operator 2 modulating operator 1, the classic two-operator FM voice. Raise the diagonal for brighter, more aggressive timbres.

The extra row and column marked F, in blue, belong to the filter, and act only while it sits in the matrix.

docs.title: Filter
docs.text:
The filter is off by default. Turn it on with the dot on the FILTER tab. Switching it on or off, or changing its engine, type, or poles, while a note plays fades rather than clicking.

The icons at the right of the tabs choose its position: on the output, where it filters the operators' mix, or in the matrix (see below). Under them, pick the engine, SVF, Ladder, or Comb. The SVF adds a type, LP, HP, BP, or Notch, picked from icons, and Poles (2, 4, or 6) for its steepness. The comb has + and - modes instead. A response curve sits beside the tiles.

Parameter Range Default Description Cutoff 20 Hz to 20 kHz (log) 2000 Filter frequency Reso 0 to 1 0.3 Resonance Drive 0 to 1 0 Pre-filter saturation Key 0 to 1 0 Octaves of cutoff per octave of the played note, around middle C Env Amt -4 to 4 oct 0 Filter envelope depth on cutoff (bipolar) Vel>Cut 0 to 6 oct 0 Velocity to cutoff depth

The FILTER ENV tab shows the filter's own ADSR as a graph above four tiles, with the same ranges as the amplitude envelope and the same defaults.

docs.title: The filter in the matrix
docs.text:
In the matrix position the filter becomes a fifth node:

  • The →F column sends operators into the filter, 0 to 1 each (M1F to M4F).
  • The F row lets the filter's output phase-modulate the operators, 0 to 8 each like the matrix (MF1 to MF4).
  • F Level (-60 to 6 dB, default 0) adds the filter's output to the mix.

The FILTER tab lists the operators sending to it, such as IN 1 2. In the output position the sends, returns, and F Level do nothing.

docs.title: Amplitude envelope
docs.text:
The AMP ENV tab shows the envelope as a graph above four tiles. Drag the handles on the graph, or edit the tiles.

Parameter Range Default Description Attack 1 to 2000 ms 5 ADSR attack Decay 1 to 2000 ms 300 ADSR decay Sustain 0 to 1 0.5 Sustain level Release 1 to 4000 ms 400 ADSR release

docs.title: Voice
docs.text:
Parameter Range Default Description Voice Mode Poly / Mono / Legato Poly Voicing Glide 0 to 2000 ms 0 Portamento (mono and legato only) Bend 0 to 24 st 2 Pitch-wheel range Gain -24 to 6 dB -6 Output level Vel>Amp 0 to 1 1 Velocity sensitivity depth

The pitch wheel moves every operator together, so the ratios hold.

docs.title: MPE
docs.text:
FM0 responds to per-note expression, as an MPE clip plays it (see Pitch Glides):

  • Pitch bend on a member channel (2 to 16) moves only the note on that channel, at a fixed range of ±48 semitones.
  • Timbre (CC74) scales the modulation amounts, from half to double.
  • Pressure lifts the note's level by up to 6 dB.

The pitch wheel on channel 1 is the ordinary wheel: it moves every note, by Bend. A keyboard set to send on any other channel has its wheel read as per-note bend at ±48 semitones, so set it to channel 1 to play with Bend.

docs.title: Macros, modulation, and presets
docs.text: FM0 sits in the standard device slot, so its parameters accept macros and modulators, and patches save and recall through the preset system.

docs.title: AI sound design
docs.text: Click the AI icon in the device header and describe the sound you want. The agent reads this device's own parameters and their real-world ranges, then writes values into them. See Per-Device AI Panel.

docs.title: Mutable Instruments Ports
docs.text:
MAGDA ships native ports of three Mutable Instruments modules, faithful to Emilie Gillet's open-source designs:

  • Materia is a port of Elements
  • Halo is a port of Rings
  • Nimbus is a port of Clouds

Materia and Halo are instruments played from MIDI. Nimbus is a granular audio processor that works on an existing signal, so add it to a track's FX chain rather than playing it from the keyboard.

docs.title: Materia (Elements)
docs.text:
A monophonic modal-synthesis voice with three exciters, Bow, Blow, and Strike, driving a modal and string resonator, followed by a stereo Space reverb.

The faceplate has four panels side by side:

  • VOICE - Contour, Signature, the transpose (labelled Coarse) and Fine, Level, and Vel>Amp.
  • EXCITER - the EXCITATION BLEND triangle beside a BOW, BLOW, and STRIKE column for each exciter's level and shaping. Drag inside the triangle to set all three exciter levels at once: Bow at the top corner, Blow at the bottom left, Strike at the bottom right.
  • RESONATOR - Geometry, Brightness, Damping, Position, and Space.
  • MODAL RESPONSE - a drawing of the resonator's partials.

The sidebar's Show the voice toggle hides the VOICE panel, and Show the modal response hides the drawing.

Parameter Range Default Description Contour 0 to 100% 50 Exciter envelope shape Bow 0 to 100% 0 Bow exciter amount Bow Timbre 0 to 100% 50 Bow timbre Blow 0 to 100% 0 Blow exciter amount Blow Flow 0 to 100% 50 Blow pressure and flow Blow Timbre 0 to 100% 50 Blow brightness Strike 0 to 100% 80 Strike exciter amount Strike Mallet 0 to 100% 50 Mallet hardness Strike Timbre 0 to 100% 50 Strike spectral content Signature 0 to 100% 10 Resonator timbral colour Geometry 0 to 100% 30 Resonator shape (bar, membrane, tube) Brightness 0 to 100% 50 Resonator cutoff Damping 0 to 100% 70 Mode decay rate Position 0 to 100% 30 Strike position on the resonator Space 0 to 100% 30 Stereo reverb amount Pitch / Fine -24 to 24 st / -100 to 100 cents 0 Transpose and fine tune Level -60 to 12 dB 0 Output level Vel>Amp 0 to 100% 100 Velocity to amplitude depth

docs.title: Halo (Rings)
docs.text:
A switchable polyphonic resonator with an internal exciter. There is no note-off: notes ring out and decay according to Damping, and the resonator rotates its internal voices as you play.

The faceplate has three panels side by side: PARAMETERS, with the transpose labelled Coarse; RESONATOR MODEL, a button per model above the POLYPHONY choice; and RESONATOR, a spectrum of the modal response. The sidebar's Show the resonator spectrum toggle hides the spectrum.

Parameter Range Default Description Structure 0 to 100% 25 Modal-to-string character Brightness 0 to 100% 50 Resonator cutoff Damping 0 to 100% 50 Mode decay rate Position 0 to 100% 25 Excitation position Model Modal / Sympathetic / String / FM / Sym Quant / String+Verb Modal Resonator type Polyphony 1 / 2 / 4 voices 2 Internal voice count Chord 0 to 10 0 Chord voicing (modal and chord models) Pitch / Fine -24 to 24 st / -100 to 100 cents 0 Transpose and fine tune Level -60 to 12 dB 0 Output level

docs.title: Nimbus (Clouds)
docs.text:
A stereo granular texture processor with four modes. It processes whatever audio reaches it, with an internal diffuser and a freeze control. Add it to a track's FX chain.

The faceplate has three panels side by side:

  • PARAMETERS - Position, Density, Size, Texture, and Pitch, over the BLEND ROUTES: Dry/Wet, Spread, Feedback, and Reverb.
  • FREEZE and PLAYBACK MODE - the freeze switch, and a button per mode: GRANULAR, STRETCH, DELAY (Looping Delay), and SPECTRAL.
  • GRAIN CLOUD - a view of the grain window and the cloud of grains.

The sidebar's Show the grain cloud toggle hides the GRAIN CLOUD panel.

Parameter Range Default Description Position 0 to 100% 50 Playback position / seek Size 0 to 100% 50 Grain size and buffer length Pitch -24 to 24 st 0 Pitch shift (Stretch mode) Density 0 to 100% 40 Grain density and overlap Texture 0 to 100% 50 Grain envelope and spectral tilt Dry/Wet 0 to 100% 50 Processed-to-dry blend Spread 0 to 100% 50 Stereo width and grain randomisation Feedback 0 to 100% 0 Output to input feedback Reverb 0 to 100% 0 Diffuser tail amount Mode Granular / Stretch / Looping Delay / Spectral Granular Processing algorithm Freeze Off / On Off Freeze the buffer and loop the current grains

docs.title: Macros, modulation, and presets
docs.text: All three ports are standard MAGDA devices, so their parameters accept macros and modulators, and patches save and recall through the preset system.

docs.title: AI sound design
docs.text:
Click the AI icon in the device header and describe the sound you want. The agent reads this device's own parameters and their real-world ranges, then writes values into them. See Per-Device AI Panel.

Materia and Halo support this. Nimbus does not — it processes incoming audio rather than generating notes, so there is no preset for an agent to design.

docs.title: Physical Models
docs.text:
Three struck physical models ship with MAGDA: Marimba, Djembe, and Bell. Each is a modal physical model driven by a strike exciter, not a sample. The ring and decay come out of the model itself, so there are no loops or release samples.

All three are 8-voice instruments. Marimba and Djembe follow the played note for pitch. Bell is fixed-pitch: the note only triggers the strike.

docs.title: Faceplate
docs.text:
The three models share one faceplate: an EXCITER column, a RESONATOR column, and a drawing of the body on the right, a tone bar, a drum membrane, or a bell in cross-section. The dot on the body marks the STRIKE POSITION; click or drag on the body to move it, which sets the same control as Position in the EXCITER column. The body flashes on each note.

The sidebar's Show the parameters toggle hides the two columns, and Show the body hides the drawing. One of the two always shows.

There is no gain control on the faceplate: set the model's level with the fader on the device's side strip.

docs.title: Marimba
docs.text:
A struck tone-bar-and-tube model.

Column Control Range Default Description EXCITER Position 0 to 1 0.3 Strike position on the bar (0 centre, 1 edge) EXCITER Tone 500 to 12000 Hz (log) 7000 Exciter brightness EXCITER Sharpness 0 to 1 0.25 Exciter transient hardness RESONATOR Decay 50 to 2000 ms 100 Bar ring time (T60)

docs.title: Djembe
docs.text:
A struck hand-drum membrane model.

Column Control Range Default Description EXCITER Position 0 to 1 0.4 Strike location (0 centre, 1 edge) EXCITER Sharpness 0 to 1 0.5 Exciter transient hardness RESONATOR Decay 50 to 3000 ms 600 Lowest-mode ring time (T60) RESONATOR Spacing 20 to 600 Hz 200 Modal frequency spacing (higher is more metallic) RESONATOR Inharmonicity 0 to 1 0 Upper-mode spreading (0 even, 1 widest)

At low Spacing the Djembe reads as a pitched tom; raise it for a more metallic, gong-like character.

docs.title: Bell
docs.text:
A struck, fixed-pitch modal church-bell model.

Column Control Range Default Description EXCITER Position 0 to 1 0.3 Strike position on the bell (0 centre, 1 edge) EXCITER Tone 500 to 12000 Hz (log) 7000 Exciter brightness EXCITER Sharpness 0 to 1 0.25 Exciter transient hardness RESONATOR Decay 300 to 40000 ms 8000 Ring time (T60); cathedral-long at the top, tine-short at the bottom

docs.title: Macros, modulation, and presets
docs.text: Each model is a standard MAGDA device, so its parameters accept macros and modulators, and patches save and recall through the preset system.

docs.title: AI sound design
docs.text: Click the AI icon in the device header and describe the sound you want. The agent reads this device's own parameters and their real-world ranges, then writes values into them. See Per-Device AI Panel.

docs.title: Poly Sequencer
docs.text:
The Poly Sequencer is a polyphonic step-sequencer MIDI device. Where the Step Sequencer plays one note per step, the Poly Sequencer can place a full chord — up to eight notes — on each step, and it switches between a melodic keyboard grid and a drum-lane grid.

The faceplate has the steps on the left and the time bend on the right. The sidebar's Show the time bend toggle hides or shows the time bend; the choice is saved with the device.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
A strip across the top of the steps holds the pattern's settings:

Setting Range Description Rate 1/4. to 1/32, with dotted (.) and triplet (T) values How fast the sequencer advances Steps 1–32 Number of steps in the pattern Gate 5–100% Default note length as a percentage of the step Dir Fwd, Rev, P-P, Rnd Playback direction: forward, reverse, ping-pong or random View Keys, Drums Switches the grid between the keyboard and drum lanes

Right-click the strip or the step ruler for Quantize and Quantize Sub; see Time Bend below.

The device header holds AI, Randomize pattern, Step record, MIDI thru (passes incoming notes through to the downstream instrument), and Copy (Click to copy pattern, drag to timeline), the same buttons as on the Step Sequencer.

docs.title: Pattern Views
docs.text:
Under the settings strip, a ruler numbers the steps and lights the one playing. Below it sits the grid, in one of two views. When the device is too short for the grid, as at the device chain's standard height, a row of step boxes stands in for it. Each box names the step's note, its chord (such as Am7) or its note count; click a box to toggle notes on that step from a pop-up keyboard, or from a list of drums in the Drums view.

The expand button at the start of the ruler (Expand into the arrangement) lends the grid to the arrangement, where it has room to work, while the step boxes stay in the device. Only one faceplate can be out at a time. Its collapse button, or Esc, puts it back.

docs.title: Keys view
docs.text: A piano-roll grid: rows are pitches (with a keyboard on the left), columns are steps. Click a cell to add or remove a note at that pitch and step — stack several in one column to build a chord. Notes draw as bars that run on through the steps tied to them. The up/down buttons beside the keyboard shift the rows by an octave, the +/− buttons zoom between one and four octaves, and the mouse wheel scrolls or zooms.

docs.title: Drums view
docs.text:
An x0x-style lane grid, one lane per drum sound. If a Drum Grid device sits downstream on the same track, the Poly Sequencer reads its pads and names the lanes to match; otherwise it falls back to a General MIDI drum map (Kick, Snare, CHat, OHat, LTom, MTom, Crash, Ride). Notes that don't match a lane appear as extra lanes you can still edit.

Right-click any step in either view for Mute Step (or Unmute Step), Clear Step, and a Pattern submenu (shift by a semitone or octave, clear the pattern).

docs.title: Per-Step Lanes
docs.text:
Below the grid, four lanes set values for every step:

  • Gate — toggle the step's gate on or off.
  • Tie — tie the step to the previous one so the note sustains without retriggering.
  • Velocity — drag to set step velocity.
  • Prob — drag to set the probability that the step fires, for humanised or evolving patterns.

docs.title: Time Bend
docs.text:
The Time Bend column reshapes step timing across the pattern, the same idea as in the Step Sequencer and Arpeggiator. Drag the curve's points and bend its segments, right-click a point for a hard corner, or start from a SHAPE. GROOVE loads a groove's curve; AMOUNT sets how much of the bend is heard and CYCLES repeats it within the pattern. The TIME | DYNAMICS switch draws a level per step instead, which scales each step's velocity as it plays; the velocities in the pattern are left as they are.

Quantize (0–100%, in the right-click menu) pulls the bent steps back toward a grid of Quantize Sub divisions (16–512) of the bend's cycle. The time bend has its own expand button, which moves it into the arrangement.

docs.title: AI Pattern Generation
docs.text: Describe the pattern you want — "4-on-the-floor kick", "lo-fi seventh chords", "hi-hat rolls" — in the device's AI panel and let its agent fill the grid. The agent reads the current view and, in the Drums view, the downstream drum lanes, so generated drum hits land on the right pads. Fields you leave alone in the request are preserved, so you can regenerate just the notes without losing your rate or step count.

docs.title: Poly Synth
docs.text: Poly Synth is a 16-voice subtractive synthesizer built into MAGDA. Four detunable oscillators, with up to eight stereo unison copies, feed two multimode state-variable filters in series or in parallel, followed by an amplitude ADSR. It plays in poly, mono, or legato modes.

docs.title: Faceplate
docs.text:
The faceplate has three panels, each with two tabs:

  • OSC and VOICE - the oscillators, and unison with the performance controls
  • FILTER 1 and FILTER 2 - the two filters, their routing, and a response curve
  • AMP ENV and FILTER ENV - the two envelopes

The Show the oscillators toggle in the device's sidebar hides the first panel, OSC and VOICE together, to make the device narrower.

docs.title: Oscillators
docs.text:
The OSC tab has a row per oscillator, under the column heads LVL, CRS, FINE, and RST. Oscillators 2 to 4 start silent (level -60 dB), so a fresh patch sounds from Osc 1 alone until you bring the others up.

Parameter Range Default Description Wave Sine / Saw / Square / Triangle Saw Oscillator waveform Level -60 to 6 dB -12 (Osc 1) Oscillator gain; -60 dB is silent Coarse -24 to 24 st 0 Pitch in semitones Fine -100 to 100 cents 0 Pitch in cents

The row starts with the waveform's icon; click it to pick another wave from a menu. The dot beside the icon turns the oscillator on and off (on by default); a disabled oscillator's row greys out. Tick RST to reset the oscillator's phase on every note-on, for a consistent attack.

docs.title: Unison and voice
docs.text:
The VOICE tab holds unison and the performance controls. Poly, Mono, and Legato run across the top.

Parameter Range Default Description Voice Mode Poly / Mono / Legato Poly Voicing Voices 1 / 2 / 4 / 8 1 Unison copies of the oscillators Detune 0 to 100 cents 20 How far the copies spread either side of the played pitch Spread 0 to 1 0.5 Stereo width of the copies Glide 0 to 2000 ms 0 Portamento time (mono and legato only) Bend 0 to 24 st 2 Pitch-wheel range Output -60 to 6 dB 0 Master output level Vel>Amp 0 to 1 1 Velocity to amplitude depth Vel>Cut 0 to 6 oct 0 Velocity to filter cutoff depth, on both filters

With Voices above 1, every note plays that many copies of all four oscillators, spaced evenly across the Detune range. Spread pans them to alternate sides, wider towards the outer copies. The copies are mixed so that more voices don't get louder. Detune and Spread dim while Voices is 1.

Unison costs CPU in proportion to the copies. In a measured worst case, all four oscillators and both filters at 6 poles, 16 held notes at 8 voices took about a quarter of one CPU core, against under a tenth with unison off.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
Poly Synth has two state-variable filters, on the FILTER 1 and FILTER 2 tabs. The dot on each tab turns that filter on or off; Filter 1 starts on and Filter 2 off. A filter that is off passes its input straight through.

Parameter Range Default Description Type LP / HP / BP / Notch LP Filter response, picked from icons Poles 2 / 4 / 6 2 Filter steepness Cutoff 50 to 18000 Hz (log) 3000 Filter frequency Reso 0 to 0.95 0.3 Resonance Env Amt -4 to 4 oct 0 Filter envelope depth on cutoff (bipolar) Drive 0 to 1 0 Pre-filter saturation

Each filter has its own set of these. More poles cut more steeply, with the resonance on the last stage only. Switching the type or the poles while a note plays fades between them rather than clicking. The response curve beside the tiles draws the selected tab's filter.

The two filters share the filter envelope and Vel>Cut.

docs.title: Routing
docs.text:
The icons at the right of the panel's tabs set the routing:

  • Serial runs Filter 1 into Filter 2.
  • Parallel feeds both filters from the oscillators and mixes them by Blend: 0 is Filter 1 alone, 1 is Filter 2 alone, 0.5 (the default) is an even mix. Blend dims in Serial.

Poles replace the 12 dB and 24 dB slopes of earlier versions. A patch saved at 24 dB now plays as 4 poles, with one resonant peak where it had two. When you open a project that used the 4OSC synth, MAGDA offers to convert each one to a Poly Synth; see Project Migrations.

docs.title: Envelopes
docs.text:
The AMP ENV and FILTER ENV tabs each show an envelope graph above four tiles. Drag the handles on the graph, or edit the tiles.

Parameter Range Default Description Attack 1 to 2000 ms 5 Envelope attack Decay 1 to 2000 ms 200 Envelope decay Sustain 0 to 1 0.7 Sustain level Release 1 to 4000 ms 400 Envelope release

Both envelopes have the same ranges and defaults. The amp envelope shapes each note's level; the filter envelope moves both filters' cutoffs by their Env Amt.

docs.title: MPE
docs.text:
Poly Synth responds to per-note expression, as an MPE clip plays it (see Pitch Glides):

  • Pitch bend on a member channel (2 to 16) moves only the note on that channel, at a fixed range of ±48 semitones.
  • Timbre (CC74) moves both filters' cutoffs, up to 3 octaves either way.
  • Pressure lifts the note's level by up to 6 dB.

The pitch wheel on channel 1 is the ordinary wheel: it moves every note, by Bend. A keyboard set to send on any other channel has its wheel read as per-note bend at ±48 semitones, so set it to channel 1 to play with Bend.

docs.title: Macros, modulation, and presets
docs.text: Like every MAGDA instrument, Poly Synth lives in the standard device slot, so its parameters can be driven by macros and modulators, and patches save and recall through the preset system.

docs.title: AI sound design
docs.text: Click the AI icon in the device header and describe the sound you want. The agent reads this device's own parameters and their real-world ranges, then writes values into them. See Per-Device AI Panel.

docs.title: Sampler
docs.text: The Sampler is MAGDA's built-in sample player. It plays one sample chromatically across the keyboard, or a map of zones spread over keys and velocities. Every voice has its own pitch envelope, filter, and amplitude envelope. It also imports SFZ, DecentSampler, and SoundFont (SF2/SF3) instruments.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Sampler has 8 voices. Every zone a note falls into plays on its own voice, so a note that answers two layered zones takes two. When all voices are busy, a playing voice is stolen for the new note.

The faceplate has four tabs, Sample, Pitch, Filter, and Amp, each a plot with its controls beside it. The Show the zones toggle in the device's sidebar opens a left panel with two tabs: ZONES, the zone list, and VOICE.

docs.title: Loading samples
docs.text:
• Drag an audio file from the Media Explorer or your file manager onto the Sampler.
  • Or click the empty waveform area, which shows a + and Drop a sample or click to load, to open a file chooser. It accepts WAV, AIFF, FLAC, Ogg, and MP3 files, and the instrument formats described under Importing instruments.

Once a sample is loaded, a strip over the waveform shows its name, its ROOT note, and a folder button that loads another. The root note comes from the file's metadata when it has one, and is C3 (note 60) otherwise. Drag or type in the root box to change it; it reads note names such as C3, F#2, or Bb1.

Dropping one sample on the device replaces the current one. Dropping several files, or a folder, builds a zone map from them (see Mapping by name). Choosing several files in the file chooser does the same.

docs.title: Sample tab
docs.text:
The waveform draws the way an audio clip does, one lane per channel. A ruler runs along the top in seconds; right-click it to switch to samples. Use the scroll bar underneath to zoom and scroll.

The START, END, LOOP IN, and LOOP OUT boxes beside the waveform set the playback region in frames. Type a value, or click the arrows to step one frame at a time. You can also drag the markers on the waveform.

The loop switch beside the tabs turns looping on. While it is on, it lights, a held note repeats the stretch between the loop markers, and the waveform shows the loop region and its markers. While it is off, the waveform shows the start and end markers, and LOOP IN and LOOP OUT are greyed out and locked.

docs.title: Expanding the waveform
docs.text:
The expand button beside the loop switch (Expand into the arrangement) opens the waveform on its own across the arrangement area, with its ruler, scroll bar, and markers. While it is out, its place on the device reads The waveform is in the arrangement, and the Pitch, Filter, and Amp tabs stay usable. Click the collapse button in the expanded view, or press Esc, to put it back.

The expand button in the device header opens the zone map over the waveform instead. Only one is ever out: clicking the other button swaps them.

docs.title: Pitch tab
docs.text:
Parameter Range Default Description Pitch -24 to 24 st 0 Transpose in semitones Fine -100 to 100 cents 0 Detune in cents Env -48 to 48 st 0 Pitch envelope depth Attack 1 ms to 5 s 1 ms Pitch envelope attack Decay 1 ms to 5 s 200 ms Pitch envelope decay Sustain 0 to 100% 0% Pitch envelope sustain level Release 1 ms to 10 s 100 ms Pitch envelope release

The pitch envelope bends each note by up to Env semitones, for drum thumps, risers, and plucks from a single sample. A negative depth bends the note down, and the plot hangs the shape from the top. At 0 the envelope does nothing. Drag the handles on the plot to shape it.

docs.title: Filter tab
docs.text:
Each voice runs its own filter. Pick the engine from the dropdown in the tab's heading: Off, SVF, Ladder, Korg 35, Oberheim, Sallen-Key, Diode, or Comb. It starts Off, and the other controls dim until you choose one.

Parameter Range Default Description Mode Depends on the engine LP Filter response, picked from icons Poles 2 / 4 / 6 2 SVF steepness Cutoff 20 Hz to 20 kHz 1 kHz Filter frequency Res 0 to 100% 0% Resonance Key 0 to 100% 0% How far the cutoff follows the played note Vel 0 to 100% 0% How far velocity opens the cutoff Env -72 to 72 st 0 Filter envelope depth Attack 1 ms to 5 s 1 ms Filter envelope attack Decay 1 ms to 5 s 300 ms Filter envelope decay Sustain 0 to 100% 0% Filter envelope sustain level Release 1 ms to 10 s 100 ms Filter envelope release

Mode is a row of icons for the responses the chosen engine has; hover one for its name. The SVF has LP, BP, HP, Notch, and Notch+, a notch at the cutoff between two resonant peaks half an octave either side. Comb has Comb+ and Comb-. Poles applies to the SVF's LP, BP, HP, and Notch: more poles cut more steeply, with the resonance on the last stage.

docs.title: Amp tab
docs.text: Parameter Range Default Description Attack 1 ms to 5 s 1 ms Time to reach full level after a note-on Decay 1 ms to 5 s 100 ms Time to fall from peak to sustain level Sustain 0 to 100% 100% Level held while the note is held Release 1 ms to 10 s 100 ms Time to fade out after note-off Level -60 to 12 dB 0 Output level Velocity 0 to 100% 100% Velocity to amplitude depth

docs.title: Voice tab
docs.text:
The VOICE tab in the left panel holds two controls:

  • Voice Mode - Poly plays a voice per note. Mono plays one note at a time and retriggers on each new note. Legato also plays one note at a time, but overlapping notes slide to the new pitch without retriggering. In Mono and Legato, a note plays the first zone that answers it.
  • Glide - portamento time in Mono and Legato, 0 to 2000 ms.

docs.title: Zones
docs.text:
A zone is a sample with its own root note, key and velocity ranges with fades, tune, gain, start and end markers, loop switch, and loop points, and a round-robin switch. Every zone a note's key and velocity fall into plays, scaled by its fades.

With a single sample, the Sampler is one zone whose markers are device parameters: you can automate START, END, LOOP IN, and LOOP OUT and link them to macros and modulators. Once there is a zone list, each zone keeps its own markers, root, and loop, and the faceplate edits the selected zone. Editing the list back down to one zone returns it to the single-sample form.

docs.title: Zone list
docs.text:
The ZONES tab lists the zones the way a rack lists its chains. Each row shows the zone's file name, or Zone N while it has no sample. Click a row to select it; the strip over the waveform then reads the file name with zone N of M.

The list has three views:

View What each row shows MIX A gain slider (-48 to 12 dB) and a button to remove the zone KEY The key range as a bar, with its fades on the shoulders VEL The velocity range as a bar, and the RR switch

On a range bar, drag an end to set the range, the middle to move it, or a top corner to fade in or out. Double-click for the whole range.

Add zone at the foot of the list adds an empty zone. Drop a sample on a zone's row to fill it; the zone keeps its ranges, tune, and gain. Dropping samples elsewhere on the list adds each as a new zone. With a zone list, loading a single sample, by the folder button or by dropping it on the waveform, fills the selected zone instead of replacing the map.

docs.title: Round robin
docs.text: Zones with RR on take turns. Of the RR zones a note falls into, only one plays, and the next note plays the next one. Zones with RR off always play. Use it to alternate between several takes of the same hit.

docs.title: Mapping by name
docs.text:
When you drop several samples or a folder, the Sampler reads a note from each file name: a note name such as C3, F#2, or Db-1 (C3 is note 60), or a number from 0 to 127. A note name wins over a number. A file with neither uses the root note in its metadata; anything left over is placed one key at a time above the highest mapped note, or from C3 when nothing is.

Each root's key range reaches halfway to its neighbours, and the lowest and highest zones extend to the ends of the keyboard. Several files on the same note become velocity layers that split the velocity range evenly, in file-name order.

docs.title: Zone map
docs.text:
The device header's expand button opens the zone map over the selected zone's waveform. Along the top are the selected zone's Root, Low key, High key, Low vel, High vel, Tune (-1200 to 1200 cents), and Gain (-48 to 12 dB).

Below them is a grid of key across and velocity up, with each zone drawn as a box and its root as a tick on the box's floor. Drag a box's edges to change its ranges, or its middle to move it; the root moves with it. Right-click a zone for Remove zone, or select it and press Backspace or Del.

Drop one sample on the grid to add a zone on the key under the pointer, covering that key alone. Drop several, or a folder, to map them by name.

docs.title: Importing instruments
docs.text:
Drop or load an .sfz, .dspreset (DecentSampler), .sf2, or .sf3 file to replace the Sampler's zones with the instrument's. The instrument's envelopes and filter go onto the device's own controls. A toast says how many zones came in and lists what the Sampler can't play under Not imported.

Envelope, filter, and velocity settings the file doesn't set go back to their defaults, so the previous sound's filter doesn't carry over. Level, Pitch, Fine, Voice Mode, and Glide keep their values.

docs.title: SFZ
docs.text:
Settings inherit through <control>, <global>, <master>, <group>, and <region>, and #define and #include work. Each region becomes a zone with:

  • key and velocity ranges, with crossfades
  • root note (pitch_keycenter), tune, and transpose. SFZ calls note 60 C4, where MAGDA calls it C3.
  • volume and amplitude, including the global, master, and group volumes
  • offset and end, and loop mode. When the SFZ sets no loop, a loop stored in the WAV file plays.
  • round robin from seq_length

The amplitude, pitch, and filter envelopes, and the filter type, cutoff, resonance, key tracking, and velocity tracking, are device-wide on the Sampler, so they come from the first region. Regions that set them differently are listed in the toast.

Layers switched by MIDI CC, MIDI program, or keyswitch keep only what plays at load time: each CC at its set_cc value, program 0, and the default keyswitch. Other features the Sampler can't play are listed in the toast rather than imported, among them LFOs, CC modulation, choke groups, velocity curves, release triggers, and random round robin (which plays in turn).

docs.title: DecentSampler
docs.text: The same settings are read from a .dspreset's groups and samples. Low-pass, band-pass, high-pass, and notch filter effects map onto the Sampler's filter; other effects are listed as not imported.

docs.title: SF2 and SF3
docs.text:
A SoundFont holds many presets, so a menu asks which one to import, grouped by bank when there is more than one bank. The chosen preset's samples are written as WAV files to a SoundFonts folder in MAGDA's data folder (set in Settings > Paths), and the zones play those files. SF3 samples are decoded, and linked stereo pairs become one stereo file.

Attenuation is scaled by 0.4, as FluidSynth and E-mu hardware do, which is how General MIDI banks are voiced. The envelopes and filter come from the zone that plays note 60.

docs.title: Macros, modulation, and presets
docs.text: The Sampler sits in the standard device slot, so its parameters accept macros and modulators, and its settings save and recall through the preset system.

docs.title: Step Sequencer
docs.text:
The Step Sequencer is a MIDI device that generates melodic and rhythmic patterns from a row of up to 32 programmable steps. Each step has a note and switches for gate, tie, glide and accent — giving you precise control over every note in the sequence.

Need chords or a drum grid?

The Step Sequencer is monophonic — one note per step. For chords (up to eight notes per step) and a switchable keyboard/drum view, use the Poly Sequencer.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Step Sequencer sits on a track's device chain before an instrument. It plays through a pattern of steps in sync with the project tempo, independent of any MIDI input. Steps can be programmed by clicking them, playing notes via step recording, or generating patterns with AI.

The faceplate has the steps on the left and the time bend on the right. The sidebar's Show the time bend toggle hides or shows the time bend; the choice is saved with the device.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
A strip across the top of the steps holds the pattern's settings:

Setting Range Description Rate 1/4. to 1/32, with dotted (.) and triplet (T) values How fast the sequencer advances through steps Steps 1–32 Number of steps in the pattern Gate 5–100% Note length as a percentage of the step duration Dir Fwd, Rev, P-P, Rnd Playback direction: forward, reverse, ping-pong or random

Right-click the strip or the step ruler for the settings that have no box of their own:

  • Quantize and Quantize Sub — see Time Bend below.
  • Velocity — the velocity of ordinary steps, 1–127.
  • Accent Velocity — the velocity of accented steps, 1–127.

docs.title: The Steps
docs.text:
Under the settings strip, a ruler numbers the steps and lights the one playing. Below it, each step has a note box, then four rows of switches. Click a switch to toggle it:

  • Gate — whether the step plays. A rest shows as a dot in its note box.
  • Tie — carries the previous note on through the step instead of retriggering it.
  • Glide — holds the step for its full length so the next note slides in from it. Tie and glide exclude each other.
  • Accent — plays the step at the Accent Velocity.

Click a note box to pick the step's note from a pop-up keyboard. When the device has the height for it, a keyboard under the note boxes sets the selected step's note instead, with Octave buttons to move it.

Shift-drag one note box onto another to copy that step. Right-click a step for Mute Step (or Unmute Step), Copy to All Steps, Clear Step and Clear Pattern.

The expand button at the start of the ruler (Expand into the arrangement) lends the note editor to the arrangement, where it becomes a piano roll with a column per step. Click a cell to put that step's note there, and click it again to rest the step; the mouse wheel scrolls and zooms the rows. Only one faceplate can be out at a time. Its collapse button, or Esc, puts it back.

docs.title: Time Bend
docs.text:
The Time Bend column reshapes step timing within each cycle, the same way it works in the Arpeggiator. Steps that would normally fire on a rigid grid follow the curve instead — compressing some and expanding others.

Drag the curve's points and bend its segments, right-click a point for a hard corner, or start from a SHAPE. GROOVE loads a groove's curve; AMOUNT sets how much of the bend is heard and CYCLES repeats it within the pattern. The TIME | DYNAMICS switch draws a level per step instead, which scales each step's velocity as it plays; the velocities set on the device are left as they are. See Time Bend for the editor itself.

Quantize (0–100%, in the right-click menu) pulls the bent steps back toward a grid of Quantize Sub divisions (16–512) of the bend's cycle.

AMOUNT and CYCLES can be linked to Macros for real-time timing modulation. The time bend has its own expand button, which moves it into the arrangement.

docs.title: Header Buttons
docs.text:
The Step Sequencer's own buttons sit in the device header:

  • AI — opens the device's AI panel; see AI Pattern Generation.
  • Randomize pattern — fills the steps with a random pattern.
  • Step record — enters step recording.
  • MIDI thru — passes incoming MIDI through to the downstream instrument alongside the sequencer output, so you can play live over the sequence.
  • Copy (Click to copy pattern, drag to timeline) — click to copy the pattern, or drag it onto the timeline to make a MIDI clip of it.

docs.title: Step Recording
docs.text: Click the step record button to enter step recording mode. Play a note on your MIDI controller and it will be placed on the current step, then the cursor advances to the next step. This is a fast way to input melodies without clicking the steps.

docs.title: AI Pattern Generation
docs.text:
The Step Sequencer can generate patterns using AI:

  1. Click the AI icon in the device header to open its AI panel
  2. Type a description (e.g. "acid techno bassline") and press Enter
  3. The agent fills the steps with a matching pattern

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text: • Arrangement loop boundary: The Step Sequencer may produce a brief timing glitch when the arrangement transport loops back to the start. This does not affect session clips or non-looping playback.

docs.title: Strum
docs.text: Strum is a MIDI device that turns a held chord into a strum, a roll or a quick arpeggio. Instead of every note starting at once, the notes start one after another, spaced along a curve you choose.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Strum sits on a track's device chain before an instrument, like the Arpeggiator. It works with any instrument, MAGDA's own or a plugin. Play a chord and Strum sends its notes on in the chosen order, spread over the Strum Length. The notes keep the velocities you played.

The panel beside the parameters shows where each strummed note lands in time for the current Shape and Cycles. It previews the timing, not a particular chord.

docs.title: Triggering
docs.text:
Trigger sets when a strum happens:
