  • Chord strums once each time you play a chord. Strum waits a moment after the first note so the whole chord is caught, and strums again if you add a note. The notes ring until you release the chord.
  • Loop strums the held chord over and over until you release it. Each new strum ends the notes of the one before.

In Loop mode, Loop Sync sets how the gap between strums is measured: Time uses Sync Interval in milliseconds, and Beat uses Loop Rate, a note value that follows the project tempo.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Range Default Description Trigger Chord, Loop Chord Strum once per chord, or repeatedly while it's held Order Up, Down, Up/Down, As Played Up The order the notes start in. Up goes from the lowest note, Down from the highest, Up/Down goes up then back down, and As Played follows the order you pressed the keys. Shape Linear, Ease In, Ease Out, Snap, Spike, S-Curve, Overshoot, Bounce Ease In The curve that spaces the notes across the strum Cycles 1–8 1 Splits the strum into that many short strums, each following the shape Strum Length 1–400 ms 90 ms Time from the first note to the last Loop Sync Time, Beat Time In Loop mode, measure the gap between strums in milliseconds or note values Loop Rate 1/1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/4T, 1/8, 1/8T, 1/16, 1/16T 1/4 Gap between strums with Loop Sync set to Beat Sync Interval 60–2000 ms 500 ms Gap between strums with Loop Sync set to Time

docs.title: Macros, modulation, and presets
docs.text: Strum sits in the standard device slot, so its parameters accept macros and modulators, and its settings save and recall through the preset system.

docs.title: First Session
docs.text: This guide walks you through creating your first project in MAGDA.

docs.title: Creating a New Project
docs.text:
1. Launch MAGDA
  2. Select File > New Project

You choose where the project is kept the first time you save it.

docs.title: Adding a Track
docs.text: Press Ctrl+T (or Cmd+T on macOS) to add a new track, or use Track > Add Track from the menu.

docs.title: Recording Audio
docs.text:
1. Set up your audio input in Settings > Audio & MIDI (Cmd+, on macOS, Ctrl+, on Windows and Linux). See Audio & MIDI.
  2. Arm a track for recording by clicking its R button
  3. Press the Record button in the transport bar
  4. Press Space to stop

docs.title: Navigating Between Views
docs.text:
Use the mode buttons in the footer bar at the bottom of the window, or F1, F2 and F3, to switch between views:

  • Live — Session view with clip launcher
  • Arrange — Timeline arrangement view
  • Mix — Full mixer with channel strips

docs.title: Saving Your Work
docs.text: Use Ctrl+S (or Cmd+S on macOS) to save. Use Ctrl+Shift+S (or Cmd+Shift+S) to save as a new file.

docs.title: System Requirements
docs.text:
Minimum Recommended OS macOS 11+ (Apple Silicon or Intel), Windows 10 (64-bit), Linux with glibc 2.39 or newer (Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 13) Latest stable release RAM 4 GB 8 GB+ Disk 200 MB 500 MB+ (for projects and audio files) Audio Built-in audio output Dedicated audio interface

Optional models, such as a local LLM or the stem separation weights, are separate downloads with their own sizes. See AI.

Intel Macs

The Intel Mac build doesn't include the ONNX runtime, so a few features are missing there: Transcribe to MIDI, the Demucs and Spleeter engines of Split into Stems (HPSS still works), the Media Library's semantic search and "find similar sounds", tempo detection with the beat tracker, and the larger command model for Fast Inference. Everything else, including the embedded local LLM, works as on Apple Silicon.

docs.title: Download
docs.text:
Download the latest release from the GitHub Releases page. Each release has one file per platform:

Platform File macOS, Apple Silicon MAGDA-<version>-macOS-arm64.dmg macOS, Intel MAGDA-<version>-macOS-x86_64.dmg Windows MAGDA-<version>-Windows-x86_64-Setup.exe Linux MAGDA-<version>-Linux-x86_64.AppImage

Each file has a .sha256 file beside it, for checking the download.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text: MAGDA checks the GitHub releases feed at most once every 24 hours on launch and shows a dialog only if a newer version is available. You can also run the check from Help > Check for Updates…. A pre-release build, such as a beta, is also told about newer pre-releases. No telemetry is sent.

docs.title: Building from Source
docs.text: MAGDA is built with CMake and requires a C++23 compiler. See the README for full build instructions.

docs.title: Audio Setup
docs.text:
On first launch, open Settings > Audio & MIDI (see Audio & MIDI) to configure:

  • Driver and Interface — Select your audio interface or built-in output
  • Sample Rate — 44100 Hz or 48000 Hz are common choices
  • Buffer Size — Lower values reduce latency but increase CPU load

docs.title: AI
docs.text:
The AI section of Settings configures the providers and models behind MAGDA's AI features: the AI Assistant chat, the per-device sound-design panels, the Media Library's Sample Analyzer, and Stem Separation. It has three tabs.

Tab Purpose Assistant Choose which providers the AI agents use, and how they trade off quality, speed, and cost Providers Add API keys for cloud providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, DeepSeek, OpenRouter) Local models Set up the embedded local model, and download every optional model

Changes wait for Apply, except downloads, removals and model folders on the Local models tab, which take effect straight away.

docs.title: Assistant
docs.text:
The Assistant tab decides which providers the AI agents actually use. A status in the tab row sums up the current choice. Setup picks how much control you want:

  • Simple — one decision that applies to every agent.
  • Advanced — a provider and model per agent role.

docs.title: Simple setup
docs.text:
Setting Description Run on Local (every agent uses a local model), Cloud (every agent uses a cloud provider), or Hybrid (a mix) Source In Local mode: Embedded (the built-in llama.cpp engine, set up under Local models > Local LLM) or Local server (an OpenAI-compatible server you run yourself) Provider Which cloud provider to use, from the keys on the Providers tab. Shown for Cloud and Hybrid Optimize for Quality or Cost in Cloud mode; Speed or Cost in Hybrid mode

In Local mode the provider and optimize options are hidden, since everything runs locally.

docs.title: Local Server (OpenAI-compatible)
docs.text:
With Source set to Local server, MAGDA talks to a server that speaks the OpenAI API, such as Ollama, LM Studio, GPUStack, or a plain llama.cpp server.

  • Model — pick the model the server should use. Refresh asks the server for its model list; you can also type a model id directly.

MAGDA looks for the server at http://localhost:11434/v1, Ollama's default address. To use another address, or a server that needs an API key, quit MAGDA and set localServerUrl and localServerApiKey in the ai block of config.json.

One server and one model serve all agent roles, the same way the embedded model does.

docs.title: Advanced setup
docs.text:
Advanced replaces the single choice with a grid, one row per agent role. Each row has its own provider and model, drawn from the keys on the Providers tab and the local backends available. Switching from Simple to Advanced seeds the grid from your simple settings, so you can start there and adjust only the rows you care about.

Agent Handles Command Turning chat requests into DSL operations on tracks, clips, and devices Music Generating musical content — notes, patterns, parts Faust Writing Faust DSP code for custom effects Chord Chord progressions and harmony Controller Controller profiles and scripts Theme Colour themes

Choosing a local provider gives a model dropdown of Embedded or Server. The Command row has a third option, Fast Inference (Command) — see below.

docs.title: Fast Inference (Command)
docs.text:
Fast Inference runs Command requests entirely on your machine with a purpose-built model rather than a general-purpose LLM. It is not a chat model: it reads one command and emits the DSL directly, with no streaming and effectively no wait.

Because it is a single-command tagger, it deliberately ignores conversation history — each request is read on its own. For follow-ups that depend on what you said earlier ("now make it louder"), a general model is the better fit.

Fast Inference works out of the box using a small built-in model. Installing the larger Command model from the Local models tab replaces it and markedly improves how well natural phrasing is understood. Cloud providers never use either one.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text: Switch on Faust DSP to have AI-generated Faust code checked before MAGDA loads it. It needs Node.js: MAGDA starts the checker on demand through npx, so there is nothing else to install, but npx must be on your system PATH. The row says whether npx was found, and Get Node.js opens the Node.js download page. See Effects — Faust validation for details.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
The Providers tab holds API keys for hosted LLM providers. The tab row shows how many keys you have added.

To add a key, pick the provider in the add row (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, DeepSeek, or OpenRouter), paste the key, then click Test to check it and Add to keep it. Test sends one small request to the provider.

Added keys are listed under API keys, each with its own Test and Remove. A provider that already has a key is greyed out in the dropdown. Choose between providers on the Assistant tab.

Keys stay on your machine

API keys are saved in MAGDA's settings file and used only to call the provider you entered them for.

docs.title: Local models
docs.text:
Every optional download lives on the Local models tab, behind the Type dropdown: Local LLM, Sample analysis, Tempo detection, Stem separation and Command model.

Intel Macs

Sample analysis, Tempo detection, Stem separation and the Command model run on the ONNX runtime, which the Intel Mac build of MAGDA doesn't include. On an Intel Mac only Local LLM is listed. Transcribe to MIDI is unavailable there too, and Split into Stems offers HPSS only.

docs.title: Local LLM
docs.text:
Sets up the embedded llama.cpp engine for fully offline AI, with no network calls and no API key.

  • Download a model… — downloads MAGDA's own model, fine-tuned for DAW operations, to a place you choose.
  • File (.gguf) — the model file. Choose… points at any GGUF model of your own.
  • GPU layers — Auto (GPU) offloads everything the GPU can take: Metal on macOS, and Vulkan on Windows and Linux when a Vulkan driver is installed (without one, the model runs on the CPU). CPU Only runs without the GPU, and Custom lets you enter a layer count for cards that run out of memory on Auto.
  • Context length — the context-window size in tokens (default 4096).
  • Load model / Unload — load the model into memory or unload it to free resources. The tab row shows which model is loaded.
  • Load model on startup — when enabled, the model loads automatically each time MAGDA launches.

docs.title: Sample analysis
docs.text:
The Sample Analyzer is the audio-tagging model behind the Media Library's semantic search and "find similar sounds". It is an optional download, separate from the LLM models.

  • The page shows the current install state and the download size.
  • Download Sample Analyzer — fetches the model. Without it, the Library still supports filename, tag, family, shape, key, and BPM filtering, but not text-based semantic search.
  • Models location — where the model is kept. Browse... moves it to another folder, Reset goes back to the default.
  • Load / Unload — bring the analyzer into memory or release it. It also preloads in the background the first time you enter Library mode.
  • Load on startup — load the analyzer each time MAGDA launches.

For how the analyzer is used once installed, see Media Library > AI Sample Analyzer.

docs.title: Tempo detection
docs.text: The beat tracker measures the tempo of samples whose file name and header don't carry one, when the Library indexes them, and lets a clip go into beat mode without you typing a BPM. Without it MAGDA falls back to an estimate that is right far less often. Download Beat Tracker fetches it, and Remove frees the disk space again.

docs.title: Stem separation
docs.text:
Weights for the machine-learning engines behind Split into Stems. The HPSS engine needs nothing here — it is pure signal processing and always available.

Model Size Splits into Demucs (4-stem) 301 MB Drums, Bass, Other, Vocals Spleeter (2-stem) 74 MB Vocals, Accompaniment

Each row shows its install state, a progress bar while downloading, and a Download / Remove button, alongside a link to the HuggingFace repository the weights come from. Models location shows where they are stored.

Choosing an uninstalled engine from a clip's Split into Stems menu opens this page directly.

docs.title: Command model
docs.text:
The larger model behind Fast Inference: a DeBERTa-v3 encoder fine-tuned to read a command and tag its intent and parameters.

  • It is not bundled with MAGDA — the download is 430 MB.
  • Without it, Fast Inference still works using the small built-in model. With it, natural phrasing is understood far more reliably.
  • Models location defaults to MAGDA's data folder. Use Browse... to keep the weights on another drive, or Reset to go back to the default.
  • The Download button turns into Cancel while a download is running, and Remove once installed. The location cannot be changed mid-download.
  • A link to the source HuggingFace repository sits under the model name.

docs.title: Audio & MIDI
docs.text:
The Audio & MIDI section of Settings chooses the audio driver and interface MAGDA plays through, which of its channels are open, and which MIDI ports MAGDA uses. Every change here takes effect as you make it: there is nothing to apply, and the window offers only Done.

MAGDA reopens the driver and interface you chose last time when it starts.

docs.title: Status bar
docs.text:
The bar at the top names the interface that is open, with its channel count (for example 2 in · 2 out), sample rate, buffer size in samples, and the latency that buffer adds in milliseconds. Its dot is green while the interface is open.

When the driver has a settings window of its own, as ASIO drivers on Windows do, a Control Panel… button opens it. Use it for options the driver keeps to itself, such as its buffer size.

docs.title: Device
docs.text:
• Driver — The audio system MAGDA talks to: Core Audio on macOS; ASIO, WASAPI or DirectSound on Windows; ALSA or JACK on Linux. The driver decides which interfaces the pickers below list.
  • Input Interface / Output Interface — The interface to record from and the one to play through. Drivers that open one interface for both directions show a single Interface picker.
  • Sample Rate — 44100 Hz and 48000 Hz are common choices.
  • Buffer Size — Lower values reduce latency but increase CPU load.

Silence after changing the sample rate

Many audio interfaces mute their outputs for a few seconds after a sample rate change while they re-sync their clock, even after the new rate is shown. Anything played in that window is lost, the metronome included, and the same happens with any other app on that interface. Wait a few seconds after switching before you press play or record.

If MAGDA closes unexpectedly while opening an audio driver, it starts the next time with the default driver instead and tells you which one it skipped. Choose a driver again here once you have dealt with the problem.

docs.title: Audio Inputs and Audio Outputs
docs.text:
The two channel lists show the open interface's inputs and outputs, stereo pairs first and then single channels. Tick the ones MAGDA should use: a ticked stereo pair opens both channels as a pair, and ticking the two channels of a pair separately opens them as two mono channels.

Double-click a channel's name to rename it, or right-click it for Rename and Clear Name. MAGDA then shows your names in place of the driver's.

docs.title: Preview
docs.text: • Audition browser files on — The output pair that browser auditioning plays through (see Preview). Point it at a cue or headphone output to audition without going through your main monitors.

docs.title: MIDI Inputs and MIDI Output
docs.text:
• MIDI Inputs — Every MIDI input MAGDA can see, each with its own switch. Turn on the controllers and keyboards you play.
  • MIDI Output — The default MIDI output, or << none >>.
  • Bluetooth MIDI… — Pairs a Bluetooth MIDI device, on systems that support it.

MIDI clock and controller profiles choose their own ports in their sections of Settings.

docs.title: Linux drivers
docs.text:
Most Linux desktops run PipeWire, which accepts JACK, PulseAudio and ALSA clients. Pick the driver for how you want to work:

Driver Device Use it for JACK Your interface Recording and production. Lowest latency, through PipeWire (pipewire-jack) or a JACK server ALSA Pulseaudio output Hearing MAGDA alongside the browser and other apps. Higher latency ALSA A hw: device Direct hardware access. Other apps can't play while MAGDA holds the device

Under JACK, MAGDA lists a card's own physical inputs and outputs only, named channel 1 onwards, and picks your hardware rather than another application. On PipeWire it uses PipeWire's JACK support directly, so you don't need to start MAGDA through pw-jack.

There is no separate PulseAudio driver: the Pulseaudio output device under ALSA goes through PulseAudio, or through pipewire-pulse on PipeWire. It's listed when the ALSA PulseAudio plugin is installed (libasound2-plugins on Debian/Ubuntu, alsa-plugins-pulseaudio on Fedora/Arch).

64 inputs and outputs under ALSA

On PipeWire, ALSA's default device can show up as 64 inputs and 64 outputs instead of your interface, and playback may break. Switch the driver to JACK to see the real interface.

docs.title: Connections
docs.text:
The Connections section of Settings is where you say what is allowed to drive MAGDA from outside it, and what MAGDA keeps in time with. Every change here takes effect as you make it. It has six tabs.

Tab Purpose MCP The endpoint an AI host connects to, and the config to paste into it WebSocket The socket a script or control surface connects to OSC Listen for Open Sound Control, on which interface and port Clients Grant each remote client what it may do, and see what it has done Ableton Link Play in time with other apps on the network MIDI Clock Send MIDI clock to hardware, or follow a clock from it

None of the first four is AI-specific. An AI assistant is one kind of client, but the same permissions cover a Lua script, a bespoke controller, or anything else holding a token. Model and provider configuration lives in AI; MIDI profiles and Lua scripts live in Controllers.

docs.title: MCP and WebSocket are two separate listeners
docs.text:
This is the thing most worth understanding before you touch either switch.

MAGDA's remote API — the thing that lets an outside program inspect and control your session — is served over two transports:

  • MCP, which is what an AI host such as Claude speaks.
  • WebSocket, which is what a script, a custom tool, or a control surface speaks, and which also pushes changes back to you as they happen.

They are genuinely separate. Each has its own switch, its own port, and its own token. Turning one on does not turn on the other, and neither needs the other to work — if you only ever use an AI host, leave the WebSocket off; if you drive MAGDA from a Python script and use no AI host, leave MCP off.

What they share is everything past the socket: the same set of operations, and the same per-client permissions on the Clients tab. A client granted edit gets edit whichever transport it arrives over.

See the Remote API Reference for connection framing, schema discovery, revisions and retries, subscriptions, errors, and the complete operation catalogue.

OSC is not one of them. It is a different protocol on a different stack, with no token, no client list, and no permissions — an OSC surface can do what OSC surfaces can do, and it will never appear on the Clients tab. It is in this section because it is another way into MAGDA from outside, not because it shares any of the above.

docs.title: MCP
docs.text:
• Enable the MCP endpoint — Opens and closes the listener immediately, not at the next launch. It listens on this machine only.
  • Rotate token — Throws this endpoint's credential away and mints a new one, disconnecting every MCP client after asking. WebSocket clients are unaffected. Clients that read the token file find the new one by themselves.

Below the switch, MCP host configuration holds the exact JSON to paste into an MCP host's config, using this install's own paths, with a Copy button. It stays correct across restarts: the helper it names finds MAGDA's current port and token each time, so neither has to be written down.

On Linux inside an AppImage, MAGDA stages magda-mcp into its data directory the first time this page is opened and updates that stable copy when the AppImage changes.

docs.title: WebSocket
docs.text:
• Enable the WebSocket API — Same immediate effect, on its own listener, also on this machine only.
  • Rotate token — The mirror image of the MCP one: drops WebSocket clients only.

Connect to shows the URL, including the ?client= query string. Name your client there — that name is what gets its own row and its own permissions on the Clients tab. A client that sends no name is lumped in with every other anonymous caller and stays read-only.

The token itself is never shown. It is regenerated every run and written to an owner-only file, shown under Token & port file with Reveal and Copy path; read it from there rather than copying it, because a token pasted somewhere permanent stops being valid the moment MAGDA restarts.

docs.title: Clients
docs.text:
A client that connects for the first time can read only. If your assistant reports that it cannot create a track or start playback, that is not a bug — nothing has been granted yet.

Each client MAGDA has heard from over either transport gets a row, listed by the name it reported and tagged with the transport it came in over. Tick what you want it to be able to do:

Permission Lets the client read Inspect the project. Always on. edit Change tempo, tracks, clips, notes, devices, and automation transport Play, stop, record-arm, loop, and seek session Launch and stop session clips and scenes hardware-midi Send channel messages and SysEx to physical MIDI outputs.

Changes apply to the client's next request. There is nothing to restart and no need to reconnect.

Each row also has Disconnect, which drops the client's current connections, and Forget, which discards its permissions. Forget does not disconnect: the client reverts to read-only and stays connected. Forget all disconnected, in the tab row, clears every client that isn't connected right now.

Grants are remembered between launches, keyed by the reported name. Two clients reporting the same name are one entry. A client that reports nothing is listed as unknown and shares one read-only entry with every other anonymous caller.

docs.title: Recent activity
docs.text: Underneath the client list is a tail of what has actually been asked for, and how it was answered — so tracks.create denied (edit) appears next to the checkbox that would allow it.

docs.title: OSC
docs.text:
MAGDA can be driven by an Open Sound Control surface — a tablet layout, a lighting desk, anything that sends OSC.

MAGDA understands a fixed set of addresses out of the box, so a stock mixer template works with no mapping step. See the OSC Address Reference for what to send and what comes back.

  • Listen for OSC — Whether the socket is open at all.
  • Listen on — All interfaces (0.0.0.0) or This computer only (127.0.0.1). OSC has no authentication, so which interfaces answer is the whole of its access control; loopback is the safe default if the surface runs on this machine.
  • Receive port — Where MAGDA listens. Committed when the field loses focus, so typing part of a port number does not rebind the socket.
  • Feedback port — Where MAGDA answers.

There is no "send feedback to" address. MAGDA reads the datagrams it receives, so it answers whoever is talking to it.

The status area below reports whether the socket is open, how many messages have arrived, and one line per surface MAGDA has heard from with its message counts and when it was last heard. A surface listed with nothing arriving and a surface never listed at all are different problems, which is why the list is there rather than just a counter.

If OSC is enabled but not listening, the port was taken by another application.

docs.title: Ableton Link
docs.text:
Ableton Link keeps MAGDA in time with other apps on the same network that have Link switched on. While Link is on, every app in the session shares one tempo, and MAGDA ignores its own tempo automation.

Setting Description Ableton Link Enabled or Disabled. Saved for you, not per project Start Stop Sync Share play and stop with the other apps in the session. Off by default Output latency offset (ms) From −500 to 500. Raise it if MAGDA sounds late against the other apps, lower it if it sounds early

When you press Play, or launch a Session clip while stopped, MAGDA waits for the session to reach the same point in the bar before it starts, never more than a bar. The Link chip in the transport blinks while a start is waiting; see Transport — Ableton Link. The footer also shows an Ableton Link pill with the number of peers while Link is on; click it to come back to this tab.

With Start Stop Sync on:

  • Anything that starts or stops MAGDA's transport reaches the session: Play, Record, Stop, or a Session launch from stopped.
  • When another app starts playing, MAGDA starts from its edit cursor, still waiting for the session's bar position.
  • When another app stops, MAGDA stops too, which also ends a take you are recording.
  • Joining a session that is already playing leaves MAGDA stopped until you press Play.
  • Loading a project stops MAGDA but not the other apps.

Only one sync source is followed at a time. Switching Link on stops following a MIDI clock, and choosing a clock to follow switches Link off.

docs.title: MIDI Clock
docs.text:
• Follow clock from — The MIDI input whose clock MAGDA follows, or None. The list offers the inputs switched on under Audio & MIDI. Following a clock switches Ableton Link off, and tempo automation is ignored while a clock is followed.
  • Send clock to — Tick each MIDI output that should receive clock. While the transport plays, MAGDA sends 24 clocks a beat, with Start, Continue, Stop and Song Position, timed to leave as the audio is heard. With no MIDI outputs connected, this says so.

A device you chose that isn't plugged in keeps its place in the list, marked (not connected). See Transport — MIDI Clock for how MAGDA plays against an external clock.

docs.title: Controllers
docs.text:
MAGDA can be driven by any class-compliant MIDI controller. Hardware knobs, sliders, pads, and pitch/mod wheels can all map to plugin parameters, macros, and LFO rates — with three complementary mapping systems:

  • Automap profiles — a controller-specific profile maps each control to a focused-device macro automatically. Plug in a supported keyboard, focus a device, and the eight macro knobs already drive that device's macros. No setup.
  • MIDI Learn — right-click any parameter, macro, or LFO Rate, choose Learn MIDI, move a controller, done. The mapping is yours and persists with the project.
  • Lua scripts — for controllers that need behaviour profiles can't express (DAW protocols like Mackie Control, motorised feedback, mode switching), load a .lua script that handles raw MIDI directly. See Lua Controller Scripts below.

Profile and Learn'd bindings can coexist — a Learn'd binding shadows automap on the same CC so your custom mapping wins. A loaded Lua script takes the input layer entirely; it owns the controller for as long as it's active.

docs.title: Controllers settings
docs.text:
Controllers have their own section in Settings, Settings > Controllers, with two tabs. Every change there takes effect as you make it.

  • MIDI Profiles — registered hardware controllers with their assigned MIDI input ports
  • Lua Scripts — .lua controller scripts (see Lua Controller Scripts)

docs.title: MIDI Profiles tab
docs.text:
One row per registered controller. Each row shows:

Part Description Status dot Green when the controller is switched on and its MIDI input is connected, dim otherwise Name Manufacturer and model, with Connected, Not connected or Disabled underneath Input port The MIDI input the controller is bound to. Click it to choose another Switch Turns the controller's profile bindings on or off. Switching one on turns off any other controller on the same input

Three buttons sit in the tab row:

  • + Add profile — register a new controller using one of the profiles in your controllers directory. Pops a menu of available profiles and adds the controller with no MIDI input; pick its input on the controller's row.
  • Upload profile… — pick a .json profile from disk and import it. Validates the JSON, copies it into the controllers directory, and refreshes the list. After upload, the new profile is available to + Add profile.
  • Open Profiles Folder — reveals the controllers directory in your file browser.

Right-click a row for Show profile in Finder (reveals the JSON file) or Remove (deletes the controller and its bindings, after asking).

Bindings created by MIDI Learn against a removed controller's port still work — they attach to the live MIDI port name, not to the controller registry entry.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
A profile describes a controller's physical layout — which CC numbers correspond to the eight macro knobs, and so on. MAGDA ships with profiles for common controllers (Launchkey Mini MK3 / MK4, generic 8-knob, etc.) and you can add your own.

When a profile is assigned to a controller and a device is focused, the profile's macro knobs drive that device's macros. Focus a different device — the same hardware knobs follow.

If you only want MIDI Learn (no automap), don't add a controller — Learn'd bindings route via the live port name and don't need a registry entry.

docs.title: Profiles directory
docs.text:
User profiles live alongside MAGDA's other configuration:

Platform Path macOS ~/Library/MAGDA/controllers/ Windows %APPDATA%\MAGDA\controllers\ Linux ~/.config/MAGDA/controllers/

On first launch the bundled profiles are seeded into this folder. Edits and additions there are durable — drop a new *.json profile in and it's available the next time you open Settings > Controllers.

docs.title: Profile JSON format
docs.text: For the full JSON schema, the resolver list (the functions that route a CC to a target — focused.macro, selected.volume, master.pan, etc.), the <vendor>.<model>.<intent> id convention, and a worked example, see the Controller Profile Format reference.

docs.title: MIDI Learn
docs.text:
To map a single hardware control to a single MAGDA target:

  1. Right-click the parameter, macro knob, or LFO Rate slider.
  2. Choose Learn MIDI. The control pulses orange.
  3. Move a knob, slider, or press a button on your controller.
  4. The binding is captured. The pulse stops; an orange dot appears.

Learn works on:

  • Plugin parameters — any device parameter (pulses on the slider).
  • Macros — track, rack, or device macros. Right-click the knob.
  • LFO / modifier Rate — right-click the Rate slider in the modulator editor.

To cancel without capturing, choose Cancel MIDI Learn (same menu, same item).

docs.title: Clearing Mappings
docs.text: Right-click → Clear MIDI Mapping (N) removes only your Learn'd bindings; automap profile coverage is left alone. After clearing a Learn'd macro, the macro falls back to its profile mapping (the dot returns to green).

docs.title: Indicator Legend
docs.text:
MAGDA shows controller coverage as small dots on macro knobs, parameter slots, and device headers.

Dot Meaning Green Profile-driven (automap) binding is active on this target. Orange A user MIDI Learn'd binding is active. Grey Profile binding exists but is shadowed by an explicit Learn override on the same CC.

A device header can show two dots side-by-side (green for profile coverage, orange for any Learn'd binding inside the device).

Above: a synth focused with an automap-mapped controller. Each macro knob carries a green dot — the automap profile is driving them, and the device-header dot mirrors the same green.

Above: the FREQ slider has an orange dot — a user MIDI Learn binding is in effect. The device-header dot turns orange to mirror it.

docs.title: Generating a Profile from Description
docs.text:
If MAGDA doesn't ship a profile for your controller, the AI Assistant can write one for you. In the AI panel, type /co to autocomplete /controller, then describe the controller after the command:

/controller Akai MPK Mini Mk3, 8 knobs on CC 70-77, channel 1

The AI generates a profile JSON, drops it in your controllers directory, and prompts you to enable it. Describe the controller in plain language — manufacturer, model, which CCs the knobs send, MIDI channel — the more specific you are, the better the profile.

To tweak the generated JSON by hand — fix a CC number, switch a knob to drive selected.pan instead of a focused-device macro — the Controller Profile Format reference explains every field.

See AI Assistant — Slash Commands.

docs.title: Lua Controller Scripts
docs.text:
Some controllers can't be expressed as a static CC → target mapping — Mackie Control surfaces, controllers with motorised faders that need feedback, controllers that change mode based on app state. For those, MAGDA hosts a Lua scripting layer: load a .lua file from the Lua Scripts tab in Settings > Controllers and it receives every incoming MIDI event for the assigned port.

The script is just Lua 5.4 (sandboxed — no io, os, require) with a magda.* API for talking back to the DAW: magda.transport, magda.session, magda.tracks, magda.devices, magda.midi. Define a top-level on_midi(event) and it fires for every event matching the assigned input port (or every input, if the port is left blank).

-- Toggle play/stop on a single CC.
function on_midi(e)
    if e.type == "cc" and e.cc == 117 and e.value > 0 then
        if magda.transport.is_playing() then
            magda.transport.stop()
        else
            magda.transport.play()
        end
    end
end

Two optional callbacks are also dispatched: on_load() once at script start, and on_tick(dt) on a periodic timer (use it to drive feedback, e.g. push the playhead position back to motorised LEDs).

Only one script can be active at a time. Loading a new script replaces the previous one. Reload picks up file edits without restarting MAGDA.

docs.title: Lua Scripts tab
docs.text:
The Lua Scripts tab lists the scripts available to you — the factory scripts you have enabled, plus every .lua file in your own scripts folder. Click a script to make it the active one. Each row shows:

Part Description Status dot Green when this is the active script; outlined when it isn't Name Script filename (e.g. launchkey_mini_mk4.lua), with active underneath when it is the loaded script Ports The MIDI input the script's on_midi listens to (none means all inputs) and the MIDI output it sends feedback to. Click either to change it

Buttons in the tab row:

  • + Add script — pick from the factory scripts bundled with MAGDA (see Factory Scripts) and add it to the list
  • Import script… — pick a .lua from disk, copy it into the scripts folder, refresh the list. You are asked before an existing file of the same name is replaced.
  • Open Scripts Folder — reveals your scripts folder in the OS file browser
  • Reload — re-evaluate the active script (or load the alphabetically-first script if none is active). Picks up file edits without restarting MAGDA.

Right-click a row for Reveal in Finder, Unload (on the active script), and Disable factory script (on a factory one).

docs.title: Factory Scripts
docs.text:
MAGDA ships with ready-made scripts for common controllers. They live inside the application rather than in your scripts folder, and are added to the list through + Add script rather than by copying files.

Script Controller launchkey_mini_mk4.lua Novation Launchkey Mini MK4 — transport, pads, knobs, scene switching launchpad_mk1.lua Novation Launchpad MK1 / Classic — session grid, scene launch, banking, User 1/2 note layouts launchpad_mk2.lua Novation Launchpad MK2 — session grid, scene launch, banking, User 1/2 note layouts 8-knobs.lua Any 8-knob controller — CC 1–8 drive the volume of tracks 1–8 foot-pedal.lua Any sustain pedal — CC 64 launches and stops the selected session clip

Disable factory script removes one from the list; + Add script brings it back. Once every factory script is enabled, the button reports that all of them are already enabled.

To modify one, add it, use Reveal in Finder to find it, and copy it into your own scripts folder under a new name.

docs.title: Scripts Folder
docs.text:
Platform Path macOS ~/Library/MAGDA/Scripts/Controllers/ Windows %APPDATA%\MAGDA\Scripts\Controllers\ Linux ~/.config/MAGDA/Scripts/Controllers/

The folder is created on first launch. Drop .lua files in there and they show up on the Lua Scripts tab. Per-script port assignments are saved alongside.

docs.title: Footer Indicator
docs.text:
While a Lua script is loaded, the right of the footer shows a pill with the script's filename and a connection dot — green when its assigned input is plugged in, dim when it's not. Click the pill to open Settings > Controllers. While the script is loaded, controller-profile pills are hidden — the script owns input.

Full API reference: Lua Scripting.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
Tip

A Learn'd binding routes through the port name, so it survives removing the controller from the list. The binding still fires whenever the named port is connected.

docs.title: Menus
docs.text:
MAGDA's menu bar has seven menus: File, Edit, View, Transport, Track, Window and Help. On macOS the MAGDA application menu comes first and holds Settings….

Items with a shortcut show it beside their name. Shortcuts follow your own mapping, set under Settings > Shortcuts; the keys below are the defaults, with Cmd on macOS and Ctrl on Windows and Linux.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Settings… (Cmd+, / Ctrl+,) opens the Settings window. It is in the MAGDA menu on macOS and at the bottom of the Edit menu on Windows and Linux.

docs.title: File
docs.text: Item Description New Project Create a new empty project Open Project… Open an existing project file Open Recent Recently opened projects, and Clear Recent Projects Recover Unsaved Project… Recover or discard work from a session that ended unexpectedly (see Recovering unsaved work) Close Project Close the current project Save Project Save the current project Save Project As… Save the current project to a new file Project Settings… Open the Project Settings dialog (title and credits, song length, sample rate, render/bounce bit depth) Collect Files… Copy every externally-referenced audio file (clips, sampler and drum-pad samples) into the project's media folder and repoint the project at the copies, so it travels self-contained. Shows progress and can be cancelled. Export Audio… Render the song to a WAV, FLAC, Opus or MP3 file: the entire song, the time selection or the loop region (see Export Audio) Export MIDI… Write the arrangement's MIDI clips to a Standard MIDI File, Type 0 (single track) or Type 1 (multi-track), for the entire song, the time selection or the loop region (see Export MIDI) Import DAWproject… Import a .dawproject interchange file (see File Formats) Export DAWproject… Export the project as a .dawproject interchange file Quit Exit MAGDA (Windows and Linux; on macOS, quit from the MAGDA menu)

docs.title: Edit
docs.text:
Item Description Undo Undo the last action, named in the menu (Cmd+Z) Redo Redo the last undone action (Cmd+Shift+Z) Cut / Copy / Paste Cut, copy and paste the selection (Cmd+X, Cmd+C, Cmd+V) Duplicate Duplicate the selection (Cmd+D) Duplicate Clip With Automation Duplicate the selected clips with the automation under them (Cmd+Alt+Shift+D) Duplicate Clip Without Automation Duplicate the selected clips without copying automation Duplicate Clip as Ghost Duplicate the selected clips as ghost clips that mirror the original's content Make Clip Unique Detach the selected ghost clips from their link group Delete Delete the selection (Del / Backspace) Split / Trim Split clips at the cursor, or trim them to the time selection (Cmd+E) Split All Tracks at Cursor Split every clip that crosses the edit cursor, on all tracks Join Clips Join two adjacent clips into one (Cmd+J) Render Selected Clip(s) Render the selected clips to audio (Cmd+B) Render Time Selection Render the time selection to audio (Cmd+Shift+B) Insert Time Insert empty time at the time selection, moving later content right Duplicate Time Range Duplicate the time selection, moving later content right Duplicate Loop Range Duplicate the loop region on all tracks, moving later content right Range Editing A submenu: Copy, Cut and Delete Time Range; Copy, Cut and Delete Loop Range; and Paste (Ripple), which makes room for the clipboard before pasting into it Select All Select all clips, or all notes of the edited clip when the editor has keyboard focus (Cmd+A, see Panel focus) Settings… Windows and Linux only (Ctrl+,)

The time-range items need a time selection, and the loop-range items need a loop region. Cut and Delete ripple: later content moves left to close the gap. See Arrangement View for range editing in detail.

docs.title: View
docs.text: Item Description Track Manager… Open the Track Manager dialog (see below) Headers on the Right Toggle track headers to the right side of the arrangement Zoom In / Zoom Out Zoom the arrangement (H / G) Zoom to Fit Fit all content in the visible area Zoom Loop to Fit Zoom to show the loop region Zoom Selection to Fit Zoom to show the current selection Enter Full Screen Toggle full-screen mode

docs.title: Track Manager
docs.text:
The Track Manager lets you control which tracks are visible in each view. Open it from View > Track Manager….

Each track has a checkbox for each view: Live, Arrange and Mix. The master channel has a row of its own. Click the checkboxes to show or hide individual tracks per view. This is useful for keeping the mixer focused on relevant tracks or hiding utility tracks from the arrangement.

docs.title: Transport
docs.text: Item Description Play Start playback. While MAGDA is playing, the item reads Pause Stop Stop playback Record Start/stop recording Loop Toggle loop playback Go to Start Move the playhead to the beginning Go to End Move the playhead to the end Add Marker Add a marker at the playhead (Cmd+M) Previous Marker / Next Marker Jump to the previous or next marker (Cmd+Alt+Left / Cmd+Alt+Right) Recent Capture Show what you just played, to choose what to keep (Cmd+Shift+C, see Capturing what you just heard)

docs.title: Track
docs.text: Item Description Add Track Add a new track (Cmd+T) Add Group Track Add a new group track (Cmd+Shift+T) Add Aux Track Add a new aux/return track Add Chord Track Add the project's chord track (disabled once one exists) Add Separator Add a separator after the selected track Delete Track Delete the selected track Duplicate Track Duplicate the selected track with clips and FX chain (Cmd+D) Duplicate Track Without Content Duplicate track structure and FX chain only, no clips (Cmd+Shift+D) Duplicate Track Content Only Duplicate the track's clips onto a new track with an empty FX chain (Cmd+Alt+D) Mute Track Toggle mute on the selected track (M) Solo Track Toggle solo on the selected track (Shift+S)

docs.title: Window
docs.text: Item Description Minimize Minimize the window Zoom Zoom the window to fill the screen Bring All to Front Bring all MAGDA windows to front

docs.title: Help
docs.text: Item Description Online Manual Open this manual in the browser Check for Updates… Ask GitHub whether a newer MAGDA release is available About MAGDA Show version and credits

docs.title: Check for Updates
docs.text:
Help > Check for Updates… asks the MAGDA GitHub releases feed whether a newer version is available, and tells you either way. MAGDA also runs the same check silently on launch, at most once every 24 hours, and only shows a dialog if a newer version is found. No telemetry is sent — the check is a plain public-releases request and carries no identifying information.

A stable release is told only about newer stable releases. A pre-release, such as a beta, is also told about newer pre-releases, so 1.0.0-beta.1 offers 1.0.0-beta.2 as well as 1.0.0.

docs.title: Interface Overview
docs.text: MAGDA's window is divided into fixed regions that stay consistent across all three views (Live, Arrange, Mix).

docs.title: Transport Bar
docs.text: The transport bar is the single row at the top of the window, and is always visible. It holds the playback controls, tempo and time signature, loop and punch, and the position displays. See Transport for details.

docs.title: Left Panel
docs.text:
The left panel has two tabs:

  • Inspector — Context-sensitive properties for the selected track, clip, note, or device. See Inspector.
  • AI Chat — Chat-based assistant for natural-language control. See AI Assistant.

docs.title: Central View
docs.text:
The central area displays one of three views depending on the active mode:

  • Session View — Grid-based clip launcher for real-time performance. See Session View.
  • Arrangement View — Traditional timeline for composing and editing. See Arrangement View.
  • Mixer View — Channel-strip mixer for balancing and routing. See Mixer View.

Switch between views with the mode buttons in the footer, with F1 / F2 / F3, or step through them with Tab and Shift+Tab.

In the Arrangement, the corner above the track headers holds the edit-tool button, the add-track button, and the zoom buttons. See Arrangement View.

docs.title: Right Panel
docs.text:
The right panel has two tabs:

  • Plugins — Browse, search, and drag plugins onto tracks
  • Samples — Browse the file system and the media library, preview audio files, and drag them into the project

See Plugin & Media Browser for details.

docs.title: Bottom Panel
docs.text:
The bottom panel switches to match the selection:

  • Empty — Nothing selected
  • Piano Roll — When a MIDI clip is selected
  • Drum Grid — When a MIDI clip is selected on a track whose instrument opens in the Drum Grid, or when you pick the Drum Grid tab for a MIDI clip
  • Chord editor — When a clip on the chord track is selected
  • Waveform Editor — When an audio clip is selected
  • Automation clip editor — When an automation clip, or a point inside one, is selected
  • Track Chain — When a track is selected, showing its FX chain

See Editors for details. Cmd+Shift+P (Ctrl+Shift+P) expands the piano roll to fill the window below the transport, and again to return.

docs.title: Footer
docs.text:
The footer bar at the bottom of the window contains, from left to right:

  • Info line — Names the control under the mouse with its help text. For a control that runs a command, such as the transport and view buttons, it also shows the command's name and its shortcut. Turn it off with Show info line in the footer in Settings > General.
  • Live / Arrange / Mix mode buttons — Switch between the three main views.
  • Ableton Link — While Ableton Link is on, a pill with the number of peers. Click it to open its settings.
  • Controllers — A pill for each controller that is switched on, or for the loaded Lua script, with a green dot while its MIDI input is connected. Click one to open Settings > Controllers.
  • Local models — Icons for the local LLM and the Sample Analyzer. The tooltip names each one's state, and clicking opens Settings > AI.
  • Bottom panel — Shows or hides the bottom panel.

docs.title: Panel Behavior
docs.text:
The left and right panels have their tabs, drawn as icons, along the bottom edge, with a button to collapse the panel beside them. Double-click a collapsed side panel to open it again. The bottom panel is shown and hidden from the footer.

Drag a panel's edge to resize it. Side panels are at least 200 pixels wide. The bottom panel can't be dragged shorter than the instrument it shows needs; when it is already shorter, the device chain scrolls instead of squeezing the instrument. Double-click the bottom panel's header to size it to suit the instrument.

docs.title: Panel focus
docs.text:
Click into the arrangement (or the Session or Mixer view), the bottom panel, the browser or the inspector, and that region takes keyboard focus. A thin accent outline shows which one has it.

Select All (Cmd+A / Ctrl+A) follows the outlined region: in the arrangement it selects all clips, and in the bottom panel all notes of the edited clip. In the browser and the inspector it leaves clips alone, so text fields keep their own Select All. Delete, cut, copy and paste act on the selection, whichever region has focus.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text: The Plugins section of Settings manages where MAGDA looks for plugins, scanning, and plugins that are kept out. Folder, format and exclusion changes wait for Apply, except that starting a scan applies them first.

docs.title: Scanning
docs.text:
The tab row shows how many plugins are available and how many are excluded, with three buttons:

  • Scan for new — Looks for plugins that have appeared since the last scan, and scans only those.
  • Rescan all — Scans every plugin in every folder again, with a progress bar.
  • View report — Opens the log of the most recent scan, showing which plugins were found, loaded, or rejected.

While a scan runs, Stop scan ends it.

Scan for new plugins on startup checks for new plugins each time MAGDA starts. It is off by default.

Plugins whose files have disappeared are dropped from the list on startup, with one exception: if the missing file lived on an external or network volume that is not currently mounted, the entry is kept. An unplugged drive is not evidence that you uninstalled the plugin, so the entry is waiting for you when you plug it back in. This covers /Volumes/... on macOS, drive letters and UNC shares on Windows, and /media, /run/media, and /mnt on Linux.

ARA plugins after updating

MAGDA hosts ARA plugins such as Melodyne only if the scan recorded them as ARA. Plugin lists scanned by older versions of MAGDA don't record this, for VST3 or Audio Unit, so after updating, click Rescan all once before inserting an ARA plugin. See ARA Plugins.

docs.title: Plugin folders
docs.text:
The folders MAGDA scans. Your operating system's standard VST3 folders, and on macOS its Audio Unit folders, are always listed, marked System. On macOS these are:

  • ~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3 and /Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3
  • ~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/Components and /Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/Components (Audio Units)

+ Add folder… adds a folder of your own, and Remove beside it takes it off the list.

docs.title: Preferred plugin format
docs.text:
When a plugin exists in several formats offers Prefer VST3, Prefer LV2, and on macOS Prefer AU. When the same plugin is installed in more than one format, the browser shows it once, in the format you prefer; a plugin that doesn't come in that format keeps the formats it has.

Projects you have already saved still load whichever exact plugin they referenced, regardless of this setting.

docs.title: Excluded
docs.text:
Plugins that crashed or failed to load during a scan are listed here with the reason and date, and later scans skip them. Remove on a row lets the next scan try that plugin again; Reset All clears the whole list.

A plugin that fails to load when you add it or open a project shows Failed to load in its device slot, and MAGDA names it, with the reason, in a warning. See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
All of MAGDA's settings live in one Settings window. Open it with MAGDA > Settings… on macOS, or Edit > Settings… on Windows and Linux. The shortcut is Cmd+, (Ctrl+, on Windows and Linux).

Only one Settings window opens at a time. Asking for it again brings it to the front on the section you asked for. Some controls elsewhere open it on the right page: the controller, Ableton Link and local-model pills in the footer, for example.

docs.title: The window
docs.text:
The sidebar on the left lists the sections. A section with more than one page shows its pages as tabs along the top, and a tab's own buttons sit at the right of the tab row.

Section What it covers Documented in General Zoom, timeline, transport, auto-save, engine, layout, behaviour and language General Appearance Theme, scale, fonts, spacing and colours Appearance Audio & MIDI Audio driver and interface, channels, MIDI ports Audio & MIDI Controllers MIDI controller profiles and Lua scripts Controllers Connections MCP, WebSocket, OSC, remote clients, Ableton Link, MIDI clock Connections Plugins Plugin folders, scanning, excluded plugins Plugins AI Assistant setup, API keys, local models AI Rendering Where exports start and how rendered files are named Rendering Paths Data, presets, capture and media database folders, external editor Paths Defaults What a new project starts with Defaults Shortcuts Keyboard shortcuts and mouse gestures Shortcuts

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
The search box at the top of the sidebar (Cmd+F / Ctrl+F) filters every section and tab by the text of their controls. Sections with nothing matching drop out of the sidebar. Esc clears the search, or closes the window when the search is already empty.

Search becomes available a moment after the window opens, once every section has finished loading.

docs.title: Applying changes
docs.text:
Most sections keep your edits until you apply them. Each section shows how many settings you have changed beside its name in the sidebar, and the footer shows the total.

Button What it does Restore defaults Shows the default values for the section you are in, as pending changes. Nothing is saved until you apply. Cancel Closes the window and drops every change you have not applied (Esc). Apply Saves the pending changes in every section and keeps the window open. OK Applies and closes (Enter).

Audio & MIDI, Controllers and Connections are different: each edit there takes effect as you make it. With one of them selected, the footer says so and offers only Done.

A few actions in the other sections also act at once rather than waiting for Apply: downloading or removing a model and changing a model folder under AI, and starting a plugin scan, which applies the Plugins section's pending changes first.

docs.title: General
docs.text: General is one scrolling page, in groups.

docs.title: Zoom
docs.text:
• Zoom In Sensitivity / Zoom Out Sensitivity — How fast the timeline zooms in and out.
  • ⇧+Zoom Sensitivity — Zoom speed while Shift is held.

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text: • New Project View — How many bars a new project shows when it opens (32 by default). This is how much is on screen, not how long the project is: that is Length under Defaults.

docs.title: Transport
docs.text:
• Stop updates playhead — When on, Stop leaves the playhead where playback stopped, so the next Play carries on from there. Off by default: Play starts again from where the playhead was.
  • Follow playhead during playback — Scroll the arrangement to keep the playhead in view. On by default.

docs.title: Auto-Save
docs.text:
• Enable auto-save — On by default.
  • Interval — How often, from 10 to 300 seconds (60 by default).

docs.title: Recovering unsaved work
docs.text:
After a crash or forced stop, MAGDA offers the previous session's unsaved project once. The offer shows its name, creation and edit times, track and clip counts, and MAGDA version. Choose Later to keep it under File > Recover Unsaved Project, where you can recover or discard it. A normal quit, including Don't Save, retires that session's autosave.

Saved projects offer a newer recovery snapshot when you reopen the project after an unclean exit. Cancel leaves both the current project and the snapshot intact. Recovery files are kept for 30 days, together with any temporary media they need. Snapshots from other builds are available in the recovery menu without a startup prompt.

Use Open Older Autosave in the recovery menu to select an .autosave file from an older MAGDA version. Creation dates that were not recorded by older versions appear as Unknown.

docs.title: Engine
docs.text:
• Render playback ahead of the audio device — Renders playback ahead of the audio device by the Look-Ahead time (5 to 200 ms, 20 by default). Off by default.
  • Keep what you play, so it can be captured afterwards — Turns on the capture buffer behind Transport > Recent Capture (the MEM switch in the transport). See Capturing what you just heard.
    • Capture Buffer — How much is kept, shown with what it costs: 5 minutes by default, up to 4 hours. Anything past the first minute is kept on disk, in the Capture history folder under Paths.
    • Capture Length — The most a capture selects for you, in bars (8 by default).
  • Unload plugins when freezing, to free their memory — When you freeze a track, the plugins rendered into its frozen audio are unloaded. On by default. See Freezing Tracks.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
• Headers on the Right — Put the track headers on the right of the arrangement. Also in the View menu.
  • Auto-Hide Main View Scrollbars — Keep the scrollbars hidden until you hover near them.
  • Compact / Medium / Large Track Height — The three heights the track-height buttons beside the arrangement's vertical scrollbar switch between.
  • Narrow / Medium / Wide Track Width — The three channel-strip widths in the Mixer.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
• Confirm before deleting tracks — On by default.
  • Auto-monitor selected track — Selecting a track sets its input monitor to Auto. See Input Monitoring. Off by default.
  • Duplicate Loop Range grows the loop (off: advances it) — When you duplicate the loop range, the loop grows to cover the copy; off, it moves on to the copy. On by default.
  • Show tooltips — On by default.
  • Show info line in the footer — Name the control under the mouse, with its help text and shortcut, on the left of the footer. On by default.
  • Open plugin window when added to a chain — Off by default.
  • Add a separator after a new chord track — On by default.
  • BEAT without a detected tempo uses the project tempo — A clip with no tempo of its own can go into beat mode without you typing a BPM. On by default.

The four New projects: switches set what a new project starts with. A project keeps the values it was created with, so changing them here leaves existing projects alone.

  • New projects: chord preview — Whether the chord track auditions chords. Off by default.
  • New projects: auto-crossfade — Whether new audio clips get an automatic crossfade where they meet a neighbour. On by default.
  • New projects: overlap plays both — Whether a new clip plays through clips that overlap it. Off, the clip on top owns the span it covers. Per clip, right-click and tick Play Through Overlap. See Overlapping clips. Off by default.
  • New projects: post-FX after fader — Which side of the fader a new track's post-FX section starts on. Existing tracks keep their own setting. On by default.

docs.title: Language
docs.text:
• UI Language — The languages MAGDA ships with, listed by language code. The new language is loaded when you apply, and a hint reminds you that a restart is needed for it to apply everywhere. See Localization.
  • Localized Font Size — An extra size multiplier for localized text, on top of Font Size under Appearance: 150% there and 120% here renders localized glyphs at 180%. Chinese defaults to 115% and Japanese to 110% until you set your own.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text: Everything that controls how MAGDA looks. Changes take effect when you click Apply or OK, with no restart.

docs.title: Theme
docs.text:
Pick MAGDA's colour scheme from the Application Theme dropdown. Three themes ship built in:

Theme Notes Dark The default. Light Light-background variant. High Contrast Black background with brighter colours throughout, for maximum legibility.

Two factory themes ship alongside them, listed below a separator: Concrete Warehouse, a muted industrial palette with amber accents, and Neon Cyberpunk, saturated pinks and cyans on deep violet. They behave exactly like custom themes, so they double as worked examples of the JSON format.

Any custom themes you have installed appear below a further separator, listed by name.

docs.title: Custom themes
docs.text:
Three buttons in the Theme group let you build and manage your own themes:

  • Get template - exports the current theme's palette as a complete, editable .json file to start from.
  • Load theme - pick an edited .json; MAGDA copies it into the Themes folder and selects it.
  • Show folder - reveals the Themes folder in your file browser.

Themes are plain JSON files in Documents/MAGDA/Themes. Each file declares:

  • name - the display name shown in the dropdown.
  • base - either dark or light. Any colour role you do not override is inherited from that base, so you only need to list what you want to change.
  • colours - a map of colour role to hex value. Roles include a six-step accent ramp (accent1 is the primary selection/active colour, through accent6) plus surface and text roles.
  • syntaxColours - optional; themes every code surface in MAGDA - the AI prompt box and the Faust source editor - covering editor background, line numbers, caret, selection, and the syntax token colours. Roles you leave out inherit from the base, exactly like colours. AI-generated themes always write this section out in full.

The filename (without .json) is the theme's id. Unknown keys and invalid colours are skipped, so a partial file is safe to load.

MAGDA watches the selected theme file while it is active: edit its JSON on disk and the change re-applies instantly, which makes hand-tuning a palette quick.

docs.title: Generate a theme with AI
docs.text: You can also describe a theme in plain language. In the AI Assistant console, type /theme <description> - for example warm sunset, dark or cyberpunk neon on black. MAGDA writes the generated theme to Documents/MAGDA/Themes, selects it, and applies it live. Edit the resulting file to fine-tune it.

docs.title: Display Scale
docs.text:
• UI Scale — A scale factor for the whole interface. Auto (from display DPI) follows the display; 100% to 200% (in 25% steps) is a fixed multiplier. Useful on HiDPI and 4K screens where MAGDA looks too small at native resolution. Cmd++ and Cmd+- (Ctrl on Windows and Linux) step the scale up and down from anywhere in MAGDA.
  • UI Font — The interface typeface. Inter (default) is MAGDA's bundled font; below it, every typeface installed on your system is listed alphabetically. This changes the typeface only.
  • Font Size — Scales MAGDA's own text without changing the size of the controls, from 80% to 150%.
  • Spacing — Tightens or loosens the padding between interface elements, on top of the UI scale: 60% to 140%, 100% by default. Lower values pack more onto the screen.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Track colour — How track headers show the track's colour: Spine, a stripe on the outer edge, or Full bar, the header's top bar.
  • Mute / solo — Draw the track header's mute and solo buttons as Icons or as Letters (M / S).

docs.title: New-Project Track Palette
docs.text:
The swatches offered when you colour tracks and clips, up to 16. Click a swatch to edit its hex value and name below the grid, + Add Colour to add one, and Remove to delete the selected one.

The palette is copied into each new project, so editing it here leaves your open project alone. Tick Apply palette to current project too to update the open project as well when you apply.

docs.title: New-Project Clip Colours
docs.text:
• New-project clip colour — Whether new clips Inherit from track or Cycle through palette.

To colour a track, right-click its header; the colour tints its header in the arrangement, Session view and mixer strips.

docs.title: Rendering
docs.text: Where rendered files go and what they are called. The audio format is chosen in the export dialog: WAV, FLAC, Opus or MP3, with a bit depth for WAV and FLAC.

docs.title: Output folder
docs.text: • Export dialog opens in — Documents, or a Custom folder you pick with Choose…. This is only where the export dialog starts. Bounces always go to the project's renders folder.

docs.title: File names
docs.text:
The Export and Bounce fields set the pattern for each kind of file, with a preview of the resulting name underneath. Click a chip under Insert to add clip-name, track-name, project-name or date-time to the field you are editing. Typing adds plain text, Backspace removes the last character or chip, and clicking a chip in the field removes it.

Pattern Default Export <project-name>_<date-time> Bounce <clip-name>_<date-time>

docs.title: Paths
docs.text: Where MAGDA keeps its files. Each folder row shows the path in use, with Change… to pick another folder, Reveal to open it in your file browser, and Use default once you have moved it.

docs.title: Folders
docs.text:
Folder Holds Default Data Logs, scripts, plugin caches ~/Library/MAGDA (macOS), %APPDATA%\MAGDA (Windows), ~/.config/MAGDA (Linux) Presets Chains, racks, devices Documents/MAGDA/Presets Capture history Recordings kept by the capture buffer The system's temporary folder Render output Set under Rendering

When you change the Data or Presets folder, MAGDA asks whether to copy the existing files to the new location. A new Data folder is marked Restart to apply: when you click OK or Apply, MAGDA asks you to save any unsaved changes and then quits, so start it again to use the new folder. A new Presets folder needs no restart.

MAGDA's settings file, config.json, stays in the default data location wherever you move the Data folder. See Resetting MAGDA.

docs.title: Media database
docs.text: The location and maintenance of the sample-indexing database: Location, a count of indexed files and of those with audio embeddings, Index presets, and Wipe database…. See Media Library — Managing the database.

docs.title: External audio editor
docs.text: The application MAGDA hands audio clips to when you choose Edit in External Editor (see Waveform Editor). Use Choose app… to pick it, or Remove to clear it. While no editor is set, choosing the clip menu item shows an alert asking you to pick one.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text: What a new project starts with. Nothing here touches the project you have open: a project's own length, sample rate and bit depths belong to it and are edited in Project Settings.

docs.title: New projects
docs.text:
• Length — The timeline length a new project starts with, in bars.
  • Sample rate — The working and render sample rate. If your audio device runs at a different rate, a note under the setting says so.
  • Bit depth for renders — 16-bit, 24-bit or 32-bit float, for audio exports.
  • Bit depth for bounces — The same choices, for bounced and frozen audio. 32-bit float keeps headroom for re-processing.

docs.title: Credits
docs.text:
The credits that describe you rather than the song — Artist, Composer, Songwriter, Producer, Arranger, Genre, Copyright and Website — are copied into every new project, so you fill them in once instead of in every song. Artist and genre also go into the tags of rendered files. Edit them per project in Project Settings → Metadata.

Title, Album, Original Artist, Year and Comment have no default: they belong to the work, and a stored value would be wrong in every project after the first.

docs.title: Shortcuts
docs.text:
Two tabs, each with Reset all in the tab row. Edits on both wait for Apply, like the rest of the window.

  • Keyboard — Every command that can take a shortcut, by category, with its keys drawn as key caps. Click a cap to record a new key, Not set to add one, and right-click a cap to clear it. A key that two commands share is shown in amber on both, with Also used by naming the other. Type in the filter box to find a command by name, or press a shortcut there to find what it does.
  • Gestures — The mouse wheel, trackpad and drag gestures for each part of MAGDA (arrangement, piano roll, drum grid, waveform, and so on). Each row shows its input; click Learn and perform a gesture to change it, and set its Sensitivity and Invert where they apply.

See Keyboard Shortcuts for the full default list of keys and gestures.

docs.title: Linking Parameters
docs.text: Linking connects modulation sources (modulators or macros) to target parameters on devices.

docs.title: Link Mode
docs.text:
Link mode is the workflow for creating modulation connections:

  1. Enter link mode — Click the link button in the corner of a modulator's or macro's card. LINK MODE shows in the track chain header while it is on
  2. Click a target — Click any device parameter in the source's scope. MAGDA links it at 30% and shows a slider over the parameter
  3. Adjust the link — Drag the slider to set the amount (0–100%). Clicking a parameter that is already linked shows the slider at its current amount
  4. Exit link mode — Press Esc or click the link button again

docs.title: Drag and Drop
docs.text: You can also create links by dragging a modulator's or macro's card directly onto a target parameter. This is a shortcut that skips the link-mode workflow.

docs.title: Link Settings
docs.text:
Each link has the following properties:

  • Amount — How much the source affects the target. A modulator's link can be negative, from −100% to +100%
  • Bipolar — When enabled, modulation swings both above and below the parameter's current value. When disabled, modulation only adds to the current value
  • On / Off — A modulator's link can be switched off without removing it

Edit a source's links on the Links tab of its modulator editor, or in the macro editor. To see everything driving one parameter, hover over it and hold Alt: a popover lists each link with its source, an amount you can drag, a BI / UNI switch, and a button that removes the link.

docs.title: Visual Indicators
docs.text:
When modulation is active:

  • Outside link mode, a bar under each linked parameter shows the modulation moving in real time
  • In link mode, the bar shows the link amount for the source you are linking instead
  • The source's link button stays lit while its link mode is on

docs.title: Linking Modulator-to-Modulator
docs.text:
Modulators can target each other's Rate to create more interesting motion than a single LFO can produce on its own. A slow LFO modulating a faster LFO's rate gives you accelerating-then-decelerating wobbles; a square-wave LFO driving another LFO's rate gives you discrete tempo shifts.

To create the link:

  1. Right-click the source modulator's card and pick the destination from Link to Parameter... → Modulators → Rate, or
  2. Use link mode with the source modulator and click the destination's Rate field in its editor.
  3. Adjust the modulation amount as usual.

A modulator's Rate can be driven by modulators and macros from the same scope (track, rack, or device). Cross-scope links — say, a track-level macro driving a Rate inside a nested rack — are not supported.

docs.title: Same-Scope Rule
docs.text: Macro→param, macro→mod, mod→param, and mod→mod links must all stay within the same scope. The scope is the parent that owns the source: track-level macros target track-level mods or any device on the track; rack-level macros target rack-level mods or devices in that rack; device-level macros and mods target only that device.

docs.title: Macros
docs.text: Macros are user-defined control knobs that provide quick, unified access to multiple device parameters.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
Each track, rack, and device has 16 macro knobs organized across 2 pages (8 knobs per page). Page through them with the arrows in the macro panel's header; click + there to add another page, and right-click the header to Remove last page.

Open a track's macros with the Track macros button in the track chain header, or a rack's or device's with the Macros button in its header. Macros also appear in the Inspector when the track, rack, or device is selected.

Drag a macro's knob up or down to change its value; hold Shift for finer steps. Click a macro without dragging to open the macro editor beside the panel, and click it again to close the editor. The editor shows the macro's name, its Value, and a list of its Links: drag across a link's row to change its amount, click Bi / Un to switch it between bipolar and unipolar, and click x to remove it.

docs.title: Range
docs.text: All macro knobs output a normalized 0–1 range. The mapping to each target parameter's actual range is handled by the modulation link (see Linking Parameters).

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
• Right-click a macro and choose Rename to give it a name (e.g., "Filter Cutoff", "Drive Amount").
  • You can also double-click the name at the top of the macro editor.
  • A macro's card shows its knob, its value, and how many links it has, but not its name; the name field appears on the card only while you rename it. The macro editor shows the name.

docs.title: Assigning Parameters
docs.text:
To connect a macro to a parameter:

  1. Click the link button in the macro's corner to enter link mode (see Linking Parameters)
  2. Click the target parameter
  3. Set the link amount on the slider that appears over the parameter

Or right-click the macro and pick a parameter from the Link to Parameter... submenus, grouped by device. You can also drag the macro onto a parameter.

A single macro can control multiple parameters simultaneously — for example, one "Brightness" knob could increase filter cutoff, reduce reverb wet, and boost high-shelf EQ gain at the same time.

The macro's right-click menu also has Show Automation Lane, Unlink for each of its links, Clear All Links, and Learn MIDI to map a hardware control to it.

docs.title: Driving Modulators
docs.text:
A macro can also target a modulator's Rate instead of a device parameter — turn the macro and you turn the LFO speed. Same workflow:

  1. Right-click the macro and pick the modulator from Link to Parameter... → Modulators, or
  2. Use link mode and click the modulator's Rate slider as the target.

In the screenshot, Macro 1 at 0.20 is dialling LFO 1's Rate down. As the macro turns, the LFO speed follows. Combine with traditional parameter links and a single knob can sweep filter cutoff, reduce reverb send, and slow the LFO that's wobbling the pitch — all at once.

On a rack, a macro can also drive the rack's Chain Select control, listed in the same menu.

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• Map the most important synth parameters to a few knobs for live performance
  • Create unified controls that coordinate multiple effects at once
  • Expose simple controls for complex multi-device setups
  • Use a macro as a "tempo" or "intensity" control that drives an LFO's rate alongside the parameters it modulates

docs.title: Modulators
docs.text:
Modulators are signal generators that modulate device parameters over time. A track's modulators can target any parameter on any device in the track's chain; racks and devices have modulators of their own too (see Hierarchical Scope).

Open a track's modulators with the Track modulators button in the track chain header, or a rack's or device's with the Mods button in its header. They also appear in the Inspector. Click + Add mod in the next free slot and pick LFO, Curve, Envelope, Random, or Follower. Modulators fill the slots in order; click + in the panel's header to add another page of slots, and right-click the header to Remove last page.

Each card shows the modulator's shape, a short type tag (such as SINE, ADSR, S&H, or FOL), its rate or time, and how many links it has. The name appears on the card only while you rename it.

Right-click a modulator's card for Rename, Show Automation Lane, Disable / Enable, the Link to Parameter... submenus, Unlink for each of its links, Clear All Links, Learn MIDI (which maps a controller to the modulator's rate), and Remove. Custom names such as "Filter Wobble" or "Swell" make a track with several LFOs and envelopes far easier to read.

docs.title: The Modulator Editor
docs.text:
Click a modulator's card to open its editor beside the panel; click the card again to close it. The editor has two tabs at the top:

  • The modulator's name — the first tab, over the modulator's controls. Double-click the name to rename it.
  • Links — how many parameters the modulator drives, over a list of its links. Each row shows the target parameter, the link amount (drag across the row to change it, from −100% to +100%), BI / UN for bipolar or unipolar, ON / OFF, and x to remove the link.

Every modulator except the follower ends on its TRIG row: Free (runs continuously), Transport (restarts when playback starts), MIDI (restarts on incoming notes), or Audio (restarts on incoming audio). For MIDI and Audio on a device or rack modulator, the settings button beside it picks what triggers it: the track itself or another track.

The LFO, Curve, and Random modulators share a rate row: the Free / Sync button switches between a rate in Hz and a tempo-synced division (such as 1 Bar, 1/4, or 1/8), and the field beside it sets the value.

docs.title: LFO
docs.text:
A low-frequency oscillator that cycles through a waveform shape. Pick the shape from the row of icons at the top:

  • Sine
  • Triangle
  • Square
  • Saw Up
  • Saw Down

Below the shape display sit the rate row and the trigger. With the Audio trigger, Atk and Rel set how the trigger follows the incoming level.

docs.title: Curve
docs.text:
A freely editable modulation shape. Use it to create complex, custom modulation patterns that go beyond standard waveforms.

The row at the top holds a Preset menu of starting shapes (Triangle, Sine, Ramp Up, Ramp Down, S-Curve, Exp, Log) and a button that opens the curve in its own, larger editor window. Below the curve sit the rate row and the trigger.

docs.title: Editing
docs.text:
• Add a point — Double-click an empty spot on the curve
  • Move a point — Drag it to a new position
  • Adjust curvature — Drag the handle between two points to bend that segment; double-click the handle to straighten it
  • Delete a point — Double-click an existing point

The editor window adds a Loop / 1-Shot switch, so the curve can play once instead of looping, along with grid and snap settings and buttons to save the curve as a preset or reset it.

docs.title: Random
docs.text: A randomised modulation source with its own shaping and smoothing controls. It runs as stepped random values or as continuous noise.

docs.title: Type
docs.text:
The Random / Noise switch at the top selects the source:

  • Random — Generates a new random value each cycle (sample & hold)
  • Noise — Continuous random signal

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• Shp (Shape) — Biases the distribution of the random values
  • Smo (Smooth) — Smooths the transitions between values (0 = hard steps, 1 = gliding)
  • Stp (Step Depth) — Amount of stepped variation between values
  • Rate — The rate row sets the speed, free-running or tempo-synced
