  • TRIG — How the modulator is (re)started

docs.title: Envelope (ADSR)
docs.text: An ADSR envelope used as a modulation source. Triggered by playback or incoming MIDI notes, it shapes a parameter through attack, decay, sustain, and release stages. The display at the top shows the envelope shape and its current state.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• A (Attack) — Rise time to peak (ms)
  • D (Decay) — Fall time to the sustain level (ms)
  • S (Sustain) — Held level while gated (0–1)
  • R (Release) — Fall time after the gate releases (ms)
  • A crv / D crv / R crv — Bend each stage from logarithmic to exponential
  • TRIG — What starts the envelope: Free (cycles continuously), Transport (starts on play), MIDI (gated by note on/off), or Audio

docs.title: Envelope Follower
docs.text: Follows the amplitude of an audio signal and uses it as a modulation source. Use it to make one parameter react to the dynamics of a track, for example ducking a pad from a kick drum. The display at the top shows the live follower output.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• Gain — Input gain into the detector (dB)
  • A (Attack) — How fast the follower rises
  • H (Hold) — Time held at the peak before releasing
  • R (Release) — How fast the follower falls

Times from one second up read in seconds.

docs.title: Detection filters
docs.text:
Band-limit what the follower reacts to so it tracks only part of the spectrum:

  • HP — Toggle on and set the cutoff to ignore low frequencies
  • LP — Toggle on and set the cutoff to ignore high frequencies

Cutoffs from 1 kHz up read in kHz.

docs.title: Audio source
docs.text: Click the Audio Source button at the bottom to choose what the follower listens to — the track's own audio, or another track's audio routed in as a sidechain.

docs.title: Modulation Overview
docs.text: MAGDA provides two complementary modulation systems: Modulators and Macros. Both allow you to dynamically control device parameters without manual automation.

docs.title: Modulators
docs.text:
Modulators are signal generators that continuously vary a target parameter over time. MAGDA includes:

  • LFO — Low-frequency oscillator with sine, triangle, square, and saw shapes
  • Curve — A freely editable shape for complex custom patterns
  • Envelope — An ADSR envelope
  • Random — Stepped random values or continuous noise
  • Follower — Follows the level of an audio signal

See Modulators for details.

docs.title: Macros
docs.text:
Macros are user-defined knobs that can control multiple parameters at once. Each track, rack, and device has 16 macro knobs (across 2 pages) that provide quick access to the most important parameters.

See Macros for details.

docs.title: Hierarchical Scope
docs.text: Modulators and macros live at three levels: on a track, on a rack, or on a single device. Each scope reaches only the parameters it owns — a track's modulators and macros can target the devices in that track's chain, but not parameters on other tracks. See Same-Scope Rule.

docs.title: Multi-Target and Multi-Source
docs.text:
• A single modulator can drive multiple target parameters simultaneously
  • A single parameter can be driven by multiple modulation sources, with their effects combined

docs.title: Track Modulator & Macro Panels
docs.text:
The Track macros and Track modulators buttons in the track chain header open the track's macro and modulator panels at the start of the chain: macros first, then modulators, each followed by its editor when you click a card. Racks and devices have the same two panels, opened from the Macros and Mods buttons in their own headers. Each panel shows its cards on pages of eight, with arrows to page through them.

The same panels appear in the Inspector when a track, rack, or device is selected, so you can edit modulation from either place.

docs.title: Internal Device Modulation
docs.text:
Some built-in devices have their own internal modulation routing that operates inside the device's audio processing.

Internal modulation and track-level modulation are independent and can be used together.

docs.title: Linking
docs.text: Parameters are connected to modulation sources using MAGDA's link mode. See Linking Parameters for the workflow.

docs.title: Automation Lanes
docs.text:
In addition to modulators and macros, any parameter can be automated with a drawn curve on an automation lane below the track in the Arrangement View. Automation lanes play back their drawn curves during transport — the parameter follows the lane's value over time, in sync with playback.

Automation is independent of modulators and macros: all three can drive the same parameter at once, with their effects combined.

docs.title: AI Assistant
docs.text: MAGDA includes a built-in AI chat assistant that lets you control the DAW using natural language. The same console runs DSL code directly with the /dsl command.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The AI Assistant is the AI Chat tab of the left panel. From top to bottom it has:

  • Header — the MAGDA mark, a model chip, and the Clear chat and Copy chat to clipboard buttons. The chip names the current AI setup and model, with a dot that turns green while a model is ready; click it to open Settings > AI. With the embedded local model, a button beside the chip loads or unloads it.
  • Conversation — your messages appear as bubbles labelled YOU → <target>, with MAGDA's replies under a MAGDA label. Copy takes the whole conversation; Clear empties it and resets the assistant's memory of every view.
  • Prompt box — where you type. Enter sends, Shift+Enter adds a line.
  • Controls row — under the prompt: the target chip (see Selection Context), key hints for Shift+Enter, @ and /, and the send button. The send button lights once there is something to send, and turns into a stop button while a request runs: click it to cancel.

docs.title: Making Requests
docs.text:
Type a request in natural language and the assistant translates it into actions:

  • "Add a MIDI track with a bass clip"
  • "Transpose the selected notes up an octave"
  • "Set the tempo to 120 BPM"
  • "Mute tracks 3 and 4"

The assistant is context-aware — it knows which tracks, clips, and devices exist in your project and what is currently selected.

docs.title: Selection Context
docs.text:
The target chip under the prompt shows what your next request is aimed at: a coloured square, the word on, and the target, such as on Bass, on Bass > Verse or on Bass > Poly Synth. The square takes the target track's colour. The square and the label do different jobs.

The square controls whether your current selection is sent at all. When it is on, the AI treats the selected track, clip, or device as the default target — a request like "add a bassline" with a track selected targets that track instead of creating a new one. Click it to turn it off, and requests are interpreted without a default target; the chip dims while it is off.

Creating a new track still works either way — just be explicit in the request ("new track", "another track") when the selection context is on.

The label opens a picker for attaching MIDI clips explicitly. It reads Add MIDI context when nothing is selected or attached. Once clips are attached it summarises them instead of the selection (Bass > Verse, Bass · all MIDI, 6 MIDI · 3 tracks).

docs.title: MIDI Context
docs.text:
Attaching MIDI sends the actual notes to the model, so it can answer about what you have written rather than guessing. Useful for "harmonise this", "write a counter-melody to these two parts", or "make the bass follow the chords in the piano clip".

Click the target chip's label to open the picker:

  • Use selection — attach the selected MIDI clips, or every MIDI clip on the selected tracks.
  • Clear — detach everything.
  • The list below shows each track with its MIDI clips indented underneath. Tick a clip to attach it, or a track to attach all of its clips. A track shows a dash instead of a checkmark when only some of its clips are attached.

Attaching context turns the selection context back on. Audio clips cannot be attached — only MIDI. Clips deleted after being attached drop out of the set on their own.

Bounded on purpose

However much you tick, MAGDA sends at most 16 clips, 128 notes per clip, and 256 notes in total, plus up to 32 chord annotations per clip. Selecting an entire project therefore cannot exhaust the model's context window — but it does mean a very large selection is sent in part rather than in full. Attach the clips that matter.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. You type a natural-language request in the chat
  2. The assistant translates your request into MAGDA's internal DSL (domain-specific language)
  3. The DSL commands are executed as actions in the project
  4. The assistant confirms what was done

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: The AI Assistant supports both cloud LLM providers and a fully offline local model. Configure them under Settings > AI: choose providers on the Assistant tab, add API keys on the Providers tab, and set up the embedded model on the Local models tab. See AI.

docs.title: Usage Tips
docs.text:
• Be specific: "Add a reverb to Track 2" works better than "make it sound spacey"
  • The assistant can handle multi-step requests: "Create 4 MIDI tracks and name them Kick, Snare, HiHat, Bass"
  • Use it for repetitive tasks: "Set all tracks to -6 dB"
  • Prefix a message with /dsl to execute DSL directly from the AI chat without making an AI call

docs.title: Drummer Agent
docs.text:
When you select a track whose Drum Grid has at least one row with a role, or a MIDI clip on such a track, the AI chat automatically switches into Drummer mode. The target chip reads Drummer · <track name>, and your requests are routed to a specialised agent that writes drum patterns instead of the general DAW assistant.

In this mode, describe the groove you want in plain language:

  • "four on the floor with offbeat open hats"
  • "a half-time hip-hop beat, snare on 3"
  • "busier hats in the second bar"

The agent works in terms of drum roles (kick, snare, closed hat, and so on), so it places hits on the pads you have labelled with matching roles. If a Drum Grid clip is selected, its current pattern is sent along as context, so follow-up requests like "add a crash on the downbeat" build on what is already there. The generated pattern is written straight into the selected clip.

Drummer mode is automatic and context-driven; there is no slash command to type. Select a non-drum track to return to the general assistant. To send a single request to the drummer from anywhere else, use /agent drummer.

docs.title: View Context
docs.text:
The console follows the view you are working in:

  • Arrangement view — requests go to the arrangement agent: tracks, clips, devices, composition and project timing.
  • Session view — there is no session agent yet, so a request sent from here gets a reply saying it isn't available. Use /agent to send it to another agent.
  • Mixer and master views — requests are routed to the mixing agent.

What you have selected narrows this. With notes selected, a request goes to the piano-roll agent; with an automation lane, clip or point selected, to the automation agent; and with a device selected, to the device agent. A Drum Grid track or clip goes to the Drummer Agent.

Each view keeps its own conversation, so switching between Arrangement, Session, and Mixer picks up the thread you left in that view rather than mixing them together.

docs.title: Mixing Agent
docs.text:
In the mixer view, the console talks to a specialised mixing agent. It can read the per-track measurement layer — loudness, peaks, stereo width and correlation, and detected frequency collisions between tracks — and ground its feedback in those numbers.

Run an analysis from the mixer's Analyze button first; a mix analysis ready chip appears beside the send button once results exist. Then ask things like:

  • "what is fighting with the bass?"
  • "is the master loud enough for streaming?"
  • "which tracks are mono-incompatible?"

The agent reads the measured findings rather than guessing from track names, and can suggest concrete moves (level trims, EQ areas to look at) based on them.

docs.title: Running DSL Directly
docs.text:
The /dsl command runs MAGDA DSL code against the project with no AI call and no network access. Type /dsl followed by the code and press Enter:

/dsl track(name="Bass", new=true).clip.new(bar=1, length_bars=4)

Press Shift+Enter to put a longer script on several lines. The reply lists what each statement did, or OK when there is nothing to report; a failing statement is reported as an error. Type /dsl on its own, or /dsl --help, for a cheat sheet of common commands, and /dsl --examples for ready-made lines.

docs.title: DSL Quick Reference
docs.text:
A few common commands to get started. For the full language reference, see DSL Reference.

track(name="Bass", new=true).clip.new(bar=1, length_bars=4)
  .notes.add_chord(root=C4, quality=major, beat=0, length=4)
  .notes.add(pitch=E2, beat=0, length=1, velocity=100)
track(name="Bass").fx.add(name="compressor")
track(name="Bass").track.set(volume_db=-6)
groove.set(template="Basic 8th Swing", strength=0.5)

docs.title: Slash Commands
docs.text:
Prefix your message with a slash command to run a tool directly or constrain the AI to a specific domain:

Command Description /groove <request> Create, extract or apply grooves (see below) /theme <description> Generate a UI colour theme from a natural-language description and apply it live /controller <description> Generate a hardware controller profile from a description of the surface /agent <surface> <request> Send one request to a specific agent, overriding the view's usual routing /dsl <code> Execute DSL directly, with no AI call

Typing / shows an autocomplete popup with available commands. Run a command with --help, or on its own, for its in-app cheat sheet, and with --examples for example prompts.

docs.title: /agent — Override Routing
docs.text:
Requests are normally routed by the view you are in (see View Context). /agent overrides that for a single message when you want a different specialist:

/agent drummer busier hats in bar 2
/agent mixer tame the low mids on the bass

Available surfaces: arrangement, piano-roll, session, mixer, automation, device, master, drummer.

docs.title: /groove — Grooves
docs.text:
/groove keeps the AI to groove operations: creating a groove, extracting one from an audio clip, applying one, or listing them. It never writes notes or clips.

/groove make a shuffled 16th-note groove with subtle delay on the off-beats
/groove extract the timing feel from the selected clip into a new groove

Grooves play as time bends. Applying one loads its curve into the selected MIDI clip's time bend, and the strength you ask for becomes the bend's AMOUNT. Grooves you create appear under Custom in the GROOVE menu.

docs.title: /theme - AI Theme Generator
docs.text:
Type /theme <description> to design a MAGDA colour theme from words - for example warm sunset, dark, cold arctic blue, retro amber terminal, or cyberpunk neon on black. The assistant produces a full palette, saves it as an editable JSON file in Documents/MAGDA/Themes, selects it, and applies it live.

Generated themes also carry a complete syntaxColours section, so the code editor and the AI console match the rest of the palette. Any syntax role the assistant does not design is derived from the palette it just produced.

The theme stays selected afterwards. Edit its .json on disk to tweak it - changes re-apply instantly - or switch themes at any time under Settings > Appearance. See Settings - Theme for the theme file format and the Get template and Load theme buttons.

Which model powers /theme is set by the Theme row of the Advanced setup on Settings > AI > Assistant.

docs.title: Per-Device AI Panel
docs.text:
Sound design happens in the device chain. Every device with an AI agent behind it shows an AI icon in its header — click it to open a docked panel attached to that device.

The panel has three rows:

  • Output area — streams the model's response token-by-token. On success the raw result is replaced by the preset's description, followed by a one-line apply status (→ applied 14 params to Poly Synth) and a yellow reminder that the result is a starting point to tweak by ear. The history persists across slot rebuilds (preset loads, plugin reloads, sidechain edits) — your last result stays put until you clear it.
  • Prompt input — type a description and press Enter to submit. Submitting cancels any in-flight generation on the same device.
  • Footer — the active model on the left; on the right a stop button while a generation runs, and Clear chat, which clears the panel for that device only.

Generations are scoped to the device the panel is mounted on. The preset name the AI chose becomes the default name when you next save a preset from the device header — just click save and hit Enter.

On a Faust device the panel writes DSP code, and a strip at its top shows whether the Faust checker is off, on or connected (see Tools). With the checker on, code that passes it is loaded and marked compilation verified. With it off, the code is put in the device's editor for you to compile. The Faust panel keeps the conversation, so a follow-up request revises the last code; Clear chat starts it afresh.

docs.title: Which devices can be designed
docs.text:
Device What the agent writes MAGDA sound generators — Poly Synth, FM0, the Drum Kit voices (Kick, Snare, Hat, Tom, Clap), the Physical Models (Marimba, Djembe, Bell), and the Mutable Instruments ports Materia and Halo Any of the device's own parameters Step Sequencer and Poly Sequencer A pattern rather than a preset Faust and Faust Instrument DSP code — the prompt reads describe an effect or instrument... Third-party plugins The parameters you nominate — see below

Beyond the sequencers, which keep purpose-written agents, sound design works by parameter introspection: the agent reads the device's parameters at runtime — names, units, real-world ranges, and discrete choices — and asks the model for values in those real units (Hz, ms, dB, semitones) rather than in normalised 0–1 terms. That is why it generalises across devices without per-device tuning.

The Sampler, Drum Grid, and effects devices have no sound-design agent.

To hide the AI icon on a sound generator or plugin you would rather drive by hand, right-click it in the Plugin Browser and untick AI Sound Designer. The setting is per device and persists.

docs.title: AI sound design for third-party plugins
docs.text:
Third-party plugins can be designed too, but not automatically: a plugin exposing hundreds of opaque parameters gives the model nothing useful to work with. You choose what it is allowed to touch.

  1. Right-click the plugin in the Plugin Browser and choose Configure AI Sound Designer... (or Configure Parameters..., which opens the same dialog).
  2. Tick the AI Agent column for each parameter the designer should be able to set. This column is separate from Visible — a parameter can be hidden in the chain and still be available to the AI, or the other way round.
  3. Optionally click AI Prompt... to add standing instructions for this plugin — how its oscillator sections are laid out, which parameters interact, anything the parameter names alone do not convey. The button gains a checkmark once a prompt is saved, and the text is prepended to every design request for that plugin.
  4. Set units and ranges for the nominated parameters, either by hand or with Detect / AI Detect. The better the ranges, the more usable the generated values. See Plugin Parameters.

The AI icon appears on the device slot once at least one parameter is ticked.

docs.title: Plugin and Parameter Aliases (@)
docs.text:
The AI chat understands @aliases as a shorthand for plugins. Type @ in the chat input to open an autocomplete list of every MAGDA device and installed plugin by its alias, such as @serum_2. Type a . after a plugin alias to list that plugin's parameter aliases, such as @eq.low_shelf_freq. Use the arrow keys to move through the list, and Enter or Tab to insert the entry.

Aliases tie a request to one specific plugin without spelling out its full name:

add @serum_2 to the Lead track

An alias is passed on as the plugin's alias token, so the DSL resolves it to the same plugin. To change a plugin's alias, right-click it in the Plugin Browser and choose Edit Alias....

docs.title: Plugin & Media Browser
docs.text:
The left panel contains two browser tools for finding and adding content to your project.

The two browsers share one search term. Type in either and the other follows, and the term stays when you switch tabs. Cmd+F (Ctrl+F on Windows/Linux) puts the cursor in the search field.

docs.title: Plugin Browser
docs.text: The Plugin Browser shows all available audio plugins organized in a tree view.

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text:
• View — Choose how the tree is organised: By Category, By Manufacturer, By Format, Favorites or Folders
  • Search plugins — Type to filter by plugin name. The filter stays applied when the list refreshes after a scan
  • Favorites — Right-click a plugin and choose Add to Favorites for quick access in the Favorites view
  • Folders - Switch to the Folders view and organize plugins into your own folders, from a plugin's right-click menu or by creating them with New Folder.... Folders stay in creation order and remain drop targets even when empty; an Unfiled bucket holds everything you have not filed.

docs.title: Adding Plugins
docs.text:
• Drag and drop — Drag a plugin from the browser onto a track header or into the FX chain to add it
  • Right-click — Choose Add to Selected Track or Add to Selected Chain

The right-click menu also offers Configure Parameters... (see Plugin Parameters), Edit Alias..., Prefer Drum Grid, Treat as MIDI FX and Show in Finder.

ARA plugins such as Melodyne are added the same way; see ARA Plugins.

docs.title: Supported Formats
docs.text:
• VST3
  • Audio Units (AU) — macOS only
  • LV2

On macOS, when a plugin is installed as both VST3 and AU, the browser shows only your preferred format. See Preferred plugin format.

docs.title: Rescanning
docs.text: If a newly installed plugin doesn't appear, rescan your plugin folders in Settings > Plugins. See Plugin Settings.

docs.title: Media Explorer
docs.text:
The Media Explorer lets you browse files on your system and preview audio before importing.

Searchable library

The same panel has a Library mode that indexes folders into a searchable database, so you can find sounds by family, key, tempo, tags, or a plain-language description. See Media Library.

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text:
The sidebar on the left switches what the browser shows:

  • Project — The current project's media folder
  • Disk — Your file system
  • Library — The indexed Media Library
  • Favourite folders — Below the other buttons. Right-click a folder in the browser and choose Add to favorites to pin it there (up to eight). Right-click a favourite to Remove from favorites or Set as default directory

In Disk mode:

  • Path box — Shows the current folder, with an up button beside it to go to the parent
  • List / Tree — Show the folder as a flat list or as a directory tree
  • Search media — Type to search the current folder and every folder inside it. Moving to another folder clears the search

docs.title: Preview
docs.text:
• Click an audio file to preview it through your monitor output
  • Preview plays the file as it is on disk, at its own tempo and pitch, unless Sync is on (see below)
  • With Auto on, ++arrowup++ / ++arrowdown++ step through results and audition each one as it is selected; ++arrowleft++ stops the preview and ++arrowright++ replays it from the start

The preview player sits under the file list. With Wave on it shows the file's name, a line of details (tempo, length, sample rate and bit depth), and its waveform. The controls below drive the preview:

  • Play / Stop - start the selected file from the beginning, or stop it. Play is greyed out until a file is selected
  • Auto - audition each file as soon as it is selected, instead of waiting for Play
  • Sync - play loops at the project tempo without changing their pitch, following tempo changes while they play. It uses the tempo the Media Library holds for the file; a file with no tempo there plays unchanged
  • Wave - show or hide the file name and waveform, giving their height to the file list. MAGDA remembers the choice
  • Volume - preview level, in dB. It is independent of the project's mixer and is not recorded into anything

Preview runs outside the project's mixer and goes straight to the output pair you nominate, so it keeps working while the transport is stopped. Choose that pair with the Preview toggle in Settings > Audio & MIDI (see Audio Settings).

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
The file-type buttons beside the search field show or hide each kind of file:

  • Audio files
  • MIDI files
  • Presets — MAGDA presets and sampler instruments (SFZ, DecentSampler)
  • Chord progressions

docs.title: Importing
docs.text:
• Drag and drop — Drag files from the explorer onto a track or clip slot to import
  • Supported audio formats: WAV, AIFF/AIF, FLAC, OGG, MP3 where a platform decoder is available
  • Supported MIDI formats: .mid files

docs.title: Multi-Select
docs.text:
• Shift-click to extend the selection to a contiguous range
  • Cmd-click (Ctrl-click on Windows/Linux) to toggle individual files in and out of the selection
  • Drag any file in the selection to drag the whole selection out

Drop targets vary by destination:

  • Arrangement View — empty area creates one track per sample; existing track appends clips sequentially
  • Session View — empty area creates one track per sample stacked into scene rows; existing track stacks clips down consecutive scene slots
  • Drum Grid — samples fill consecutive pads from the drop target

docs.title: Chord Panel
docs.text:
Chord Engine device

The Chord Panel is the Chord Engine device's view, docked beside the clip editors. Everything it does is described in full on the Chord Engine page; this page covers where the panel appears and how it differs.

The Chord Panel is a real-time chord analysis and suggestion tool. It detects chords as you play, identifies the musical key, lists matching scales, and suggests what chord to play next.

docs.title: Where it appears
docs.text:
The panel opens on the right of the bottom panel when the clip you are editing is on a track with a Chord Engine:

  • beside the Piano Roll, for a MIDI clip on a track whose chain holds a Chord Engine;
  • beside the chord editor, for a clip on the chord track, which always has a Chord Engine.

It reads and drives that track's Chord Engine, so the chords it detects are the ones played on that track. Drag a suggestion straight onto the editor beside it to place the chord (see Placing Chords).

The collapse button in the panel's bottom-left corner (Toggle chord panel) folds it to a narrow strip at the right edge, and the same button on the strip brings it back. Drag the panel's left edge to make it wider or narrower; dragging it very narrow folds it, and double-clicking the edge toggles it too.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
The panel is divided into three columns:

Column Content Chord (left) The chord you are playing, with its degree in the detected key, then the History of recent chords Suggestions (centre) Suggestion tiles in two groups, Diatonic and Beyond the key, or the AI's progressions Key / Scales (right) Detected key, a button to browse scales, and the matching scales

A footer spans the bottom with the controls that shape the suggestions. Unlike the device in a chain, the docked panel shows no keyboard under the chord name.

docs.title: Chord Detection
docs.text: Play notes on the track and the panel displays the detected chord name in real time. Recent chords appear in the History section below; the bin button beside it clears the history and resets detection. See Chord Detection.

docs.title: Key Detection
docs.text:
The detected key (e.g. "C minor") is shown at the top of the right column, found with the Krumhansl-Schmuckler key-finding algorithm. See Key Detection for how it works.

Why the detected key might not match any chord you played

The algorithm detects the tonal centre from the aggregate pitch content, not from specific chord names. For example, playing G minor and Bb major together contributes pitch classes (G, Bb, D, Bb, D, F) which can correlate strongly with C minor's profile — even though you never played a C minor chord. This is musically correct: G minor and Bb major are the v and VII chords of C minor.

docs.title: Scale Detection
docs.text:
Below the key, the panel lists the top matching scales, ranked by how well the pitch classes you've played match each scale's note set.

  • Click a scale to see all diatonic chords built from it.
  • Shift-click a scale to select it for filtering. You can select multiple scales — their pitch classes are merged and used to filter chord suggestions.

docs.title: Suggestions
docs.text: The centre column shows chord suggestions ranked by musical relevance, in two groups: Diatonic (in key) and Beyond the key (secondary, borrowed and substitute chords). Each tile shows its Roman numeral degree. Press a tile, in the suggestions or the history, to hear it through the track's instrument. See Suggestion Generation.

docs.title: Footer Controls
docs.text: Control Description Novelty Slider from safe to wild: the balance between diatonic (0%) and non-diatonic (100%) suggestions Extensions Toggles for the extensions the suggestions may use: 7th, 9th, 11th and 13th. Alt adds borrowed chords and tritone substitutes. Scale filter The funnel button: filter suggestions by the detected scales

docs.title: Browse
docs.text: The browse button beside the key (Browse scales) swaps the suggestions for a list of every scale, with root-note buttons to narrow it to one key. The back arrow (Back to suggestions) returns to the suggestions.

docs.title: AI Mode
docs.text:
Switch to the AI tab, with the icons at the top of the suggestions column, to generate chord progressions from text descriptions. Type a prompt describing the style or mood (e.g. "Soulful I-iv-V7", "Jazzy backdoor voicing") in the prompt at the foot of the panel and the AI returns labelled progressions as rows of chord buttons. Press a chord to audition it, or drag it onto the editor beside the panel.

See Chord Engine — AI Tab for full details.

docs.title: Drum Grid Editor
docs.text:
Displayed in the bottom panel when you select a MIDI clip on a track whose instrument opens in the Drum Grid — a Drum Grid device does by default. Switch between this editor and the Piano Roll with the two tabs at the left of the header. Right-click the Drum Grid tab and choose Use Drum Grid by default for instrument to make another instrument open here too.

Shows a step-sequencer-style grid:

  • Rows represent drum pads / MIDI notes
  • Columns represent time steps
  • Click an empty cell to add a hit; double-click a hit to remove it
  • Shift + drag along a row to stamp a run of hits, one per grid step
  • Velocity per hit is adjustable in the velocity lane, or with Shift + wheel (see Auditioning Hits)
  • Live input highlight — with the track's input monitoring on, pad rows light up as you play them and the played row scrolls into view

Header controls

  • Piano Roll / Drum Grid — Switch editors for the clip
  • Overlay tracks — Show other tracks' notes as a ghost overlay (Layer clips from other tracks), same as in the Piano Roll. Ghost hits land on the row matching their pitch; notes that do not map to a pad row are skipped.
  • Edit tools — Pointer, Pencil, Slice, Glue, and Erase (keys 1 to 5), shared with the Piano Roll. With Erase, click or sweep over hits to remove them.
  • Time Bend — Show the clip's time bend (see Time Bend)
  • Key — The song key chip, shared with the Piano Roll
  • Loop — Toggle the clip's own source loop on or off
  • Grid division, AUTO, SNAP — Pick the grid subdivision, let it follow the zoom level, and toggle snap-to-grid
  • Clip power — Enable or disable the clip
  • Maximise — Pinned to the far right, this toggle expands the editor to fill the window. Click again to restore. Shared with the Piano Roll.

Sidebar controls

  • Chord track — Show the chord track's chords in a lane above the grid
  • Monitor — Hear hits as you click them (see Auditioning Hits)
  • Fold — Collapse the grid to only the pads in use, hiding empty lanes (Fold to used pads)

Right-click the grid for Copy, Paste, Duplicate, Delete, Slice... (see Slicing Notes), the default length and velocity for new hits, and Quantize.

docs.title: Velocity and Control Lanes
docs.text:
The drawer at the bottom of the editor holds the velocity lane. Drag the bars to set hit velocities. Click a pad row's name to select the row: the velocity lane then shows only that row's hits (VEL · selected row).

The buttons at the left of the drawer switch it to CC and pitchbend lanes, which you add with the + button the same way as in the Piano Roll. The menu offers Pitchbend, common controllers (CC 1 (Mod Wheel), CC 7 (Volume), CC 11 (Expression), CC 64 (Sustain)), and Custom CC...

docs.title: Auditioning Hits
docs.text:
The Monitor toggle in the sidebar previews hits through the track's instrument. With it lit, clicking a cell or pressing a pad sounds that note. It works the same as in the Piano Roll, and the setting is shared between the two editors. The play button at the end of each pad row always auditions, whatever the toggle state.

Shift + wheel over a hit edits its velocity, exactly as in the Piano Roll.

docs.title: Pad Rows
docs.text:
Each pad that holds a sound has a mute button on its row, which mutes the pad's mixer channel.

When any pad carries a role, the rows group under KICK, SNARE, HATS, and PERC headers, in role order; pads without a role join PERC. Click a header to fold its group.

docs.title: Row Labels and Roles
docs.text:
Each pad row can carry a custom name and an instrument role. The role is a semantic label (what the pad is: a kick, a snare, a closed hat) and shows as a small coloured pill next to the row, abbreviated to a short tag like K, S, or HH.

Right-click a row to set both:

  • Set instrument - choose a role from the submenu, or None to clear it.
  • Rename label... - give the row a custom name.
  • Clear label - remove the custom name.
  • Clear role - remove the role (leaving the pad unlabelled).

Roles are also what the Drummer agent reads and writes, so labelling your pads lets the AI place hits on the right voices.

The available roles and their short tags:

Role Tag Role Tag Kick K Ride R Snare S Ride Bell RB Snare Rim SR Crash CR Clap C Tom High TH Closed Hat HH Tom Mid TM Open Hat OH Tom Low TL Pedal Hat PH Perc 1-4 P1-P4

docs.title: Drumkits
docs.text:
A drumkit saves a grid's row layout - each pad's note, custom label, and role - so you can reuse it across projects. Right-click a row to manage kits:

  • Save as drumkit... - name and save the current grid's row layout.
  • Apply template - apply a built-in template or one of your saved drumkits to the current grid.

Drumkits store pad metadata (notes, labels, roles), not the samples themselves.

See Drum Grid for the DrumGrid device itself, including per-pad sample loading, each pad's chain, and envelopes. Each pad that holds a sound also has its own channel in the Mixer.

docs.title: Editors
docs.text:
The bottom panel displays an editor that auto-switches based on the current selection. Select a MIDI clip and it shows the Piano Roll; select an audio clip and it shows the Waveform Editor, and so on.

Editor Shown when you select Piano Roll A MIDI clip Drum Grid Editor A MIDI clip on a track whose instrument is MAGDA's Drum Grid, or is set to Prefer Drum Grid (in the track header's or the Plugin Browser's right-click menu) Waveform Editor An audio clip Chord editor A clip on the chord track Automation clip editor An automation clip Track Chain A track or device

For a MIDI clip, the Piano Roll / Drum Grid tabs in the toolbar switch between the two editors.

Double-click a clip to open the bottom panel on it, and double-click again to close it.

docs.title: Shared Controls
docs.text:
The Piano Roll, Drum Grid Editor and Waveform Editor share one layout: a toolbar across the top and an icon rail down the left edge.

  • The toolbar's right-hand end carries the same controls in each: Maximise to fill the window, the clip's Power switch, the grid (division, AUTO and SNAP) and Loop, which turns the selected clip's own loop on or off.
  • The rail holds each editor's view toggles, such as Fold in the Piano Roll or the spectrogram in the Waveform Editor.

docs.title: Inspector
docs.text:
The Inspector panel is on the right side of the window. It displays context-sensitive properties for the currently selected item.

Its sections fold: click a section's title to fold or unfold it. A folded section stays folded as you select other items, until you restart MAGDA. The FX, Latency, Mods and Macros sections start folded each time you open MAGDA. When an inspector is taller than the panel, the panel scrolls.

docs.title: Track Inspector
docs.text:
Displayed when a track is selected. From the top:

  • Name — Click to rename. The track colour shows as a spine beside the name, or fills the name field when Track colour is set to Full bar in Settings > Appearance. Click the spine, or right-click the name, to choose a colour. A track with no colour has no spine. The switch at the right enables or disables the track
  • Mix — Volume and pan, M (mute), S (solo), R (record arm), input monitoring, and the automation button, which lights when the track has automation
  • Automated — Appears when the track has automation and lists the automated parameters. The automation button folds it away
  • Routing — Audio and MIDI input and output selectors
  • FX — The track's FX chain, one row per device (a rack shows as one row). Click a row's dot to bypass the device; click its chevron to unfold up to three of its parameters, chosen in the Mini FX column of the Configure Parameters dialog. Third-party plugins have a button that opens their window. The section header shows the track's total latency
  • Sends — The track's sends with their levels; the + in the section header adds a send
  • Mods and Macros — The track's own modulators and macros, see Mods and Macros
  • Clips — How many clips the track holds

Which of these a track shows depends on its type: a group or aux has no record or input routing, for example. With several tracks selected, the inspector names how many, and mute, solo, record arm, enable, and colour apply to all of them.

docs.title: Master Inspector
docs.text:
Displayed when the master is selected:

  • Header — The master's channel layout and how many devices its chain holds, with a mute button
  • Output — Volume and a live peak meter. Click the peak readout to reset it
  • FX — The master chain, in the same rows as the track inspector's FX section
  • Latency — The master chain's total latency in milliseconds and samples, and the devices that add the most (up to five)
  • Mods and Macros — The master's own modulators and macros

docs.title: Clip Inspector
docs.text:
Displayed when a clip is selected. The header shows the clip's colour spine and name over a summary line: the clip type, Session for a Session View clip, the take, its length in bars, and the sample rate (audio) or note count (MIDI). Double-click the name to rename the clip. Click the spine, or right-click the name, to choose a colour: None, Inherit from Track, or a palette colour. A clip with no colour has no spine. Beside the name sit Save to library, which saves the clip's settings or MIDI file to the media library, and the power button that enables or disables the clip.

Position and loop values are expressed in beats (shown as bars and beats). The sections below appear for the kinds of clip they apply to.

docs.title: Clip
docs.text:
• Clip — Start, End and Length on the timeline
  • Loop — The loop switch, with the loop's start and end and its Phase (or offset)
  • Takes — For a clip with recorded takes, the take to play

docs.title: Mix
docs.text:
For audio clips:

  • Volume, Pan and Gain
  • Reverse — Play the clip backwards
  • Gain envelope — Show the clip's gain envelope

docs.title: Warp & Pitch
docs.text:
For audio clips. The switch in the section header turns warp markers on or off.

  • Beat / Free — Beat follows the project tempo in bars and beats; Free plays the file at its own rate
  • Stretch engine — Off, Signalsmith, SoundTouch, or SoundTouch HQ
  • Transient sensitivity — How readily transient markers are detected
  • Tempo and Length — The source tempo in BPM, with buttons that halve or double it, and the length in beats
  • Speed and Analog — In Free mode, the playback speed, and analog pitch, which resamples instead of time-stretching
  • Pitch — Transpose in semitones and cents
  • Key — The source's key root

docs.title: Pitch
docs.text: For MIDI clips: Transpose buttons that move every note down or up an octave or a semitone (−12, −1, +1, +12).

docs.title: Fades
docs.text: For audio clips: fade-in and fade-out lengths, each with its curve shape. Crossfade in and Crossfade out appear where the clip overlaps a neighbour, and the switch in the section header crossfades automatically where clips overlap. A Session View clip has a Launch fade instead, which smooths the start (0 keeps the transient).

docs.title: Time Bend
docs.text: For MIDI clips: the clip's time bend curve.

docs.title: Labels
docs.text: For audio clips: the clip's labels, placed with the Label tool in the waveform editor.

docs.title: Launch
docs.text:
For clips in Session View:

  • Quantize — Bar / beat snap for launch timing
  • Follow action — Action when the clip ends: None, Play Next, Play Previous, Play Random, Stop, Play Again
  • Delay (beats) - Delay between the clip ending and the follow action firing (0 - 64 beats)
  • Loops - Number of loops the clip plays before the follow action fires

Delay and Loops appear once a follow action is set.

docs.title: Note Inspector
docs.text:
Displayed when one or more MIDI notes are selected in the Piano Roll. The header names the note (or how many are selected) over the clip's name. Shows:

  • Pitch — MIDI note number and name
  • Velocity — Note velocity (0–127)
  • Start — Note start position
  • Length — Note duration

When multiple notes are selected, the inspector shows ranges (e.g., "C3–G5") and allows batch editing.

docs.title: Automation Inspectors
docs.text:
Selecting automation points shows the parameter's name over how many points are selected, with the Value and Position of the selection. With several points selected, editing the value moves them all by the same amount.

Selecting an automation clip shows its name over a summary line (the automated parameter and the clip's length), with the Start, End and Length of the clip, and the Loop switch with the loop's length. Right-click the name to choose the clip's colour.

docs.title: Device Inspector
docs.text:
Displayed when a device, rack, or chain is selected in the track chain:

  • Header — The device type (for example its plugin format, Instrument or Effect, and the manufacturer) over the device's name
  • Facts — The device's Category (for MAGDA's own devices), its Latency, and, for a device with a sidechain input, where its Sidechain comes from
  • Mods and Macros — The device's or rack's own modulators and macros
  • About — A short description, for MAGDA's own devices

The device's parameters live on the device itself, in the track chain.

docs.title: Mods and Macros
docs.text:
The track, master, and device inspectors each show the selected item's own Mods and Macros, using the same cards, knobs, and editors as the track chain. Edits made in either place show in the other. Click a card to open its editor below the cards.

Clicking a modulator or macro in the chain selects its owner and opens that item here, unfolding its section. Post-FX devices, analysis devices, and the chord track have no mods or macros, so they show none here either.

docs.title: Media Library
docs.text: The Media Library is the searchable, indexed side of the left browser panel. Where the Media Explorer walks your filesystem folder by folder, the Library lets you index folders once and then find sounds by family, shape, key, tempo, tags, or a plain-language description of what you want.

docs.title: Disk and Library modes
docs.text:
The buttons in the left panel's sidebar switch what the browser shows:

  • Project and Disk - the filesystem browser (Media Explorer), opened on the project's media folder or on your disk. Navigate folders and preview files as they sit on disk.
  • Library - the indexed sample database. Searches and filters run against everything you have indexed, regardless of which folder it lives in.

You index folders from Disk mode and then search them from Library mode.

docs.title: Indexing folders
docs.text:
The Library is empty until you index something. In Disk mode, right-click any folder:

  • Index this folder - shown when nothing under the folder has been indexed yet. Scans the folder and adds every supported file.
  • Scan for new files - skips files already in the database and only processes ones it has not seen.
  • Re-index this folder - re-derives every file from scratch, ignoring the cache. Use this after a tagging-model change or if entries look wrong.
  • Change folder location... - point an indexed folder at a new path on disk without losing its entries.
  • Remove from media library - drops the folder's entries from the database. The files on disk are untouched.

Always move indexed folders with Change folder location...

If you move or rename an indexed folder in Finder, Explorer, or your file manager, every entry under it points at a path that no longer exists and the rows are flagged missing. Use Change folder location... to relocate an indexed folder so the database follows the move and your entries stay intact. If a folder has already been moved by hand, you can recover it: re-index it at the new path, or fix individual files with Recover missing file....

Indexing is manual

There is no scan-on-startup or live filesystem watcher. The Library only changes when you index, re-index, or scan for new files. When files on disk change after indexing, their rows are flagged (see Row status) so you know to re-scan.

docs.title: The Index Folder dialog
docs.text:
When you start indexing, the Index Folder dialog lets you attach tags to every row in that scan:

  • Tags - free-text tags applied to all files in the folder (for example a pack name).
  • Use folder name - adds the folder's own name as a tag (on by default).
  • Use subfolder names - adds each subfolder along the path as a tag (off by default).

Press Start to begin. Indexing runs in the background; you can keep working while it scans.

docs.title: What gets indexed
docs.text:
Kind Extensions Analysis Audio .wav, .aif, .aiff, .mp3, .flac, .ogg, .m4a Full: BPM, key, family, shape, duration, tags MIDI .mid, .midi BPM, duration and shape. A file carrying MAGDA's chord markers is indexed as a chord progression Presets .vstpreset, .aupreset, .fxp, .fxb, .mps Path, format, and parsed metadata only

For audio, MAGDA derives what it can from the file itself (tempo, key, duration, whether the sound is tonal) and from naming conventions in the path (a kick_120bpm.wav in a .../Drums/Kicks/ folder picks up the tempo and a drum family hint).

docs.title: Searching and filtering
docs.text:
In Library mode the search bar and filter strip drive the results table.

  • Search media (top bar) - a plain-language semantic search. Type a description like warm analog bass and press Enter to rank results by how close their sound is to your text. This uses the AI Sample Analyzer and runs on Enter rather than per keystroke. Clearing the box restores the unfiltered view. The search term is shared with Disk mode and the Plugin Browser.
  • File-type buttons (top bar) - the audio / MIDI / preset / chord progression buttons double as the kind filter in Library mode, narrowing results to a file type.

The filter strip below adds structured filters that combine with the search:

  • family - a closed set: drum, bass, lead, pad, keys, guitar, orchestral, vocal, fx, texture.
  • shape - one-shot, loop, or sustained.
  • key - root note from C to B.
  • bpm - min and max boxes for a tempo range.
  • tonal - switch to limit results to pitched (tonal) material.
  • tags - type a tag and add it as a chip; the field suggests tags already in your library as you type. Several chips are AND-combined against each row's tags (for example drum and 808). This works whether or not the Sample Analyzer is installed.

Results are paginated at 100 rows per page. The footer shows which rows you are looking at (for example 1–100 of 312, with the total shown when you are browsing by filters alone) and the page number, with arrows to move between pages.

docs.title: Results columns
docs.text:
The table shows Name, Family, Shape, BPM, Key, Dur (duration), and Tags. Drag column headers to reorder them, and use the header's right-click menu to toggle column visibility. The Tags column is hidden by default in the docked panel and shown by default in the pop-out window.

The Family and Shape cells are clickable pills: click one to reassign a row's family or shape from a menu, without opening the full edit dialog.

docs.title: Row status
docs.text:
A narrow column at the left of each row shows its state:

  • Nothing - the file on disk matches what was indexed.
  • A ring - the file changed (modified time or size) since it was indexed. Re-scan to refresh it.
  • A filled dot in the error colour - the file is no longer at its indexed path, and the row is marked missing. Use Recover missing file... to point the row at its new location.
  • A dot in the accent colour - you have edited the row's fields.

Hover over a row or select it and the column shows a play button that previews the file.

docs.title: Previewing results
docs.text:
Library rows audition through the same preview player as the Media Explorer, using the same Play, Stop, Auto, Sync, Wave and volume controls. Clicking a row loads it, and with Auto on it plays immediately.

Keyboard auditioning works on the results table as well:

  • ++arrowup++ / ++arrowdown++ move through rows, loading each one as it is selected
  • ++arrowleft++ stops the preview
  • ++arrowright++ replays the current row from the start

With Sync off, preview plays each file at its own tempo and pitch. With Sync on, a row with a BPM plays at the project tempo, keeping its pitch; a row without one plays unchanged.

docs.title: Editing entries
docs.text:
Right-click a row (or a multi-row selection) for per-row actions:

  • Edit row fields and tags... - edit the family, shape, key, BPM, and tags by hand. With multiple rows selected this becomes Edit selected row fields and tags... for bulk edits.
  • Reset to detected - discard manual edits and re-derive fields from the file itself. With multiple rows selected this becomes Reset selected rows to detected.
  • Delete file metadata - forget the tempo and key the Library holds for the file, both detected and your own, along with its warp markers. The row stays, and the next scan or BEAT press on a clip measures the file again.
  • Save current clip values to library - if the file is open as a clip in the project, write that clip's BPM, key, and related values back to the Library row.
  • Recover missing file... - browse to the new location of a file flagged missing.
  • Find similar sounds to "..." - find sounds whose audio resembles the selected one (see below).
  • Analyze selected rows - run the AI Sample Analyzer over the selection.
  • Delete selected rows - remove the rows from the database (the files on disk are untouched).

The table header's right-click menu also offers Remove duplicate file rows... to clear out repeated paths.

docs.title: AI Sample Analyzer
docs.text:
The Sample Analyzer is an optional AI model that listens to your samples and adds two capabilities:

  • Semantic text search - the Search media box can rank sounds by a plain-language description instead of relying on filenames and tags.
  • Find similar sounds - right-click a row to surface other samples that sound like it, ranked by audio similarity.

It is built on CLAP (Contrastive Language-Audio Pre-training), which embeds audio and text into the same space so the two can be compared.

Not the CLAP plugin format

The CLAP used here is a machine-learning model for matching audio to text. It is unrelated to CLAP the audio plugin standard, which shares the acronym but is a different thing entirely.

docs.title: Installing it
docs.text:
The analyzer is a separate download, not bundled with the app. Open Settings > AI, go to the Local models tab and choose Sample analysis as the type, where it shows the download size and a Download Sample Analyzer button (see Settings > AI). Once installed, Load brings the models into memory (they also preload in the background the first time you enter Library mode).

Intel macOS

The Sample Analyzer runs on the ONNX runtime, which is not part of the Intel macOS build. On those builds it isn't offered, and semantic search and find-similar are unavailable; everything else in the Library works.

The Sample Analyzer icon (a database icon) in the footer status bar shows the current state. Its colour reflects the state and the tooltip names it: not installed, installed (downloaded but not loaded), loading, or loaded.

docs.title: Without the analyzer
docs.text: Indexing and the Library still work without it; you simply lose semantic search and find-similar. Filename, tag, family, shape, key, and BPM filtering all work on their own. When you index a folder without the analyzer installed, MAGDA warns you and lets you continue. You can install the analyzer later and run Analyze selected rows to backfill the audio analysis on rows that were indexed without it.

docs.title: Adding sounds to your project
docs.text:
Drag rows from the Library into the project exactly as you would from the Media Explorer. Drop targets behave the same way:

  • Arrangement View - an empty area creates one track per sample; an existing track appends clips sequentially.
  • Session View - an empty area stacks samples into scene rows; an existing track fills consecutive scene slots.
  • Drum Grid - samples fill consecutive pads from the drop target.

Select multiple rows (Shift-click for a range, Cmd-click / Ctrl-click to toggle individual rows) and drag any one of them to drag the whole selection.

Linux drag-and-drop

On macOS and Windows, dragging out of the Library is an OS-level drag, so you can also drop files into Finder, Explorer, or a plugin's file slot. On Linux the drag is internal to MAGDA, so it targets in-app destinations such as tracks and the Drum Grid.

docs.title: Pop-out window
docs.text: The Open in window button (top of the filter strip) detaches the Library into its own resizable window, which is useful when you want a tall results list alongside the arrangement. The pop-out shows the Tags column by default.

docs.title: Managing the database
docs.text:
The database is a rebuildable cache; your audio files on disk remain the source of truth. Its settings live under Media database in Settings > Paths (see Settings):

  • Location - Reveal shows the database folder, Change... moves it, and Use default returns it to the default location.
  • A statistics line showing how many files are indexed, and how many have audio analysis from the Sample Analyzer.
  • Wipe database... - clear every indexed entry and start fresh. This does not delete any files on disk.

docs.title: Piano Roll
docs.text:
Displayed in the bottom panel when a MIDI clip is selected. Provides a grid for editing notes:

  • Horizontal axis — Time (bars and beats)
  • Vertical axis — Pitch (MIDI note numbers, with piano keyboard on the left)
  • Vertical zoom — Drag the zoom strip on the far-left edge (beside the octave labels and keyboard) up or down to change the note row height. The zoom level is remembered per clip.
  • Double-click an empty cell to add a default-length note at that position and pitch
  • Alt + drag on empty grid to draw a note of variable length. The drag distance sets the note length. The Pencil tool does the same without the modifier.
  • Drag a note to move it in time or pitch; Alt + drag a note to copy it
  • Drag edges to resize note length
  • Shift+Ctrl + click a note to delete it directly. If the note is part of a multi-selection, the whole group is erased. Acts as a rubber tool.
  • Control lanes at the bottom for velocity, CC, pitchbend and MPE (see Control Lanes)
  • Live input highlight — with the track's input monitoring on, the keyboard lights up notes as you play them (MIDI or computer keyboard) and scrolls a held note into view

docs.title: Toolbar
docs.text:
Toolbar controls

  • Piano Roll / Drum Grid — Switch this clip between the Piano Roll and the Drum Grid Editor
  • Layer clips — Show other tracks' notes as a ghost overlay (see Overlay Tracks)
  • Edit tools — Pointer, Pencil, Slice, Glue and Erase (see Edit Tools)
  • Time Bend — Show the clip's time bend in a panel beside the grid (see Time Bend)
  • Key — The project's key, with scale highlighting (see Scale Highlighting)
  • Maximise — Expand the editor to fill the window. Click again to restore.
  • Power — Enable or disable the clip
  • ABS / REL — Toggle between absolute (timeline) and relative (clip) time. Hidden for Session View clips, and locked to relative while an arrangement clip loops.
  • Grid — The grid division (click it to pick one), AUTO to follow the zoom level, and SNAP to snap to the grid
  • Loop — Toggle the clip's own loop on or off

Rail

Stacked on the left edge:

  • Chord track — Show the chord lane above the grid (see Chord Timeline)
  • Monitor — Hear notes as you click them (see Auditioning Notes)
  • Fold — Collapse the grid to only the pitches in use (see Fold)
  • Show take lanes — At the bottom, when the clip holds recorded takes (see Take Lanes)

docs.title: Edit Tools
docs.text:
Pick a tool in the toolbar, or press its number key. Holding the key switches tool only while it is held, and holding Alt switches to the Pencil.

Tool Key What it does Pointer 1 Select, move and resize notes Pencil 2 Draw notes on the empty grid Slice 3 Cut a note where you click Glue 4 Join a note to the next note of the same pitch Erase 5 Delete notes by clicking or sweeping over them

docs.title: Auditioning Notes
docs.text:
The Monitor button sits at the top of the rail. When it is lit, notes sound through the track's instrument as you work on them:

  • Click an existing note to play it.
  • Alt + drag to draw a note and hear it for as long as you hold.
  • Double-click to add a note and it sounds once.

The toggle is off by default, so ordinary selection stays silent. Its state persists as you switch clips and move between the Piano Roll and the Drum Grid Editor within a session.

docs.title: Control Lanes
docs.text:
The drawer at the bottom of the editor shows one kind of lane at a time. Pick it with the three buttons at the top of the drawer's header column:

  • Velocity — One bar per note. Drag the bars to set note velocities; selected notes edit together.
  • CC and pitchbend — The clip's CC and pitchbend lanes, stacked so they are all visible at once. Add one with the + button at the bottom of the header column: the menu offers Pitchbend, common controllers (CC 1 (Mod Wheel), CC 7 (Volume), CC 11 (Expression), CC 64 (Sustain)) and Custom CC... for any controller number. Each lane shows its name with a close button, and the pitchbend lane has a Range field for the bend range in semitones.
  • MPE — Pitch glides on the notes, with Slide and Pressure lanes below (see Pitch Glides (MPE)).

Drag the drawer's top edge to resize it. The drawer grows automatically as CC lanes are added. A pencil or curve stroke in a lane is one undo step.

docs.title: Editing Velocity with the Wheel
docs.text:
Hold Shift and scroll the wheel over a note to nudge its velocity, in steps and clamped to 1-127. If the note is part of the current selection the whole selection scales together; otherwise only that note changes. Shift + wheel over the empty grid edits the current selection. A small v NN readout appears by the cursor while you drag, and a full wheel spin collapses into a single undo step.

While a note is hovered or a selection exists, this gesture takes over from the usual Shift + wheel horizontal scroll.

docs.title: Fold
docs.text: The Fold button collapses the vertical axis to only the pitches that are actually used in the clip, hiding the empty rows in between. Every remaining row is labelled, and the view re-centres on the used notes when you toggle it. Folding is handy on sparse parts — a bassline or a lead — so you can see all the notes without scrolling. With Fold on, dragging a note vertically snaps through the used-pitch rows. While the key is lit, Fold keeps the key's rows as well. The same control exists in the Drum Grid Editor as Fold to used pads.

docs.title: Scale Highlighting
docs.text: The key button in the toolbar shows the project's key. Click it to pick a root note and Major or Minor, choose No Key, or turn on Highlight scale and fold to key. While the highlight is lit, rows in the scale stand out, the root's rows are marked, and notes outside the scale are hatched, along with their velocity bars.

docs.title: Take Lanes
docs.text: When a MIDI clip holds more than one recorded take, click Show take lanes at the bottom of the rail to reveal the folded take strip below the grid and comp the takes together. See Recording Takes & Comping.

docs.title: Pitch Glides (MPE)
docs.text:
Choose MPE in the control-lane drawer to edit per-note expression. In this mode you draw pitch glides directly on a note: the glide curve bends the note's pitch over its length, independently of other notes. Right-click a glide for Clear Pitch Glide. Playback uses MPE, so each gliding note gets its own MIDI channel — point the track at an MPE-capable instrument to hear it.

Below the grid, the Slide and Pressure lanes edit the selected note's slide and pressure curves within the note's length. Select one note to edit them; with no note or several selected, the lanes are read-only. Each edit is one undo step.

docs.title: Overlay Tracks (Ghost Notes)
docs.text:
Click the Layer clips button in the toolbar (next to the Piano Roll / Drum Grid tabs) to overlay MIDI from other tracks as ghost notes. The menu lists every other track that has MIDI clips; tick as many as you like — the menu stays open while you toggle, and Clear All removes them all at once.

Ghost notes render dimmed in the source clip's colour, aligned on the shared timeline, and are never interactive: they are reference material for harmony and counterpoint while you edit the active clip. The overlay selection persists while you switch clips or move between the Piano Roll and Drum Grid Editor.

docs.title: Time Bend
docs.text: The Time Bend button opens the clip's time bend in a panel beside the grid. The bend moves when notes play without changing them as written: the grid dims each note where it is written and draws it where it plays, updating as you shape the curve. GROOVE and BAKE sit above the curve, to load a groove and to write the bend into the notes. See Groove & Time Bend and Time Bend.

docs.title: Slicing Notes
docs.text:
The Slice tool cuts a note in two where you click. To cut notes into equal pieces, select one or more notes, right-click and choose Slice.... A popup shows how many notes are selected and a SLICES control. Set how many equal pieces to divide each selected note into (2 to 32, default 4), then click Apply or press Enter.

Each selected note is split into that many equal-length pieces end to end, keeping the original pitch and velocity. The slices land on the same track in place of the original notes, and they become the new selection so you can immediately edit or slice them again. The action is undoable (Ctrl+Z to revert). Click Cancel or press Esc to dismiss without changing the clip.

Slicing is available in both the Piano Roll and the Drum Grid Editor.

docs.title: Chord Timeline
docs.text: The Chord track button in the rail shows a chord row above the note grid with chord annotations. It is on by default when a Chord Engine is on the track, and the choice is remembered per clip. Chords can be placed by dragging from the Chord Engine's suggestion grid, or detected from existing notes with the refresh button (Recalculate chords from notes). Annotations are linked to their MIDI notes and update automatically when notes are moved, resized, or deleted. On tracks other than the chord track, a second button compares the row against the chord track's progression. See Chord Engine — Chord Timeline for details.

docs.title: Track Chain
docs.text:
Displayed in the bottom panel when a track or device is selected. Shows the track's FX chain as a horizontal strip of devices:

  • Drag devices to reorder them in the chain
  • Click a device to select it and show it in the Inspector
  • Drag plugins from the Plugin Browser onto the chain to add them, or click the + at the end of the chain
  • Right-click a device for Add to New Rack and Delete; Backspace deletes the selected devices
  • Racks are shown as containers with nested parallel chains

See FX Chain & Racks for working with devices, presets, and racks.

When you select a Drum Grid pad's channel, the panel shows that pad's chain, and devices you add land in the pad's chain.

docs.title: Header Controls
docs.text:
The header runs across the top of the panel. From the left:

  • Track macros / Track modulators — show the track's own macro and modulator panels at the start of the chain
  • Add rack / Add multiband rack — create a new rack on the track
  • Gain staging — start a gain-staging pass
  • Presets — the track preset box and the floppy disk that saves one
  • Track name
  • Post-FX panel, Oscilloscope, Spectrum Analyzer, Levels — show the post-FX panel, and add or remove each analyzer there
  • MIDI light, M (mute), S (solo)
  • Volume and pan
  • Power — switch the whole track chain on or off
  • Fold — the chevron at the far right

The master shows no MIDI light, solo, pan, or power. On a pad channel the presets, gain staging, multiband rack, and power buttons are hidden. The chord track shows only its name, volume, and its audition control.

docs.title: Folding the Header
docs.text:
Click the chevron at the right end of the header to fold it to a thin, darker strip; the controls fade out as it folds. The MIDI light stays visible on the strip. Click anywhere on the strip to bring the header back.

Right-click the strip (or the chevron) for a menu that shows or hides the Post-FX Panel and adds or removes the Oscilloscope, Spectrum Analyzer, and Levels analyzers.

MAGDA remembers whether the header is folded between sessions. Folding applies to the track chain only; the other bottom-panel editors keep their toolbars.

docs.title: Waveform Editor
docs.text: The Waveform Editor is the audio clip editor in the bottom panel. It opens when you select an audio clip and shows the clip's source file, where you trim and loop the clip, place warp markers and labels, and draw its gain envelope.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
• Toolbar across the top (see Toolbar).
  • Rail down the left edge. Its buttons switch the spectrogram and the transient markers on and off; the button at the bottom opens and closes the properties panel.
  • Ruler and waveform in the middle. The waveform draws in the clip's colour, one lane per channel.
  • Properties panel on the right (see Properties Panel). Drag its left edge to resize it.
  • Scroll bar along the bottom. Drag its thumb to scroll and its ends to zoom.

docs.title: Toolbar
docs.text:
• Clip name on the left.
  • Tools in the centre. While the waveform is showing, they are Pointer, Label and Marker (see Warp Markers and Labels). While the gain envelope is showing, they are Line, Pen and Flat (see Gain Envelope).
  • Maximise expands the editor to fill the window; click again to restore.
  • Power enables or disables the clip.
  • Grid - the grid division (click it to pick one), AUTO to follow the zoom level, and SNAP to snap to the grid.
  • Loop turns the clip's loop on or off. On a free clip it puts the clip into beat mode first (see Looping).
  • Gain envelope shows or hides the clip's gain envelope.

docs.title: Editing the Clip
docs.text:
With the Pointer:

  • Drag the left edge of the audio to trim the clip's start, and the right edge to trim its end (when the clip doesn't loop).
  • Hold Shift while dragging an edge to stretch the clip instead of trimming it.
  • When the clip loops, drag the phase marker to change where playback starts in the loop, and drag the ends of the loop in the ruler to change the loop region.
  • Drag in the body of the waveform to zoom around the pointer.

Double-click the ruler above the ticks to fit the view to the loop, or to the whole clip when it doesn't loop. A double-click on the ticks themselves places the edit cursor.

Right-click the waveform for Show Pre-Marker Audio and Show Post-Marker Audio, the slice commands (see Slicing), and Reset Beat Grid Origin once the grid origin has been moved. When the clip holds recorded takes, the menu also offers Expand Takes / Collapse Takes and the comp commands; see Recording Takes & Comping.

docs.title: Warp Markers
docs.text:
With Warp on (in the properties panel or the Inspector), warp markers pin points in the audio to positions on the timeline. They draw as hairlines with a flag at the top. See Warp Markers for what they do.

  • Add - choose the Marker tool and click the waveform. A dotted guide follows the pointer to show where the marker will land. The tool is greyed out while Warp is off.
  • Move - drag a marker to stretch the audio on either side of it. Alt + drag moves it without stretching.
  • Delete - double-click a marker, or right-click it and choose Remove Warp Marker.

docs.title: Gain Envelope
docs.text:
Click the gain envelope button in the toolbar to show the clip's gain envelope. The waveform dims, the sample markers hide, and the curve draws in the clip's colour over dB guides. An empty envelope is a flat 0 dB line. The envelope ranges from silence up to +6 dB.

Draw it with the envelope tools:

Tool What it does Line Drag a straight ramp. The default tool Pen Draw the envelope freehand Flat Click a grid cell to hold it at one level

Each stroke is one undo step. The same tool edits the envelope on the clip in the arrangement while it is shown there. Whether the envelope is shown is saved with each clip.

docs.title: Labels
docs.text:
Labels name a part of the source file - a verse, a breath, a hit - without changing how the clip plays. A label is a named, coloured region, or a single point.

  • Add - choose the Label tool, then click to place a point label or drag to label a region.
  • Move or resize - drag a label's flag on the top edge of the waveform to move it, or drag its ends to resize a region. Moving a label never stretches the audio.
  • Edit - right-click a label for Rename Label..., Colour and Delete Label. Double-clicking a label also deletes it.

Labels are saved with the project, follow linked ghost clips and pasted copies, and travel with the file into the Media Library. The Inspector lists a clip's labels in its Labels section.

docs.title: Spectrogram
docs.text:
The spectrogram button in the rail swaps the waveform for a spectrogram, which shows the frequencies in the audio over time, from 30 Hz to 20 kHz on a logarithmic scale. Stereo files show the sum of both channels. The choice applies to every clip and is remembered between sessions.

The waveform stays on screen until the spectrogram is ready, which on a long file can take a moment. Markers, labels and the envelope draw on top as usual.

docs.title: Transients
docs.text: The transient button in the rail shows or hides the transient markers MAGDA detects in the audio. How many it finds is set by Sens in the properties panel, or Transient sensitivity in the Inspector; even at the lowest setting the strongest onsets still show, so hide them with the button when you don't need them.

docs.title: Properties Panel
docs.text:
The panel on the right gives quick access to the clip's settings without switching to the Inspector:

Section Controls Clip WARP, BEAT and REV (reverse) Stretch Speed, the stretch Mode, the source BPM and length in Beats, and its Key Pitch Semi (semitones) and Analog Transients Sens (detection sensitivity) Fades Fade in and out, with curves and behaviours, and the crossfade lengths Mix Vol, Gain and Pan

A bookmark button saves the clip's current settings to the Media Library. See Audio Clip Properties for what each setting does.

Selecting several audio clips at once keeps the editor open in a multi-clip mode, where the Fades section edits all of them together.

docs.title: Clips on ARA Tracks
docs.text: On a track with an ARA plugin, the plugin plays the raw file, so the editor stands down MAGDA's own processing: Loop and the gain envelope button are greyed out, warp markers and the loop phase marker can't be edited, and Shift + dragging an edge trims instead of stretching.

docs.title: Edit in an External Editor
docs.text:
To do destructive editing in another application (Audacity, iZotope RX, and so on), right-click an audio clip and choose Edit in External Editor. MAGDA hands the clip's source file to the application you have configured, so changes you save there are reflected back in MAGDA.

Set which application to use under External audio editor in Settings > Paths (see Settings). If none is set, MAGDA asks you to choose one first.

docs.title: Controller Profile Format
docs.text:
A controller profile is a small JSON file that tells MAGDA how a piece of hardware is laid out and what each control should do by default. Profiles live in MAGDA's controllers directory (~/Library/MAGDA/controllers/ on macOS — see Controllers → Profiles directory) and load on app launch.

This page is a reference for anyone writing or editing a profile by hand — community contributors, advanced users, plugin authors. Most users never need to look at the JSON.

docs.title: File shape
docs.text:
{
  "id": "novation.launchkey_mini_mk4.macros",
  "vendor": "Novation",
  "name": "Launchkey Mini MK4 — Macros",

  "controls": [
    { "controlId": "knob_1", "kind": "knob", "cc": 21, "channel": 1 },
    { "controlId": "knob_2", "kind": "knob", "cc": 22, "channel": 1 }
    // …
  ],

  "defaultBindings": [
    { "controlId": "knob_1", "resolverKind": "focused.macro", "args": { "macroIndex": "0" } },
    { "controlId": "knob_2", "resolverKind": "focused.macro", "args": { "macroIndex": "1" } }
    // …
  ]
}

docs.title: Top-level fields
docs.text: Field Required Description id ✓ Stable, dot-separated identifier. Convention: <vendor>.<model> (lowercase, underscores). The id is what MAGDA uses internally — multiple files with the same id collide last-wins. vendor Display name of the manufacturer, shown beside the model in Settings > Controllers. name ✓ Display name of the model. controls ✓ Array of physical controls the hardware exposes. Must contain at least one. defaultBindings Array of "what each control does out of the box". Optional — a profile that only declares controls is still valid; bindings just won't fire automatically.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
Each entry describes a physical control. MAGDA listens for the matching MIDI message and routes it to whatever the control is bound to.

Field Required Description controlId ✓ Stable name used to reference this control from defaultBindings. Free-form; convention is knob_1, pad_3, slider_a, etc. kind ✓ What the control physically is. Free-form string but conventional values are knob, slider, pad, button. Used for UI hints. cc ✓ MIDI CC number, 0–127. channel ✓ MIDI channel, 1–16, or -1 for "any channel". feedbackCc If the controller accepts colour / state feedback on a different CC than its input, set it here. Most don't.

docs.title: Default bindings
docs.text:
Each entry says: when this control fires, route the value to this resolver.

Field Required Description controlId ✓ Must match a controlId from controls. resolverKind ✓ Which resolver runs when this control fires. See the table below. args Per-resolver arguments. JSON object of strings (numeric values are still strings).

A binding referencing a non-existent controlId is dropped at load with a warning. Upload profile… on Settings > Controllers > MIDI Profiles catches it too, and refuses the file until it is fixed.

docs.title: Resolvers
docs.text:
A resolver is a tiny function that runs every time a bound control fires. It returns a concrete target (a parameter, a macro, a track property) based on the current state of MAGDA — focused device, selected track, etc. — so the same hardware control can drive different things depending on context.

This is the difference between a profile and a MIDI Learn binding: Learn pins a control to one specific parameter, the profile/resolver path makes it follow context.

MAGDA ships with five built-in resolvers:

docs.title: focused.macro
docs.text:
Drives one macro of whichever device currently has focus.

Arg Type Description macroIndex string of int ("0"–"15") Which macro to drive. Devices have 16 macros total (8 per page × 2 pages).

Example:

{ "controlId": "knob_1", "resolverKind": "focused.macro", "args": { "macroIndex": "0" } }

The eight knobs of a typical 8-knob controller usually map to macroIndex "0" through "7" — they always land on the focused device's first eight macros, regardless of which track or device that is.

docs.title: selected.volume
docs.text:
Drives the volume fader of the currently-selected track. No args.

{ "controlId": "fader_1", "resolverKind": "selected.volume", "args": {} }

Useful for a generic-purpose volume fader on a controller — point it at the selected track and re-select tracks to "move" the fader.

docs.title: selected.pan
docs.text:
Drives the pan of the currently-selected track. No args.

{ "controlId": "encoder_pan", "resolverKind": "selected.pan", "args": {} }

docs.title: master.volume
docs.text:
Drives the master bus volume. No args.

{ "controlId": "fader_master", "resolverKind": "master.volume", "args": {} }

docs.title: master.pan
docs.text:
Drives the master bus pan. No args.

{ "controlId": "encoder_master_pan", "resolverKind": "master.pan", "args": {} }

docs.title: Multiple profiles per controller
docs.text:
A single piece of hardware doesn't have to be one profile. A Launchkey Mini might be useful in two different ways: knobs driving the focused device's macros, or knobs driving the selected track's volume / pan / sends. Each of those is a different intent, and each is its own profile JSON.

The architecture supports this — what matters is that each profile has a distinct id. The convention is <vendor>.<model>.<intent>, dot-separated at every segment:

novation.launchkey_mini_mk4.macros     ← knobs follow focused device
novation.launchkey_mini_mk4.mix        ← knobs control selected-track mix
